Question: Why do some people act less intelligent than they really are?
Answer: I once had a girlfriend who systematically acted less intelligent than she really was, especially when her friends and family were near. Her main reason to do so was that she wanted to fit in, and to some extent I understood her. Because actually, she needed to fit in. Her parents — my neighbors, alas — were, and are, “common sense people.” They never read a book, are not interested in culture whatsoever, hate Nature (I will come back to this interesting feature in a minute), hate intellectuals, and Science in general. “Common sense” is their Science, your honor. And thinking is a city in China. When her father tries to talk to me about our trees — this is the big problem, we have trees in our garden ! — it feels like talking to a wall. An aggressive wall, that is. (He becomes frantic if he finds leaves and twigs in his cement garden, and so does his wife.) He does not listen to what you say, even if he would be able to understand what you are saying. (He’s not.) He lives in this entirely fabricated delusional world, by his own “common sense” rules. And that is the world in which Ebba grew up — constantly fighting against her father’s one-dimensional reasoning, against his bullying and stupidity. Her mom is much friendlier, but intellectually much alike her husband. To rebel especially against her father, Ebba developed a drug problem, was thrown out of the house, and lived on her own as a young teenager. But smart as she was, she obtained a college degree in the end. Still, the friends she had tended to be more like her parents, probably because she met most of them in bad times. So every time her friends and family were near, she acted just like them, ignoring her real thoughts, and swallowing any objections against their constant no-brainer truths. When we were an item, she refused to enter any kind of even slightly intellectual conversations, because she wanted to be like them — she needed to be like them and fit in. So I guess the short (but honest) answer is: survival of the fittest. SOURCES: the image is mine.

Question: How can Missouri ban terminating ectopic pregnancies, when they are deadly to the mother?
Answer: The irony of the term. Ectopic pregnancies are not actual pregnancies, since by definition the embryo attaches outside the uterus. Most of the time, the embryo ends up in a fallopian tube, but it can also occur in an ovary or the abdominal cavity. Only when the embryo is in the abdominal cavity, it theoretically could survive. That is to say, in 1 out of 10,000 to 25,000 pregnancies, an abdominal ectopic pregnancy occurs — which means that per year, we have roughly 20,000 to 50,000 cases per year worldwide — and in the history of medical literature only a dozen cases are known in which an embryo survived. (Sigh.) On the other hand, if one leaves an ectopic pregnancy untreated, the chances of survival are very (very) small. Either the embryo is naturally aborted, the patient’s body consumes the embryo, or the embryo dies at some point and stays in the body. Which means there is lump of dead flesh sitting in there, rotting. So how can Missouri ban terminating ectopic pregnancies, when they are deadly to the mother, knowing that there is a smaller chance for an embryo to survive an ectopic pregnancy than to survive a jump from the top of the Eiffel tower ? Because the Missouri legislators are so obsessed by their holy book of Faery tales — which were historically never written as true stories in the first place — that they consider ”the gift of life” as a god-given thing. (Which is pretty ironic, given the fact that many untreated patients die.) There are four exceptions, of course: then one is allowed to open a backdoor and let the doctor in. God will close his/her/its/whatever eyes if a god-fearing man/woman/whatever breaks the rules (this happens all the time with, e. g., abortions). That’s the way the Hebrew beliefs “work.” The short answer: they are evil hypocritical morons. Question: Why do some people dislike you for literally no reason at all if you have been kind and decent and engaging?
Answer: One month ago, my daughter received a message from Esther, a girl in her 6th grade class. It said that “she was de-friending every single person of the class, because they had hurt her soul so many times, and she simply did not need them anymore.” (They are all going to middle school now, and most of them to different schools. Esther has made a decision at the very divide of their young lives.) It sounds like a sad dramatic story in the make — Esther, whose soul was tortured by the other kids. But we also know Esther’s mom (who is the spitting image of her daughter). And Esther’s mom is toxic. And she poisons her daughter. Esther’s mom has no friends, and she is convinced that the world is against her. That she is a victim. But Esther’s mom is hiding something — especially for her daughter. And the thing she is hiding is the fact that she wants to be a victim, that she wants to complain about the fact that ishe s all alone in the world — she is the martyr in her own carefully devised life story. And that Esther has to be a victim too. My daughter once was invited to Esther’s house and play with her in the afternoon, and we gladly accepted the kind invitation, because making new friends — Esther was new in school — is fantastic. When we came back to get our daughter, Esther’s mom said: “We will probably not see you again, I guess, because that’s how it always goes. I guess Esther won’t be invited by you to come and play with your daughter, but that’s the way it is.” She really believed she was a victim, but she victimized herself. And her daughter. And seeing how she is molding her own daughter into martyrdom, I think it’s fair to say she is bordering Munchausen-by-proxy — she psychologically tortures her daughter in order to get the attention, and especially the pity she so deserves. We did not know what to say (because people like that never hear what you are saying), and while we were waiting for our daughter, Esther’s mom mentioned the fact that her son — Esther’s little brother who had gladly played along — had COVID. “But I thought I better not mention it, because otherwise you would not like us.” (Sigh.) Esther is twelve years old today, and she is de-friending everyone else in 6th grade. Because she is convinced that nobody likes her, that everybody hates her for some invisible reason. (Later, we found out that Esther had to change schools because “nobody liked her.” Double sigh.) But Esther has become the mirror image of her mom — she refuses to join in games “because nobody wants her to join anyways,” she refused to go to birthday parties “because nobody wants her at the party anyways.” Esther is a Munchausen-by-proxy victim, already completed distorted by her mom. And things will only get worse. SOURCES: the art is my own.

Question: What are some things that people don’t tell you about being pregnant and giving birth?
Answer: That OB/GYNs sometimes widen the vagina during childbirth (through the making of an incision), to facilitate the delivery. Those darn so-called episiotomies. Our daughter was on the way but relative to the pelvic dimensions of my girlfriend, she was also pretty big (especially the head). And as the OB/GYN was old school, he (rather quickly) proposed to “make a cut.” My girlfriend is a urologist herself, and she knew all too well what can happen when OB/GYNs “make a cut” — they are the worst surgeons in a hospital, and often mess up patients in the most incomprehensible ways — but on the other hand, the baby’s head was big and she had been in labor without an epidural for quite a while. So she gave in. And before my medically unexperienced eyes, she was locally sedated through an injection down there, and the OB/GYN made an incision in the tissue between the vaginal opening and the anus to widen the vagina, and there was blood. A lot of blood. (There were never excrements though — for which I am very grateful.) After our baby was born, he stitched her up again, but needless to say, it took some time for my girlfriend to recover and before everything turned back to normal again in the vaginal zone. In the end, I learned that during childbirth — and even when its pretty gross — Most anything goes. SOURCES: The anatomy of the human gravid uterus exhibited in figures. See page for author, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Question: When you went to the hospital, did the staff not take you seriously and you ended up deathly sick as a result?
Answer: This patient was something else. She didn’t have a job, lived in the lower echelons of society and was obviously mentally challenged. She also had a kidney stone. She claimed to be suffering from severe abdominal pain and subsequently visited her General Practitioner, but he brushed her off with Ibuprofen because “it was obviously the kidney stone.” But the pain was simply too intense to cover up with a simple GP-woven Ibuprofen blanket, so she called her urologist’s office, and insisted on coming over right away. When she explained her symptoms, the urologist knew at once that this was not related to the kidney stone. And then the patient said the most remarkable thing — “It’s so painful that I asked my dad to drive slower on the way to the hospital.” The urologist immediately asked if that was because of the bumps in the road. (It was.) She then applied pressure on a specific point on the right-hand side of the patient’s abdomen and then quickly released the pressure, and the patient’s reaction confirmed the urologist’s hypothesis. (The patient loudly screamed.) “It’s not the kidney stone. You have acute appendicitis. And you will need emergency surgery right away.” The patient first refused the operation (bearing her GP’s “diagnosis” in mind, and because she did not really understand what was going on), but the pain quickly grew worse and she was feverish as well. So when a general surgeon (and an emergency ultrasound) confirmed the urologist’s diagnosis, she eventually gave in, and not much later the appendix (and a huge amount of pus) was removed. If she had waited any longer upon listening to her GP, his (enormous and unforgivable) mistake could have very well ended up fatally for her. Because her pain was not kidney stone related at all (as the GP should have known) — And the road was really bumpy. SOURCES: (for the image) Annals of Surgery, vol. 197, No. 5 (1983), pp. 495–506.

Question: If your partner cheats, do you blame them, the other person, or both?
Answer: You have to attend a party, because if you do not want to attend, you spoil everything yet again. And even when you tell her you are feeling really sick — because you really are — she immediately blames you for spoiling “the one evening she so was looking forward to.” And so you go. You try to blend in among the others (who all know she is cheating on you, but never tell you because it is not their problem), and stand by the bonfires with a glass of warm wine, feeling almost like the worst you ever felt in your entire life. It is Winter, but the outside cold is nothing compared to what is going on inside. And then the real shame still has to come: you are feeling so sick that you have to go inside, while you know all too well that your wife will not join you, because her lover is standing next to the fire. And you are breaking down in little pieces. And inside a movie is playing: SHRECK. (You don’t even like the movie, but you have no choice. And as you are almost dying, nothing really matters. But you know you will have to sit it out, because she wants to stay as long as she can.) Sitting in between toddlers, preteens and preschoolers, and going down due to something which is almost converging to Cabin Fever, you feel you are an embarrassing witness to a marriage which is gone — as all the others know. But here’s the most painful thing. You knew all too well what was going (without proof), they all knew what was really going on (with proof), she knew what would happen very soon, and he was watching you, hoping she would not have second thoughts. And as he very well knew what was going on, I blamed him as well — but only secondarily. She was the one who made me sick. SOURCES: Google images.[1]

Question: Is British tap water safe for an American?
Answer: When I was a kid, my family once spent three days in Bristol, and in a local restaurant, we ate “fresh” vegetables which turned out to be rinsed in tap water. Both my parents and my two sisters became really sick in the evening — vomiting and diarrhea with a small fever on the side — and they had to stay in bed for most of the next day. And let’s not even speak of the enormous amount of bad cancer cases in British people due to the aggressive damage tap water does to the locals. Traveling in Great Britain — and please don’t even consider Ireland, because the tap water can turn all funny on you and change you into a Leprechaun, or even much worse: a Banshee ! — is actually only possible if you bring your own swimming pool filled with American tap water with you (which happens all the time). The Cambridge American Cemetery contains some 8,500 graves of mostly young American WW2 soldiers, and just to be clear: those boys did not die during battle (who would a deserve a medal for that kind of shame) — they died after drinking British tap water.[1] And now on a more serious note — I lived in both the US (various states) and Europe (various countries), and I can tell you that the chlorinated tap water of the US tastes like swimming pool water in Europe — mainland and Great Britain. Both US and British tap water are very safe to drink though — The British version only tastes much better. SOURCES: the footnoted site and Google images.

Question: As a doctor, what's the most shocking thing to transpire while delivering a baby?
Answer: The baby was actually delivered almost perfectly, but nobody had noticed that something was going on in this young woman’s body. She was barely twenty-one at the time, alone, and she had traveled from a country in war to the promised land to become a single mother. The shock came only slightly later. In the first months of her mothership in the promised land, she was the happiest mom in the world (although she mourned the father of her baby, who had fallen just like so many others). Finally, there was a chance. Finally, there was a future. And then she noticed some blood in her pee, and although she wanted to dismiss the red clouds amongst the clearest skies in her young life, she knew that the constant pain might not be a coincidence after all. So she sought for an opinion, and not much later she got it. And now she was a mother with cancer, and the Sun stopped shining altogether (because this cancer was bad). And time and again, the young mother walked to the urologist’s office in the hope to (finally) hear some good news, but without an exception, the news got worse. First there was the kidney cancer (removal), then there was a cancerous lymph node mass (removal), then new cancerous lymph node growth (removal), and then even worse. The baby had not even reached the age of one when the cancerous mass had grown into the vena cava — a large vein which carries blood to the heart from other parts of the body — of the mother whom she would never really know. Because the cancer was literally strangling the way to her mom’s heart. And the struggle would be over soon. Question: When was the first time you realized that a teacher cannot always be right?
Answer: My daughter was 9 at the time. She came home from school and said she had learned about the seasons, about Winter and Summer. Question: What is the most dangerous type of cancer? Why do you think so? What is the survival rate for this type of cancer if it is treated properly with surgery and chemotherapy/radiation therapy (if needed)?
Answer: It’s a little glitch. A tiny thing that is slightly different, and you didn’t notice it at first. It surfaces one day, and you don’t really mind. (It doesn’t even hurt.) The GP basically says the same, and still he wants you to have some more tests. Because some people in your family have died young. Because a glitch can point towards a defect. And a defect can point towards disaster. The glitch turns out to be a thing, and the thing turns out to be a node. The node is swollen because it is cancerous, and the cancer has traveled from a breast to sit inside the node. Where it has waited all along before it could possibly spread to distant parts of the body. Possibly. And the waiting starts, after new images have been taken. The images will check for new glitches — inside the body this time. Checking if the cancer cells have traveled beyond the lymph nodes, checking if the clock can promise time. (It has started to hurt now, though. Never a good sign.) And the images show new glitches — dozens of them, all over the place — and the hurting in hindsight explains more than words. (But she doesn’t tell them.) She will die in a matter of weeks. And her eyes turn glassy now and her skin color fades, and people start avoiding her altogether. For she radiates bad luck — she radiates angst, and all the children of the world should never see this (because it hurts). And even he did not address her — the early monster of the street — when the cancer comes too close, and, when it finally stops hiding: A scream — Before they finally meet. What is the most dangerous type of cancer ? — The cancer that hides before the final glitches come. Before they finally meet. SOURCES: painting by Mikhail Nesterov.

Question: Have you ever met somebody so stupid that they made you question how they survived this long?
Answer: One of my good friends turned stupid from the moment he met his current wife (of whom I deeply hope it is not his last). He is way smarter than she is in every compartment of the thinking tank, but she manipulates him every which way. The last time I saw him, I told him that we (my family) just visited a Dutch amusement park called Efteling (centered about old German and Scandinavian fairy tales) — and he immediately said that he was “so waiting for the moment that his family — his wife and two children of 3 and 6 years old — could also finally visit the park.” I was totally amazed about this remark, as people visit this park all the time with toddlers, but before he could even give his opinion, his wife did the talking — “Kids of 3 years old obviously cannot really enjoy such an amusement park — and they will forget EVERY SINGLE THING they experienced.” My subsequent question made her silent for a while — “So you do not plan to send Charles [the 3-year-old] to school soon ?” She did not understand my question, and became somewhat angry. “Why wouldn’t we — he will be learning A LOT OF THINGS in kindergarten !!” I could not stop myself anymore, so I gently whispered: “Oh, I thought that this did not make any sense because he will forget EVERY SINGLE THING he experiences at that age. Hell — why even play with him at all, for that matter.” She — very angry by now — shouted: “BECAUSE HE ENJOYS IT !!!” My friend knew I checkmated her, but did not say a word. And he will wait two or three more years before he will visit the park, because her psychology reigns over their relationship. They won’t travel far in the coming years for the same reason, and he will also keep quiet. Because he turned stupid all of a sudden (she was stupid all along). In my world, this is totally absurd — life happens now, and not in three or for years, especially if it involves children — you don’t count to 20 million when you are playing hide-and-seek. The boy called Charles (and his older sister) would experience the best day of their life and that’s the only thing which matters. Not the incoherent ramblings of a modern fairy tale witch. Question: As a lifeguard, did you ever see something that made you say, “You can’t be serious…?”?
Answer: My daughter spends one week per year with my parents and her two nieces in a little cabin in the Southern part of a Northern country. It’s an unbreakable tradition that has been going on for almost 10 years, and it’s still going very strong. Swimming is a very important item on the everyday agenda if the weather allows it: there’s a fabulous pool on the site, and not using it would almost be a crime. My parents are not the only grandparents with grandchildren who rent a cabin or a hotel room in the ambient castle, and this time a grandmother was sitting in a lounge chair, watching her granddaughter in the pool. The girl was seven years old and not a great swimmer. And yes, a lifeguard was there as well. At some point grandma went back to the cabin because she had forgotten something, while her granddaughter was still in the water, and this was the single worst decision in grandma’s entire life. Because a lifeguard has to watch everyone — she had to watch one single person. When it involves young children, three minutes is enough to destroy most everything you ever loved. And when water enters the equation, one mistake is all it takes. And when grandma came back, Zoë was gone. After an episode pf panic, a lifeguard quickly found Zoë at the bottom of the pool — unresponsive. She was declared dead not much later, after many dramatic tries to resuscitate the poor girl who had been alone for three minutes which would last for a lifetime. Sometimes mistakes do happen in and around swimming pools. Parents overestimate the swimming capacity of their children, grandparents need to pee “and will be back in a second,” children hide too well and barely seek, some parents with very young children even drink and nap. The lifeguards have seen it all before. But this time was different — This time someone’s baby died. SOURCES: John Everett Millais, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Question: What are the most insane things that American tourists do abroad?
Answer: I was in Hangzhou, China in July with my daughter and girlfriend (for both business and pleasure), and although Hangzhou is a big, modern and breathtaking city with more than 13 million inhabitants and absolutely astounding historical sites, it is not well known — not even among experienced travelers. There is virtually no tourism at all (most foreigners are there for business or for working at the university), and so many of the locals have never seen a foreigner before. In my case, I turned out to be an extremely curious foreign specimen to the Hangzhou people: I am a white, 6′3′’ tall, blond and blue-eyed man with stubbles (Chinese men cannot grow beards), and so I was constantly photographed and filmed (especially by young women). We noticed one (and only one) American party of tourists, and we needed no proper introduction to know they really were American. (The sheer size often is a dead give-away.) [Our favorite local restaurant.] Besides the typically loudness, there is always the also-typical American arrogance which makes one ashamed to be from the West as well — “Why isn’t there some DECENT FOOD around here ? Look at these restaurants — so DISGUSTING !!” Some days later, we saw them again by sheer coincidence. They had found the only McDonalds in the neighborhood, and so they were eating there. It was in more than one way a signature statement of American tourism. Why enjoy the absolutely delicious local food with an open mind, when you can have American junk food instead, right ? (Wrong.) SOURCES: the pictures (of the famous laughing monk, and people in our favorite local restaurant) are my own.

Question: If your 3-year-old tells you there's a monster in their room, do you dismiss what they're seeing or feed into it asking them to describe what it is they saw?
Answer: On April 27, 1985, 53-year-old Marine Hedge came back home after a pleasant evening out with a male friend. The man spent the rest of the evening in her company until he left her to go home himself, and she was ready to go to bed. It was 1 AM. Before she closed her eyes, she thought she heard a distinct noise in the bedroom closet, and she remembered the scary bedroom monster that had lived in the closet of her old bedroom back when she was a toddler, and that had haunted her dreams for so many nights. And she had to smile about her silly young self. Then there was that sound again, and this time she did not imagine it. Suddenly the closet door opened, and the bedroom light was switched on. And she saw a bearded madman who had stepped out of the closet, and he jumped on her and immediately started to strangle her with all his brutal might. The last thought she ever had before the lights disappeared, was that the bedroom closet monster had been real all along. Some time later, her desecrated body was found in a remote ditch. She had become a victim of the BTK serial killer Dennis Rader, who had sat in her bedroom closet for hours on end, waiting, until her male friend finally left.[1] So if your 3-year-old tells you there's a monster in his or her room, under the bed or inside the bedroom closet, I would not dismiss it right away, and have a peek just in case. You never know what was hiding there all along — Waiting just for you. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. For the image of Marine Hedge, I consulted Findagrave.[2] The image of Dennis Rader was taken from AP News.

Question: What hard truths of life does everyone need to realize?
Answer: It was an evening in November, and the crickets stopped making any noise. It wasn’t really cold, but Summer was certainly over. We decided to have a quick drink in a pub, because I had to leave for a while the next morning. In the restaurant, everything felt okay. In the car afterwards, the mood had quieted down. As if it had never been there. I remember we talked about trivialities, but only later I realized that my trivialities mattered a great deal to her — that is to say, my every wording of everyday (non-)problems hit her very hard. As if I was an enemy. And here is a simple truth: I did not notice her reaction at all. This was small talk, and I thought we were doing okay. The actual cool down would come within an hour. After we had hit the ice berg. One. Fucking. Hour. And I can say this to you: I knew we hit it, in the car, when driving back home. I realized more than everything else that we had hit something. Something invisible that took away the skin, but left everything underneath to bleed, something invisible that I could almost touch, but did not feel at the time being. We were sinking. The ice berg would surface only many months later, but I knew that suddenly there was pain while I could not see a wound — she was keeping it hidden from me. And in the months that followed — the months in which she proceeded to develop her relationship with a lover — I tried to keep the sinking pieces afloat with all my (legendary 😉) might, but the water was too cold, and while I was looking for a door to climb onto, they had already reached the shore (and forgot about me all along). So yeah, the water was cold, but it also wakes you up. And when I woke up, I knew what I had to do. And I also knew it meant I had to fight my ex-lover who had turned venomous on me. This was more than a decade ago. Hundreds of thousands of dollars in between. And a cancer that spread, and that ended her life. But not mine. SOURCES: the drawing is mine.

Question: My wife is keen for me to get a vasectomy. I am leery of getting this done. Has any man experienced serious discomfort/side effects from this procedure?
Answer: My girlfriend (who is a urologist) does them all the time, and basically there are three types of men that come for a vasectomy: men who do not want to have children, men with children who do not want to have more children, and men who want to fool around without subsequent pregnancies. The first and the third kind are rare, the second kind is not. And of the second type, in most cases there is a dark governing power behind the “decision” of the male patient to get a vasectomy: territorial pissing. In most cases, it is actually the wife of the patient who wants the vasectomy — not because she does not want to have more children per se, but because she does not want her husband to have children with another female (in case of a divorce, or cheating). She wants to control his afterlife so to speak — his hypothetical life after her. Often, these wives refuse to take the birth control pill themselves (for largely unscientific reasons), and would NEVER be sterilized themselves (you never know what happens in the future) — it’s hubby who has to take the bullet. And guess what also often happens — Men who enter the consultation room with the new wife, asking for the vasectomy (orchestrated by wife No. 1) to be undone. Because the second wife wants kids of her own — territorial pissing, remember ? And that sounds like some serious discomfort to me. SOURCES: GIF found through GIFer.

Question: What is the biggest mistake one can make?
Answer: Some word tricks influence us more than they should, but one example definitely stands out. One that everybody — literally everyone you know — uses to emphasize stuff. Isn’t that too bad ? It isn’t actually, because “too bad” implies it is more than bad, and more than bad is still bad. So “too bad” does not exist. And maybe you think that your friend is “too fat,” but more than fat is still fat, so if you think she is really fat, she can’t be “too fat.” And of course, I agree that the use of “too” could make sense if we use reference points, but we usually don’t, do we ? So don’t worry if you are too skinny or too dumb, too uptight or too obtuse, or too sorry for whatever they are blaming you for. They are simply trying to confuse you through a three-letter word — Too bad. SOURCES: image found through Google images.

Question: If God asks you on Judgement Day, “Why didn't you believe in me,” what would you say to him?
Answer: I am not sure which god you mean exactly — there are thousands, and yours is a copy of some of them — but anyway, I would ask him/her/it/frog about cancer. Cancer in kids, to be precise. Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Is being overweight physically uncomfortable? I'm obviously talking about fat. I’d like to know how being overweight feels physically, like when fitting clothes, walking, exercising, breathing, and maintaining hygiene.
Answer: Kathy D. enters the ER because she is hurting all over the place. She is a real patient — not a figment of my imagination. She is morbidly obese and she can hardly walk. She is morbidly obese and she can hardly talk. After some medical examinations, it turns out she is having a renal colic — one of the most painful conditions in the medical dictionary — and the kidney stone has to be removed somehow, because it is too large. A surgical procedure is out of the question, because she is also too large — hospitals in this country do not have specialized units to handle people this big — only veterinarian hospitals have the appropriate mechanic cranes to lift horses and the like. And not enough staff is available to lift fat flabs weighing more than half a human while the surgeon is risking her or his life under the flab to fix the patient. So the kidney stone has to be removed through a so-called lithotripsy — a non-invasive procedure in which focused ultrasonic energy or shock waves are sent directly to the stone, so that the shock waves break it into smaller stones that will eventually pass through the urinary system. (Here ends the theory.) This will happen the next day. In the morning, Kathy D. has to go to the toilet (Number two), and so she stumbles to the little cubicle in her hospital room, where she is barely able to squeeze through the door opening (what is the matter with this country — why are door openings so small ?). Once seated, she defecates, and then the usual shit (pun intended) starts once again: she can hardly reach her bottom because of her sheer circumference, so she has to clean up through the front side. In her case — again due to the fact that her bottom is so far away — she can only clean part of it. Some shit marbles and stains always stay (as the surgeons and nurses will soon see). She also smells the other smells coming from the many mildew sites that have formed in the many skin folds her body has — as if they were brain wrinkles of a rotting corpse. And she hates them. (Her husband claims he loves those rotting brain wrinkles, and even has named some of the largest ones. And she knows it’s not okay. She also knows he is a feeder, but he loves her for who she is. Or so he claims, because she is the one feeling bad all the time.) Not much later, the nurses enter her room to wheel her into the OR. In her case it is highly nontrivial, since she cannot be mechanically lifted into the hospital bed. (She sure hopes they don’t smell her, but she knows they do.) And that’s not the end of it. Her immense fat layer is just too thick for the shock waves to travel through, so that the surgery does not work out in the end. She has to go home and lose some (read: a LOT of) weight. And her husband knows she is hungry. SOURCES: Google images.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How do doctors handle patients who think they’re not sick when they really are?
Answer: Sometimes patients really do know that they are (very) sick, but are afraid to say it out loud — as if the very naming of their condition will make matters worse. Cancer or erectile dysfunction are two typical examples. Many people have the big C or the flaccid ED, but never mention it in public. My girlfriend once had a patient who downplayed his bout of prostate cancer because he did not want to live with the consequences of a radical prostatectomy — he was very young, and a life with erectile dysfunction sounded like hell for him. So he followed an alternative herbal route instead, designed by his older brother. Whatever she tried to tell and explain her patient — the man would never listen, and time and again fell into his brother’s alternative medicine trap. When he finally came to his senses, too much time had gone by. His procrastination in denial had given the cancer enough elbow room to spread. Some people are simply afraid to acknowledge the beast that is torturing them inside. Patrick Swayze, for instance, refused to admit in public that he was suffering from metastasized pancreas cancer. He had no problem with admitting that he had pancreatic cancer, but he brushed off the metastasis whenever it was mentioned. As if the very denial would kill the adjective. In fact, although he was officially diagnosed with stage 4 pancreatic cancer in mid January 2008 — one of the worst imaginable cancer diagnoses with a bleak five year survival rate of 1%[1] — he really seemed to believe later on that since doctors had removed a metastatic pancreatic tumor in his liver, the metastatic adjective could be removed from his diagnosis as well. But that’s not how it works, and Swayze chose to deny it for himself and in public, because that was his way of coping with a dark truth that was unstoppable. He was “kicking it” instead.[2] For some people, saying the word is admitting the sentence. But that’s not how adjectives are killed. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the most disrespectful thing a doctor did to you?
Answer: Some of the most disrespectful things which happen to patients are totally unknown to them. Some doctors do stuff you wouldn’t even believe, and never tell you in the end. One such example is an OB/GYN in my girlfriend’s hospital who cut off a ureter while performing a hysterectomy, and did not even realize that he did it. Something was obviously very wrong, so he called up a urologist and urged her to intervene. And she was the one who reconnected the ureter. (The patient will never know.) Now if you know about some of my writings, you might think that you read about this case before, but actually you haven’t: this only happened the other week. And that is the hideous side surrounding such tragic incidents — which happen all the time in case of OB/GYNs — they keep performing surgeries whom they do not master, and the butchering keeps on going. Some general surgeon or urologist will help them out in the end, until some general surgeon or urologist won’t be available one day. (Will the patient then be notified afterwards ?) And then we have the evil doctors who do unethical stuff while hiding under the medical radar. One urologist — not an OB/GYN, this time — told us that he performed digital vaginal examinations on all of his female patients, every single time they visited him. Upon some questioning from our side, he confirmed that he also performed them on teenagers, even during their very first consultation. Without any medical indication whatsoever. (And I know I wrote about this doctor before, and I will do it again to create awareness. There are legal terms for this kind of behavior, as you and I well know.) These cases embrace the most disrespectful instances of all. The stuff that most everyone in the Operation Room (or private practice) knows — While no one tells you. SOURCES (for the image): Gynecological diagnosis (1910), Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Question: What are the craziest experiments done in the name of science?
Answer: In the 1950s, Dr. Curt Richter, a Harvard graduate and psycho-biologist at the famous Johns Hopkins University (Baltimore, Maryland), decided to transform a daring thought into a psychological lab experiment which defied most ethical borders of Science. It involved rats. EXPERIMENT A: Richter threw the rats into large reservoirs half filled with water. Even the best swimmers gave up and sank after an average of 15 minutes a piece. EXPERIMENT B: Just before the rats gave up in exhaustion, Richter pulled them out, wiped them dry, and let them rest for a few minutes. Then put them back in the water again for a second round. Some of them lasted for almost 60 hours before drowning. Richter explained the results as follows: “The rats in Experiment B believed that they would eventually be rescued, so they embraced “hope” with every strength in their bodies.” (Wow.) None of the rats died in the experiments, by the way — at least, that is what many modern-day reports about the Richter experiments claim. But let me tell you: none of it is true. Nine of the twelve rats in the first experiment actually swam for many hours in a row (some of them for days) before giving up — only three of them gave in very early.[1] Meaning that Richter’s interpretation in the end is your utter nonsense — he interpreted the experiments through one of the most infamous un-scientific and self fulfilling clouds of disillusion ever seen on the psycho-meteorological stage (and everybody bought it). And secondly, Richter actually really let the rats drown if they were exhausted. (So much for hope.) SOURCES: Richter, C. P. (1957). On the phenomenon of sudden death in animals and man. Psychosomatic Medicine, 19, 191–198, and the footnoted sites. The image was found through Google images.[2]

Question: What are the symptoms of early stage dementia or Alzheimer's disease? Is it possible for a person to appear normal for years while having these diseases?
Answer: The mother of one of my best friends was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s at a point in her life when nobody had a single clue as to what was going on. The very moment at which my friend noticed someone was wrong — one single moment, instead of an abundant number of signs — was almost breathtaking. She was (and still is) a retired high school Math teacher, and a very intelligent woman. She read books in various languages, played bridge on a competitive level, had her own fishing boat which she often steered overseas (she’d bought it with her husband who died from late stage pancreatic cancer right after he retired, and it meant the world to her), helped her grandchildren with their mathematical shenanigans — the works. And that was her strength — the very guise to hide what was happening in her mind. You see, intelligent people are always much better in covering up the dementia mess — they virtually always are diagnosed much later than your average Joe. They can find answers to the everyday questions which become everyday challenges for those who suffer from dementia, through deduction, and they can do it for many years before they are caught. To add insult to injury, the mother of my friend always was absent-minded, and that made the fact that her mind was wandering off medically even harder to detect. And then, one day, my friend was staying in her house with his family — as he often did on weekends — and he was looking for a wine glass in a cupboard. And found a pile of unopened letters. And when he asked his mom about the pile, she could not explain it — as if it was a magical cupboard apparition. As if she had never seen it before. When my friend started opening the letters, the truth dawned on him like a wrecking ball, because he realized nothing would be the same again after that very moment. Unpaid bills. Warnings. Fines. Reminders. More fines. More than a hundred of them, stretched over so many, many months. And only in hindsight he could see that certain remarks she had made in the last five years, certain strange looks in her eyes that he had never seen before, certain things she did not say which she would have said, acknowledged his darkest fear while his tears were falling on the cold granite floor. That the Alzheimer monster would evaporate her very mind and memories rather sooner than later, and that she would wind up as an empty shell with a one-minute brain — And a life filled with sorrow. SOURCES: portrait by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What should people know?
Answer: My former Parents-in-Law often gathered wild mushrooms in the woods not far from their house, and then prepared them for dinner. I always blatantly refused to eat them, which enraged especially my former MIL, because it was as if I did not trust her (I didn’t). I had never forgotten about one infamous mushroom story which happened to good friends of ours. The man was a bio engineer and professionally versed in the wonderful world of toadstools, and he gathered wild mushrooms all the time. Till one fateful day when his family was having this marvelous mushroom dinner, and his youngest son started complain about pain in his testicles. Not much later, his oldest son joined in. And then his wife stated — a little confused — that she was feeling dizzy. My friend knew all too well what was happening and started feeling light in the head himself, and before he could transport his children and wife into the car, his boys had already lost consciousness. He reached the hospital just in time (before losing consciousness himself), and was able to explain to an ER doctor what had happened before the lights went out. It turned out in the end that he had picked a rare variant of one of the usual kinds he gathered, and the toxicity of this rare brother depended on the season. And during this time of year, it was really poisonous. They barely survived their toadstool adventure, after a stomach pumping, a long stay in the hospital, and an abdominal Aftermath which lasted for a long time. So yeah, I always refused to eat my PIL’s mushroom picks, since they were mushroom illiterates and since my friend who was a professional almost died in the act — the stakes of this game were simply too high. And one day it really happened. My former PIL’s had gathered some mushrooms in the woods once again, prepared them and ate them, served with a glass of red wine (or two). And then didn’t feel so good afterwards. My PILs did not die, nor did they end up in an ER, but there was dizziness and there was vomiting, and a lot of abdominal inconvenience. They did not want to talk about it though, and at long last blamed the wine. I guess that in the end, some grapes just can’t be trusted. SOURCES: GIF found on Reddit/GIFs.

Question: Does childbirth hurt?
Answer: A colic occurs when there is an obstruction within a hollow internal organ, such as the intestines, gallbladder, rectum, kidneys, ureters, and uterus. To try to get rid of the obstruction, the smooth muscles inside the walls of the hollow organ contract vigorously around it, and these spasms cause pain. These smooth muscles are involuntary (we cannot control their function) and are controlled by the unconscious part of our brain function using the autonomic nervous system.[1] (In some way it’s our instinct that govern the colic.) And this is where our story gets really interesting. Most people attribute the intense pain associated to labor mainly to the stretching sensations of cervix and uterus, but that is definitely not so: sensory denervation of the uterus occurs during pregnancy and cervical sensory denervation occurs at the onset of labor, so that actually there are no such stretching sensations whatsoever during childbirth — the stretch receptors are totally gone.[2] But where does the actual labor pain come from ? Labor pain occurs due to vasoconstriction within the uterus. When the uterus contracts, there is a reduction in blood flow to the uterus causing hypoxia:[3] This decrease in blood volume causes pain because although the uterus is denervated, the surrounding blood vessels remain innervated, and the disruption of homeostasis causes an imbalance in the system, which results in sensations of pain. So the original “uterine colic” is the bad guy — he (eventually) causes the pain. On a related matter, renal colics are generically considered to be (much) more painful than “uterine colics,”[4] and to add insult to injury, the psychological strength of the pregnant patient determines a big part of the personal perception of childbirth pain. (The lower the pain threshold, the worse the perception.) That’s one reason why the breathing method really works. In the end, childbirth usually really hurts (of course), but it is not the worst pain in the world, nor the most painful medical condition in the world (of course) — if that is the question. Otherwise, who would go for a second baby without an epidural ? SOURCES: the footnoted sites. For the image: Emile Beau: Grossesse gémellaire. Ouvrage: Atlas complémentaire de tous les traités d'accouchements, Edition: Paris : Masson, 1865. Auteur: LENOIR, Adolphe, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Question: He’s a nice guy but I’m not physically attracted to him. Should I give him a chance or let him go?
Answer: Anne is a cardiologist and a colleague of my spouse. She had a long relationship with Ed who considered Anne to be the love of his life. Ed is the kind of man who can prepare the best marinated steak using a secret family recipe, cook it on a BBQ to perfection, open the best French wine whom he acquired from a small local vineyard only the lucky few know, and make a toast through the telling of some original anecdote about his life. Ed is the real deal. He has one thing against him though: he isn’t good looking. It’s one of his only ordinary qualities. But his larger-than-life charisma easily makes up for it. Or so we thought. One day, he called my girlfriend in tears. “Anne has left me for a cardiac surgeon called “Sandy.” I’m totally devastated.” And he really was. He stopped taking care of himself and his surroundings, stopped preparing the perfect marinated steaks, and stopped enjoying his fabulous wine. Usually he is alone, or goes to a local pub to spend the evening drinking on his own, because he still does not understand what has happened. After two years, his heart still is shattered to little pieces, and I am sorry to say that some of these pieces are gone forever. Because Anne — a cardiologist, of all people — swept them away. Some time after the phone call, my girlfriend got to talk to Anne in the hospital, and her side of the story was bitterly cold: “Sandy is simply better looking. I knew him well as a student, and when I heard that he was separating from his wife, I immediately made my move and called him.” It sounded unreal. On the one hand, you have this interesting, intelligent, funny, loving and original man — admittedly, not the most handsome man around, but still someone who would give his life for Anne — and on the other hand, we have a cardiac surgeon, a stranger who is chosen solely because of his looks. And she called him immediately ? Which brings me to your question: “He’s a nice guy but I’m not physically attracted to him. Should I give him a chance or let him go ?” Let him go. Because only then, does he have a chance. SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What was the biggest shock when you became a lone parent after splitting with your partner?
Answer: Cold calculation. It was already a big shock to me when she started to change without telling me why, over a period of 6 months. Long silences, anger and resentment towards me, and long toilet breaks in which she was texting an unknown person. The restroom-texting was a new thing, by the way — she never did that before it all began. So yeah, big changes. When she broke the news to me that she had been cheating all along, the moment was very intense, but actually not as shocking as the very beginning of the downwards spiral, which had started on an evening in November. Suddenly everything was different. Suddenly her eyes became angry. Suddenly her love for me had started to fade. Suddenly. The news hurt but somehow I had expected it all along, so I finally became angry (and that was a good thing). What REALLY shocked me though, was her hunger for money. As if it wasn’t enough that we were breaking up, that our belongings had to be divided — and even worse: our friends and family as well — it turned out that while I had been trying to save our marriage, she had been calculating (with the help of lawyers) how much money she could gain. So she turned out to be a different person altogether — a person I did not want to know anymore. Somehow she was diseased, and that was the very end for me. In the last summer before that fateful November, she started talking about having babies, and for the first time this became an item on the common bucket list we never had. But I was probably the luckiest man in the world that our relationship exploded before a baby ever arrived on the scene, because baby dreams become nightmares in the darkness of divorce. Because a decade later, she was totally erased by the disease inside her. And maybe that’s the biggest shock: we almost were the parents of an unborn disaster — A miserable act in the dead circus. SOURCES: painting by Kevin Foote.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the saddest truth about smart people?
Answer: That despite the fact they are very smart, their thoughts, opinions and arguments are “equal” to the thoughts, opinions and arguments of the not-so-smart people. It’s the democracy of thought: people form opinions which should be based on correct arguments and factual facts, but those that find that thinking is for thinkers, reading for educated people and knowledge totally useless, have opinions as well. Based on incorrect arguments and not-so-factual facts. I once had a discussion with a woman who became almost violent when I claimed that smoking is undeniably bad for your health. She — an avid smoker — immediately fulminated that “her grandfather died at the age of 95, and he had smoked all his life, and a lot !” For her it was a proof, for me it was irrelevant. And still, her opinion is just as valuable as mine and yours, despite the fact that you and I factually and provable know that she are wrong. The typical Dunning-Kruger opponent (very common among the not-so-smart) cannot understand your arguments, so will not change his or her mind. He or she has “arguments” of his or her own, and has every right to think what he or she is thinking. As if truth is democratic. SOURCES: sculpture The Thinker by Auguste Rodin. CrisNYCa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a therapist, what is the most difficult thing you’ve had to tell a client?
Answer: Two years ago, my girlfriend had a patient who posed her the most unexpected request she might have ever received. He had only one testicle due to an episode of testicle cancer, and the remaining testicle had taken a huge kick from one of his cows (this guy was a farmer). The testicle looked like a melon, but it was still alive and kicking (pun intended). So he told her his decision: “I am seventy years old, and my wife an I do not share the bed anymore. You don’t need to spend any extra energy on saving my testicle. Just remove it, and I will be just fine.” It’s what he would have done on his farm with a ram or a bull, so there wasn’t that big of a problem in his eyes. Just amputate the thing — it had no function whatsoever anymore. But that was not the case. The urologist tried to explain that he needed the testosterone in order to function as he functioned today — as a functioning man, that is. But that’s not how he saw it, so he dismissed her arguments and demanded that she remove the melon. A bull without testicles would not grow an udder, right ? But she did not give in as well, because this was not a farm, and his biological knowledge of these things only went so far (as in most farmers, for that matter). So she repeated time and again that with an empty scrotum he would suffer from fatigue, hot flashes, muscle loss, poor facial hair growth and what have you. That without the remaining testicle he would turn into a woman in menopause — higher voice and all — and that lifelong hormone treatment would be necessary to keep his chemical works in balance. It took forever before he finally accepted her viewpoint. And yes indeed, she was not a therapist, but often (ethical) surgeons have to engage with their patients on a psychological level in order to converge to the correct therapy — not the one that earns them the most money. And if you were wondering about the outcome — The melon lived. SOURCES: Dissections of the male anus and urogenital system: two figures, with the arteries and blood vessels indicated in red. Colored lithograph by J. Roux, 1822. Wellcome Collection. (© public domain)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How “monstrous” can your thoughts be?
Answer: Although it’s well past midnight, he finally parks the car and steps out. It’s a three-hours drive back home and he has to work tomorrow morning, but the call is too strong to disobey. It’s still very warm and moist, and the silence of Nature around here is overwhelming — almost mystical. It’s his favorite place in the whole wide world, and coming to this sacred place time and again feels like a religious experience, only much more spiritual and still very real. As he slowly walks closer to the “altar” — that’s how he calls the small open space in the woods where he collects his belongings — he starts smelling the sweet fetid smell of decomposition, although his new treasure has been here for only two days. But he doesn’t care. It’s part of the game, and no smell can stop him. He will come back for another two or three weeks, unless the wild animals ruin the game (as they have done before). The smell is much stronger now, as he is almost there. And then he sees her. Lying there on the altar, undressed, legs wide open, her glassy eyes staring at the skies, but seeing nothing. (She is so beautiful.) Her jaw is crushed — he needed to overpower her, and one carefully aimed hit with a piece of oak is usually all it takes — and she misses a nipple (he couldn’t stop himself). Her face is really bloody, but he has water, soap and a towel with him to clean her up. Some make-up will make her all shiny again, as she so deserves. She was still alive when he brought her here, but after he engaged with her for the second and third time, he knew he could not keep her alive. The ultimate possession was taking her life while looking into her eyes and seeing the panic and despair, until all emotion faded into one last stare. He stopped counting his possessions — thirty, fifty, more ? — but she is one of the finest specimens of them all. She looks great, her skin feels great, and her hair is fabulous. She can be everyone he wants her to be, and she never says no. (He wonders when they will finally catch him — Ted Bundy, the ultimate ladies’ man — though. Murdering is totally consuming him, and it’s basically taking over his life. And he knows he will never stop. Never.) And even now, after two days, she still feels simply smashing inside. The empty look of her lifeless eyes and the mesmerizing feeling of her putrid flesh make him finish too early, but that’s totally okay for the night is still young. And so is she. SOURCES: image found through Listverse (image credit: Abrams Press/Amazon Prime Video).[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Have you ever met someone really privileged who shocked you?
Answer: Meet Marlee and John. Marlee is a dermatologist and John is a journalist. They are hippies “avant la lettre.” They love smoking marihuana, talk about Nature and the Universe, John is one of those guys who has a fabulous vinyl collection and a vinyl record player in the living room as the central vantage point of their philosophy — the works. And Love and Peace, of course ☮️ If they would be muppets, they would be musicians in the Electric Mayhem Band. But they are not. Their children go to a privileged Catholic school that has the factual reputation of being snobby, discriminating (especially towards poor people and people of color), cruel and condescending, but one thing is certainly true: many of the school children have rich and/or influential parents. A second thing is true as well: not a single one of the parents of these children is a member of the Electric Mayhem Band. No Love and Peace ☮️ for these guys. Apparently, the philosophy of Marlee and John is a guise for what really matters in their lives: money. And that is what their misguided hippie children are learning at school as we speak — “You can sing and dance at home, but you will learn the lashes of life at school. And the many, many connections into networks of those that have power, and dollars.” No more flower power for the children — No more Electric Mayhem. SOURCES: photograph found through Google images.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why do people with cancer sometimes appear to be OK on the outside?
Answer: My friend Ingrid was diagnosed with breast cancer when she was in her thirties, and it was not really a big surprise, as mutated BRCA genes run in her family (with many fatal consequences). So she decided to have a preventive double mastectomy, because she wanted to live. Unfortunately people with faulted BRC genes lack the tumor-repressing capacity normal BRCA genes have, so when cells start to go berserk in their body, they can do so without the body appropriately reacting. And so the cancers can grow and rage without obstruction. Six months ago, Ingrid felt a little bump in her groin, and she immediately suspected what was going on. And she was right: swollen cancerous lymph nodes. Further medical examination and imaging showed that the cancer had spread to her liver, and that the primary cancer still was breast cancer. So even with the double mastectomy and all the chemo, some breast cancer cells had managed to escape, and started to cluster far away from the breast area. And that’s exactly what the lymph nodes were signaling eventually. The thing is: in the beginning, the cancer clusters are very small (consisting of a couple of thousands of cells) and do no harm whatsoever. And it’s often only when the first real symptoms show up, that the damage has been done. And that’s the case with Ingrid. She has been diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer, and only has a couple of years left. Despite all the surgeries and therapies, the cancer had never completely left her body. And prepared a bleak sentence instead. SOURCES: Papilla of breast, anterior view. Skin surrounding the papilla has been partly removed. From “Atlas and Textbook of Human Anatomy,” 1914, Vol. 3, fig. 826, by Johannes Sobotta and J. Playfair McMurrich. Artist: K. Hajek.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How was your medical mystery finally diagnosed correctly?
Answer: A urologist in my girlfriend’s department had to perform an operation on a young woman to repair a uterine prolapse. The patient suffered from an abnormal weakening of the vaginal muscles which eventually resulted in a full uterine prolapse — the uterus literally hanging out of the body through the vagina. And for some unknown reason, she also complained of severe abdominal pain. To repair the prolapse, a surgical mesh was to be implanted to keep the patient’s uterus in place. The uterus was in such a bad shape though that the urologists first talked to the patient and asked her if her uterus could be removed — pregnancy after a mesh has been implanted can cause new and severe complications, and the patient already had children — but she refused. Before the mesh could be implanted though, an old prolapse pessary — which had been there to hold the prolapsed womb initially into place — had to be taken out first. But it did not look like a pessary at all, due to its weird shape and enormous size. “It was HUGE. Like a giant donut. Simply incredible.” When my girlfriend’s colleague subsequently tried to remove the colossal donut pessary, a putrid stench suddenly emerged, and an enormous amount of stinking pus — “almost a bucket” — washed away from the patient’s vagina. The surgery then had to be stopped, because the infection which caused the pus — and her mysterious abdominal pain ! — had to be treated first. And after hearing about the details of her condition, the patient decided not much later that the uterus indeed had to go — No more pus buckets for her. SOURCES: OBG Management 33 (2021), 20—27.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What were the last words you heard someone say before they died?
Answer: My last words to Jenny had been formulated more than a decade ago, so I never even tried to talk to her when she was sitting there, exhausted, desperate, and also totally passive because it was too late to escape what was coming. That was two years ago. The venue was a coffee shop, I was waiting for my daughter (and she was waiting for her son), and I had a lot of work to do. So I opened my portable computer, and started writing up things. And behind me, Jenny was sitting on a bar stool in a state of emptiness I had hardly ever seen before. INTERMEZZO: I knew she had cancer. But I did not know she was this sick (and none of it was my business). Here was a virtually unrecognizable woman who was moving like Jenny, dressed like Jenny, but the spark in her was gone. And the cancer had spread. So yeah, I continued to work and think hard, while Jenny’s statue was sitting there behind me, staring into the future that lay ahead. And it was so close she could almost see it. Almost. When my daughter was finally there, I had a final peek at the empty ghost who once was my wife, and then we left, totally again pulled into our own lives, and leaving Jenny behind in the life she had aggressively chosen for at the very point when our roads diverged in a wood. In the week after she died, I received a message beyond the grave which said that I was not to attend her funeral. Apparently, she had expected me to talk to her before she died — after all the nonsense she did to me — and I remained silent in the last coffee shop stand. So I did not attend the funeral in the end. And that was okay for me. SOURCES: painting by Kevin Foote.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I wrapped a bandage too hard around my finger. Should I be worried?
Answer: A friend of ours noticed one morning that some hair was wrapped around one of the fingers of her baby. It’s called a “hair tourniquet” — human hair (or some other type of thread) tied around a finger, toe, or male genital. It’s kind of what you have right now. And usually there’s no problem whatsoever, but as the term “tourniquet” suggests, the affected digit cannot receive an adequate blood supply for a while, and this is never good. In rare cases the digit even has to be amputated. So you want to take care of your hair tourniquet right away. But be aware — In the case of our friend’s baby, its little finger top looked badly swollen and almost black, and so our friend decided to free the finger ASAP. Not much later, her baby started to convulse, and went into cardiac arrest. When the paramedics arrived, there was not much they could do. By removing the hair tourniquet, a blood clot from the finger top was released into her baby’s little body, and caused severe thrombosis. And snapped its little life in seconds. Our friend only wanted to help her baby. (It turned out differently though.) SOURCES: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do nurses wear diapers?
Answer: The answer is NO (I take it that you mean during long surgeries), and I am highly surprised and somewhat taken aback that someone answered positively on this question, claiming he/she wears them systematically during operations which take 10 hours and more. Defecation and all. (My guess is that this person is a pervert.) In any case, of all the OR nurses and doctors we know, none of them ever wears a diaper — not even when they are still coping with the aftermath of a bad stomach flu and the like. All these people are highly trained professionals, and all these people know exactly when they can leave the table, and when they cannot. And just to be very clear: in situations which involve high stress (and great responsibility), your bowel movements and bladder summersaults are controlled by a first-things-first mechanism which simply is stronger than your basic instincts. In such cases, your mind does not leave any elbow room for No. 1 and No. 2 — The life of the patient comes first. SOURCES: Whoisjohngalt, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What’s the most extreme thing you’ve seen a “helicopter” parent do?
Answer: Wes was the new boy in my daughter’s class, and from the very beginning it was clear that Wes was special. According to his mom, that is. For Wes was one year younger than the other kids, and even now he needed to be stimulated with more advanced Math, French and what have you. According to his mom, that is. Nobody really knew why he had to change schools in the beginning of sixth grade, but it was clear that mom had something to do with it. The people of the old school were not convinced that Wes needed all this pushing — he was a bright kid, but there was no indication whatsoever that he needed the “extra training.” History basically repeated itself in the new school: his new sixth grade teacher did not like the way he was ordered to push the little boy, and he also saw no reason to do it. Wes had a lot of stress, and the constant projection of his mom’s frustrations in her own life’s course onto his little self made everything worse, all the time. When the class of 2024 graduated, all the students were officially lauded in no particular order, with a personal laudatio. And then it happened: my daughter was the first to be called, and lauded as the most creative (art-wise) student, who also had the most exceptional grades of all. And Wes’s mom imploded. She had a long talk with the teachers afterwards, extremely angry and erratic, and she has not spoken with us since. Because as always, the teachers have made a mistake. Many mistakes. My daughter is going to high school in a couple of weeks, and so is Wes — to the very same school. His mom has already resumed the negotiations — with the new people in the new school, that is. And they will see once and for all what no teacher in the past has seen in Wes, and it will finally reduce his constant stress (and awakening depression) because he so deserves the recognition. But she does not understand that it isn’t the recognition of the teachers he so craves for — It’s hers. SOURCES: the painting is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Which are the weirdest medical cases till now?
Answer: On the weekend, we went for a swim on the camping site where we have a little trailer house, and in and near the swimming pool was a family with children, and one of these children was obviously severely “syndromal.” The boy looked almost exactly like the patient on the left-hand side in the image below. Both my girlfriend and I knew immediately what the cause of his particular appearance was, and in my case, it was the very first time I had ever seen such patient. (It may have been the first case for my girlfriend as well, but I’m not sure.) Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS). It’s a rare genetic disorder caused by a loss of function of certain genes on chromosome 15 — and I know this abstract nonsense doesn’t say much about the patient for those who are not acquainted with PWS, but I can you tell you this: these patients are cursed. PWS patients are characterized by a constant craving for food (or anything which looks like food, or can be eaten in general), are usually mentally impaired and typically suffer from behavioral issues. They often also share some generic characteristics related to appearance:[1] Often, affected individuals have a narrow forehead, small hands and feet, short height, and light skin and hair. This boy was a textbook case. I guess he was about eighteen years old, but this poor morbidly obese boy was wearing a diaper, and was constantly annoying his brothers, sisters and parents (because he wanted food), and at times was aggressive as well. PWS patients are so consumed by their constant hunger, that they would eat anything to satisfy the craving — think rotten meat, think garbage bags, think dead animals, think stones, think frozen food. And even if it’s normal food, they cannot (and will not) stop. Many a PWS patient has eaten him -or herself to death because of lack of surveillance, and that’s the big burden of those living with these patients: they will do anything to find food. They will lie, they will cheat, they will steal, they will try to break the lock on the fridge. That’s also why it is almost impossible to keep your PWS girl or boy at home — it’s a night-and-day job to keep them alive, and at some point you will fail miserably. The average life expectancy of PWS patients is close to twenty-five years (!!!), so the very sight of this boy made us kind of sad, knowing what was coming rather sooner than later — An unfinished life. SOURCES: the footnoted site and Google images.[2]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do doctors know when their patient is lying?
Answer: This happened a couple of months ago. A male patient enters the ER with abdominal pain because he is severely constipated, but the very cause of his medical problem turns out to be urological. He has a conglomerate of very painful cauliflower-like genital warts in and around his anus, and it makes him postpone No. 2 every which way. Hence the constipation. But this patient is weird. Even before his first medical interview with the urologist is over, he starts undressing to show his genitals and behind. As if he is eager to show them. As if he is excited. His condition turns out to be Syphilis, but the medication will save him nevertheless. (Without medication, Syphilis is life-threatening.) But now here’s the problem: the patient acts as if he does not know how the warts got “there” in the first place, since “he is a decent citizen.” When his urologist asks him — rather blatantly, but in the privacy of the consultation room there is no reason to lie about one’s case — whether he is homosexual, he almost erupts and immediately becomes so aggressive, that a male trainee is asked to join the interview. Every single further question about the touchdown location of his genital warts is dodged, and it is obviously that the man is lying, possibly in a bout of self-denial about his own personal preferences. He is not like that. Period. And still, that is the location where the bad guys entered the building. Most probably, at this point you are asking yourself why the urologist is asking these questions. The answer is that the patient’s sexu🙄l partners need to be contacted and warned about his condition, and need to take the appropriate medication (penicillins) in order to prevent that they succumb to the disease they might be suffering from. This patient refuses to help in any way, though. And genital warts really do mark the spot. SOURCES: Tertiary syphilitic ulceration of the scalp (on the left) and Face of a woman with a typical “syphilitic nose” (on the right), St Bartholomew's Hospital Photographic Society, Wellcome Collection (CC BY 4.0 attribution).

Question: What happens when humans swallow animal sperm?
Answer: People eat animal sperm all the time (bull testicles have been consumed for ages, for instance), and engaging with pets and their produce has always been around in one way or the other. In particular, humans are animals and swallowing human semen is quite a common practice in your average household (and an excellent contraceptive approach to marital life), and basically what is swallowed is a healthy addition to one’s everyday diet. So in the end it’s very simple: a good load of protein never hurts — And some like it hot. SOURCES: Google images.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Has anybody lost their kid due to termination from CPS?
Answer: “The saddest thing that I'd ever seen were smokers outside the hospital doors.” You might be acquainted with this Editors song, but that’s almost exactly what happens all the time in cases described by the question. My uncle is a social worker and visits them all the time. Parents who lost their kids through termination from CPS. These are “parents,” by the way — the quotation marks are important. Teenage parents, people with drug and/or gambling addictions, general retards who flunked every class they ever had, but still “think” (the quotation marks again) they can run a household, people who “think” having babies is a right — just like buying teddy bears, or pets. People who can’t spell responsibility. People with psychiatric issues so severe, that a baby would not never make it. And still they want those babies. My uncle tries to help these people paying bills, looking for a job, stop gaming 10 hours per day, thinking outside the conspiracy box trap, feeding the kids (if there are any left), using contraception — you name it. Without people like my uncle, these guys and galls are lost. But they are not the greatest victims — the greatest victims are the children. They grow up in loveless households where mom and dad can hardly write nor read, have no idea whatsoever how to help their kids in school matters, and consider Doritos and Pepsi a decent school meal. Most of them are mentally so much behind that it takes a miracle to convince them that kids need to brush their teeth, that reading is a good thing, and that it’s not okay for their 12-year-old daughter to “engage” with a 17-year-old friend. Many of these kids will make the very same mistakes of their parents, although they vow to be different. That’s often how child abuse works — cyclically and very hard to escape. The most frustrated and sad thing is the Editors song though. My uncle, visiting the Andersons again. They have 6 children (although both “parents” are only 24 years old), and have lost every single one of them through CPS termination. When Mary Lee Anderson opens the door to let my uncle in, he sees her belly, and immediately knows what is going on. And number 7 will also be taken away from them in no time, because the very fact that she is pregnant shows how desperate the situation really is. For Mare Lee will never understand — She loves them teddy bears. SOURCES: painting by Rhys Knight (and suitably edited).

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is your biggest “only in the USA” moment?
Answer: We were spending our holidays in the states and my daughter was still very young. It was very hot that day, and so we decided to have a quick swim before going for dinner. At the swimming pool we undressed our daughter — who was three at the time — to get her in her bathing suit, so that at some point she briefly did not have any clothes on. And to our astonishment, an American woman addressed us about “how inappropriately it was what we were doing.” And she wasn’t the only one who was staring at us. Apparently the American people looked at us through some kind of filter in which they could not see that my daughter was just a toddler, and not a grown-up. Apparently they associated “our behavior” with different things than we did. And all this happened in the land of child beauty pageant contests — Welcome to America. SOURCES: GIF found through Google images.[1]
