Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's the most despicable thing you've seen a doctor or nurse do?
Answer: One urologist once told us that he performed digital vaginal examinations (DVEs) on his female patients, as a fixed routine when they medically consulted him. Even if there was no indication whatsoever to do a DVE. He insisted on doing it to teenage patients to “know the patient a little better” — because that’s just the doctor he is. In fact, it’s exactly the teenage patients that keep him thriving to remain the digital artist that he is — it takes only one finger to make someone medically happy. He knows all too well that most patients would never suspect him of indecent behavior, as his consultation room is the perfect venue to perform a DVE on a teenage female without any questions being raised. And how wrong could it ever be to let the experienced urologist digitally search his young female patients for medical conditions in the first place ? This urologist is the perfect helping hand, and what’s even more — He always does it with a smile. SOURCES: Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a professor, has there been a student you instantly recognized as a genius in the first week of knowing them?
Answer: You can’t discover a genius through simple Math puzzles, or IQ tests (and that’s what many answers get totally wrong). IQ tests were actually introduced to examine people who are at the other end of the spectrum, such as Down patients. And that works really well. But they are way too simple for identifying brilliancy or geniuses (and that’s why Mensa is such a hilariously example of the cyclic irony of stupidity). IQ tests are very simple. Too simple. In general, it often takes a (true) genius to identify a (true) genius, by the way. One famous example is that of Jacques Tits — a Belgian mathematical genius who entered university at the age of 14, was not allowed to obtained his Master in two years, so had to wait the full 4 years but essentially wrote his PhD thesis while waiting. He later was awarded a Wolf prize and an Abel prize (the mathematical equivalent of the Nobel prize), became one of the legends of Group Theory and Geometry, and is considered to be one of the great mathematicians of the 20th century. And yet he is not the hero of our story. The hero is a student of his when Tits was still teaching at the Free University of Brussels, and who quickly became the main character in his Group Theory classes, blowing Tits away. So Tits sent the boy to Alexander Grothendieck, at that moment the most famous mathematician in the world, and one of the greatest ever. And just like Tits, Grothendieck immediately acknowledged the raw unparalleled power of this boy, and so became his PhD advisor. Under Grothendieck, the boy grow to his full potential, and then eventually even became (much) stronger than his master. One of his main accomplishments is the proof of the hardest of the so-called Weil conjectures — the dream of Grothendieck (and his frustration later on), and arguably the most famous mathematical problem of the time, only solvable by the singular genius of this young Belgian man who would perform many more mathematical miracles in his career. Jean-Pierre Serre, himself one of the greatest mathematicians of the 20th century, would later say that this man was the greatest ever, that the difference between the boy’s genius and the best of the rest was almost impossible to describe, because it was unworldly. His name was (and still is) Pierre Deligne. And IQ tests (and those who devise them) cannot grasp people like that — they never could. They are just very, very easy tests which give you a score without much meaning — Unless the score is very, very low. IMAGE CREDIT: Andrea Kane.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How crazy is your mother?
Answer: When my father-in-law announced that he wanted a divorce on the very day his youngest son became 18, my mother-in-law’s life was obliterated. But that’s what self-denial usually does near the end of the road. She knew that he had cheated on her all along with multiple nurses and interns, and still she had always ignored that in some way because he was the father of her children, and because he was the love of her life. When he was on call, his pager beeped without exception because of some undefined emergency urological call (usually made by some young female trainee for non-medical reasons, but still urological in some sense). He did that all the time. So when he announced the divorce, she was gutted. He was a man of next-to-no words, but still she must have been very blind not to see that the many things she had tried over the years to meet his demands were hardly even relevant to the questions he had asked — if you are too different, there is no perfect answer to the questions you do not understand. So they divorced, and she tried to commit suicide by hanging herself. And she was found after a minute or so, and saved. And then a horrible nightmare of healing began of wounds that are still open to this very day — fifteen years later. She has not thought about a single man since. (He has touched many women though.) But sometimes they still turn up. Matchboxes — once the very center of his attention, but now an instigator of angst, because he had collected them for years, and now they keep appearing in his house every which way. Because she still has a key — that’s what shame does to you after 30 years of cheating — and she still uses it as well. Planting matchboxes in his living room, under the sofa, in the kitchen on the stove, in his bedroom under his favorite pillow which has become tired of so many screams. She thought she married the love of her life, but he was just a handsome guy who became the father of her children, and who happened to collect matchboxes. And somehow they didn’t match. SOURCES: the image is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do people know they have cancer?
Answer: My former friend Jenny never had the slightest clue before she found something insignificant which turned out to be huge. Even warning signs such as back pains only become warning signs in hindsight. So when the GP told her the little bump was a cancerous lymph node, she was more than surprised — but not devastated, because she still had a chance. As a young healthy woman (or so she thought) with young healthy children, it was only fair to have a long future ahead. The bump was a traveler though, and it came from the primary breast area. And as the lymphatic system is a hub for cancers to travel around our body, things became more tedious. Only weeks later, it turned out that the traveler had gone even further, and had reached distant regions in the body long before any bump was found, so that the long future ahead transformed into a new truth — Five years at most. Jenny would never see her kids grow up. She would never see them graduate. Her new future would be captivated by desperate tries to keep her alive in a rising see of pain which would destroy her inner self, and only would leave a shell of memories which became more distant by the minute, as the shadows came ever closer. In the end, only empty eyes remained which would stop seeing near the end of August. As it all started with a minor bump, and a diagnosis. Which changed into a sentence soon. SOURCES: The Great Wave off Kanagawa, 神奈川沖浪裏, Kanagawa-oki Nami Ura. (© Public domain)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the saddest thing that happened to you that you never shared with others before?
Answer: it did not happen to me. Today, we visited the best theme park in the world for my daughter’s birthday (on Saturday). For us, it was the perfect day. But not for everyone. Because for some time, we noticed another family with kids, and one of the kids was sitting in a wheelchair. The girl seemed confused and too tired to be enchanted, too sick to be engaged. At first we thought it was one of those patients that should not have been born in the first place — you know, those poor babies that lacked oxygen for a minute or so, and entered the world as the sort of concentration of pain and misery that would never have even one day to really enjoy. But we were wrong, and she was different. She lacked any facial hair (including eyebrows), and she was obviously too weakened to walk by herself, but she talked — whispered might be a better word — to the sister who was pushing her, and to her parents, and what she said was sane. She likely was a very young cancer patient who was battling her sickness and therapies, and who was trying to enjoy a day away from the pain she was in, and forget about the existential struggle. Because some cancer patients die young. I could not tell her age — she probably was fourteen or fifteen, but in the land of the tallest people in the world, she could have been twelve or thirteen as well. Too young to die in any case. And too proud to tell just how much she was suffering — Even when surrounded by fairy tales. (And all those happy people.) Some, some die young, But you better hold on. So many things I need to say to you — Please don't, don't let me go. And we said we would die together. (Song by Laleh) SOURCES: painting by Alessandro Sicioldr.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Should teachers be allowed to prevent students from using the restroom?
Answer: My daughter dreamed of doing ballet as a very young girl, so when she asked us if she could join a local ballet school, we immediately said yes. One day — she was six or seven at the time — we fetched her from ballet school and all of a sudden she complained that she really had to pee during class, and that the ballet teacher had not allowed her to go, even when my daughter had clearly said that it was ever so urgent. And that was the beginning of the end. Not much later, we took her off ballet because the sheer ballet interpretation of discipline turned out the be a variation of middle-aged torture. (Pain should never be a part of the learning process, Miss Baryshnikov.) Kids so small should be allowed to go to the restrooms when they have to go, and even when they would be older, there is a basic universal principle which you should not touch — When you have to go, you have to go. SOURCES: Google images.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's wrong with my anus? There's a small lump on top of my anus, like a big skin tag, it's the size of a pistachio. It doesn't hurt at all, I don't bleed or anything, I've had it for many months. What could it be? Should I be worried?
Answer: I have suffered from similar symptoms for more than a decade, but in my case, the lump protruded from my rectum whenever I had to go (No. 2). Unfortunately, I also have irritable bowel syndrome, which means I have to go all the time. And this guy hurt me so bad that I often almost fainted in the act. Bled a lot. Pushed it back afterwards. Then had to go again less than an hour later. Bled a lot. Almost fainted. Pushed it back. (You get the picture.) It ruined my life. Finally I had it examined, and it turned out to be a pre-cancerous polyp (of about 5 inches long), which had lived in my rectum. If I had waited any longer, it would have turned cancerous. (Not as bad as the patient of my girlfriend’s who turned up with a uterine prolapse (uterus dangling between her legs) which she had been living with for 5 years. But still.) So go the a doctor as soon as you can. (Trust me on this one.) SOURCES: Medical Illustration & Animation. (© Scott Bodell)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's something that sucks about being a man?
Answer: A couple we know really well, had a big fight in a pub they frequented almost daily. When they returned back home, the woman — who could be very aggressive when drunk — closed the glass door of their house as hard as she could while her spouse was right behind her, and it caught one of his hands. His hand broke the glass, and was even stuck in the door for a while, and when he finally managed pull it out, most of the flesh of the upper part of his hand was gone. The gash was erupting blood, the wound was horrible. So they called us, and my girlfriend took him to her hospital and immediately performed emergency surgery on his hand. Our female friend never even said sorry, but if he would have done even a fraction of what she had done to him, he would have spent half of his life in jail. He never officially accused her of (a very serious case of) spousal abuse, because he knew that in a court, he would lose since he was a man, and her every lie would be believed. Come Spring, she decided she wanted him to leave (because her horoscope girlfriend had told her so), and she demanded 100% legal and physical custody of their two young children. He was heart-broken by the whole matter, but she warned him that if he so much as opened his mouth and tried to fight for a better deal, she would accuse him of domestic violence and the like, and that he would end up in jail before he could even begin to understand what was going on. And since he was a man, he knew she was right. SOURCES: Annals of Surgery, vol. 197, No. 5 (1983), pp. 495–506.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Who has witnessed a medical miracle?
Answer: A patient, in so much pain that he can barely walk. He knows he has prostate cancer, and although he is consumed by what is happening inside, his urologist says that he is okay, and that no further action is needed for the time being. What he does not know is that his urologist does not want to help him. That fixing this patient will take too much time (if it’s possible at all), and there’s not enough money involved. Still, the patient panics and asks for a second opinion in another hospital. To add insult to injury, not only the pain has become unbearable, but he is also severely constipated. And if he tries to go, crying, some stuff oozes out of his rectum but it’s certainly not excrements. When he is medically examined by his new urologist, she discovers that the stuff is pus. Tumor pus, to be exact. And that when she so much as briefly touches his rectum, the stinking stuff comes shooting out, because that’s where the tumor is. The original prostate tumor. It has gotten so big that it is trying to exit his body through his behind. (That’s what procrastination does to cancer.) But there is also a second big surprise: although the tumor is one of the biggest ever seen, the cancer has miraculously not spread. Although the patient’s abdomen is filled with tumor tissue, this patient still has a chance to live for a long time, if he is properly medically helped. And this time, he is. SOURCES: Dissections of the male genitals, upper thighs and pelvic region: two figures, with the arteries, blood vessels and veins indicated in red and blue. Colored lithograph by J. Roux, 1822.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What do very old people (90s plus) think about?
Answer: Isaac Newton — the greatest and most influential scientist of all time — stated in his formulation of the three fundamental laws of physics:[1] A body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant speed in a straight line, except insofar as it is acted upon by a force. Essentially, a physical body that moves wants to stay moving, and a physical body at rest wants to stay at rest. And that is what happens to very old people. As the burden of their body starts slowing them down — essentially because of muscle atrophy, a vast spectrum of conditions, and organs that are failing them in the battle against gravity (Newton, yet again) — a cyclic disaster is initiated that is impossible to stop. The mind and body slow down until they are too often at rest, and since being at rest turns out to be the least painful and exhausting thing to do, they want to keep resting. While the exact opposite — movement of the mind and body (in that order) — is what should help them to keep moving in the first place. And if one is used to resting all the time, every waking activity becomes tiring. Walking, talking, thinking, seeing, listening, reading, loving, giving, losing, and in the end: living, become exhausting because the universe is pulling at you until you finally dissolve. What do very old people (90s plus) think about ? About trying to keep moving — All the time. SOURCES: the image depicts the death mask of Isaac Newton.[2]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: If I win 8 million at the casino and leave immediately, what will be the consequences?
Answer: Las Vegas has been one of my heimats since I was a kid, but only once have I ever experienced who the more important people in the world were. (Not us, by the way.) We were upgraded into a floor which was only reachable through a special card, and our specific room wat set for $4,700 a night. Three living rooms, two kitchens, one golden jacuzzi. In the other apartment (only two apartments per floor), I noticed a very famous Hollywood actor entering with a new girlfriend, but we did not see nor hear anything. (Her legs were great.) It was Leo or Brad, by the way. (You choose.) SOURCES: People’s magazine.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Did divorce ruin your life?
Answer: As someone who keeps the wounds of the past wide open in order to visit them whenever I want — and this might sound like the beginning of an answer that acknowledges the question — I can only say that it did not. But some people took some of the rot with them for no particular reason (or so I thought). And then my former wife died from cancer. And a family ordered me to go to my ex-wife’s funeral, while there was nothing left between us. In fact, I had asked that particular family member explicitly not to go herself (to respect my former in-law family), but she ignored my question altogether and went to the cremation all the same, cried her heart out so that everyone could see it, and then called me on the phone. And she described every single detail of the funeral into the voice mail app of my phone, so that I would feel the pain I was supposed to feel according to her sick mind (I didn’t). (My daughter cried.) That pain had been buried more than a decade ago, and that’s what some people don’t accept afterwards, even if someone dies. Even if your ex-wife disappears in the mist of metastasis. Even if you witnessed the demise (but never asked for it). The divorce ruined many things at some point (for years), but then life moves on and so do you, and still some people have the audacity to rip your life apart because they think you have to be involved in the after-life of your marriage. Because for some people that’s what it was always about — Selling the drama. “And to christ: a cross, and to me: a chair — I will sit and earn the ransom from up here.” SOURCES: painting by Mikhail Vasilyevich Nesterov. Lyrics by Live.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Has someone told you something that still bothers you today?
Answer: As someone who keeps the wounds of the past wide open in order to visit them whenever I want — that’s how I can easily visit my former two-year-old self in class — I remember the very pain of the letters that formed the words and sentences I never wanted to hear. Many of them — perhaps all of them — but that doesn’t mean they still bother me as of today. They simply exist, and have a particular taste if I think of them, or when I visit the past. Which I do from time to time (but not because I miss it). But in more recent times, what bothered me the most was that a family member demanded me to go to my ex-wife’s funeral, while there was nothing left between us. In fact, I had asked that particular family member explicitly not to go (stirring up things after so many years hurts more than it helps, if you ask me), but as the number one super-hero-narcissist she was and is, she simply went to the cremation, cried her heart out so that everyone could see it, and then called me on the phone. In the evening, and very drunk. And she tried to describe every single detail of the funeral into the voice mail app of my phone, so that I would feel the pain I was supposed to feel according to her sick mind (I didn’t). I had never heard so much self-love hurt. Although she was a close witness of the ordeal I went through when my marriage was ripped apart, she never understood nor learnt a thing. It was just a part of her everyday life, which consisted and consists of everyday tears and everyday pain, wrapped up in the misery of others. Because that’s what it was always about — Selling the drama. And to christ: a cross, and to me: a chair — I will sit and earn the ransom from up here. SOURCES: painting by Mikhail Vasilyevich Nesterov. Lyrics by Live.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Have you ever witnessed a "Don't tell me how to raise my child" moment?
Answer: I had made the virtually lethal mistake to mention to a mother that smoking cigarettes inside one’s house or one’s car is very bad for the people who also happen to live in the house, or sit in the car — especially if they are children. The woman, who was a very good friend of my former MIL, immediately became aggressive towards me, and even began shouting almost at once. The problem was that not only she was an avid smoker — this woman loved to smoke ! — she had also smoked for many years in her own house, near her young children (and she still did). But instead of looking into the mirror and change her ways, she made a little twist in her head and decided to change the rhetoric altogether — as if that was even possible: “Do you think I would ENDANGER my own children ? Are you saying I am a BAD MOTHER ?!!” I tried to explain to her that this made no sense at all, but she was so angry with me — “the snotty professor” — that she refused to listen to my every word. She was convinced that she was a good mother (because she deeply loved her children), and being a good mother to her children implied that smoking inside her house and car was NOT bad for their health, because she would NEVER harm her children. Only, that’s exactly what she had done for many, many years. SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are some sad truths about life?
Answer: Nicole is the 74-old-mother of one of my best friends, and on Saturday she had a long talk with us because she needed someone to talk to. It was at the birthday party of her grandson — who also is my godson (terrible term) — and her oldest sister was there as well. Aunt Lynn, a proud educated woman of 87 whom Nicole considers to be her mom, rather than her sister. Aunt Lynn has been a single and extremely independent woman for most of her life, and I have known her at a personal level for at least fifteen years. But something has changed. She still drives a car, but since about a year, she often gets lost when she tries to visit her little sister (only a couple of blocks down the road), and has to drive back. She always dressed meticulously in the past, following old etiquette rules, but nowadays she often walks around in her pajamas, not really realizing what she is doing. Or what day it is. She also virtually stopped bathing. My friend’s family is conservative, and the word “dementia” has never been mentioned in conversations — she “forgets a lot” and “has a hard time remembering what she was talking about” — but not the word (as if saying the word will only make matters worse). The last time I saw Aunt Lynn (before Saturday), it was unclear to me how bad her memory was affected by her condition, and also on Saturday, I thought she was doing really well for a 87-year-old. Until she ordered drinks. All of a sudden, she grabbed my friend — her nephew — by the arms, and ordered drinks for some people. And on the verge of being aggressive, she urged him to hurry up, because she was tired of waiting. We thought she was kidding at first. Only, she wasn’t. Her sister Nicole was extremely worried (because the mental deterioration of Aunt Lynn has progressed really rapidly in the past months), and she tried to convince her sister to call it a day, and head back home with her. But Aunt Lynn refused altogether, and stated “that this was HER house, and that SHE would decide what happened IN HER HOUSE.” Only it wasn’t her house at all — it was my friend’s. She never lived there (not even close). In the end, Aunt Lynn was so confused that she joined her little sister to go back home, speechless and confused, as if she was a toddler who needed a nap. And I saw the tears in Nicole’s eyes, and realized that an era was nearing its very gloomy end. And that nothing will be left of Aunt Lynn’s mind apart from scraps and pieces, wrapped up in aggressive episodes of frustration, while every next tick of the clock will obliterate her even further, and every next question will confuse her even more. And that is the saddest thing about Aunt Lynn. That if she will even take a few more steps down the ladder of oblivion, suddenly all letters and sounds will be lost, and only the bleakest emptiness will remain — And with any luck, one last smile. SOURCES: painting by Mikhail Vasilyevich Nesterov.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why do commercial airline pilots always announce the altitude at which the plane will be flying, when giving their initial greeting to the passengers?
Answer: It’s actually a brilliant psychological life hack. Many passengers are really afraid of flying — aerophobia, as it is called — and so the airline pilots, especially on long hauls, reassure those passengers by giving them some extra information about the current status of the flight in (usually) a warm and kind voice. By hearing the pilot, the passengers now have connected to the pilot (who is a real flesh-and-blood knowledgeable human being), and by hearing some technical information, the passengers get the feeling that those numbers are the numbers they should be — everything is okay ! But that’s not the end of it: by simply hearing that they are flying at an altitude of 30,000 feet, aerophobic passengers get a feeling of relative safety, since they are far above the ground now, and that’s not where the accidents happen — The height marks the spot. SOURCES: image found through GIPHY.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do lots of wife’s cheat while at work?
Answer: In my research institute I have barely seen it, although there is one professor who (in)famously sleeps with his PhD students. (In fact, he married one of them after divorcing his first wife, but the cheating never stopped.) In my girlfriend’s hospital though (and the other hospitals she worked in), the vastness of cheating from both wives and husbands is nothing less than breathtaking. One doctor — dr. Peterson, an orthopedist and serial cheater with a wife and kids at home — at some point simultaneously had a relationship with two nurses who found out about each other, and engaged in a cat fight at a party which I happened to attend. Nowadays, Peterson has a relationship with an anesthesiologist called dr. Paris (who also is married with children), and the running joke among the nurses is that “it turns out he was in Paris again on the weekend.” This is just one of many examples, but usually the relationships develop between female nurses and male doctors — in the mind of many (but not all) nurses, being married to a hospital doctor and bear his children lifts them to the highest echelons, and endows them with the status they always dreamed of. But being in Paris on a regular basis is also rather nice, of course. SOURCES: the drawing is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, what’s the biggest miracle you’ve ever witnessed in the emergency department?
Answer: An Egyptian woman insisted that her husband’s sperm be checked. To her, it was an emergency because she wanted to get pregnant and have a baby, but nothing happened at all. The semen sample was a disaster in its purest form, because it was dead. Not a single living sperm cell was found swimming in the sample, and after further investigation the emergency received a name, in the form of a rare congenital condition in which patients are infertile from birth. He could never have kids in the first place. But now the miracle enters the picture. Because this couple already had three kids. And although her husband believed that he was the biological father of his children, this very idea was scientifically not possible. His wife, on the other hand, knew only too well that the truth was slightly different (although she had never known herself until now that his suckers did not swim, and never did). Because back in Egypt — where they lived when all their children were conceived — a medical miracle had happened. Three times. And it involved living sperm. SOURCES: image taken from GIFer.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Is it safe to stick your finger in your own anus?
Answer: Medical doctors perform digital rectal exams all the time to check out the state of a patient’s prostate, or to diagnose hemorrhoids, so obviously there is no harm to it whatsoever, as long as we are talking about fingers. One patient in my girlfriend’s hospital once entered the ER with a potato stuck in his behind. That wasn’t the primary problem, though: the patient had tried to get the potato out of his rectum by inserting a knitting needle in there and trying to prick it into the potato. He believed that he would be able to pull out the potato in this way, but the only thing that happened was that he severely damaged his rectum with the needle. (He never explained how the potato got in there. Most of these patients “fall.”) My girlfriend and I once had a friendly encounter with a female specialist friend, and the latter happened to have extremely long nails. She loved to examine me down there, and although it was very pleasing in the heat of the moment, it was also very itchy and scratchy afterwards, as if my rectum had been perforated by a crab. Is it safe to stick your finger in your own anus ? It is very safe indeed. You want to be careful about the crabs, though. SOURCES: image found through Alamy.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are your thoughts on the Olympics' decision to allow Imane Khelif to compete in the women's boxing competition despite previous controversies surrounding her gender eligibility?
Answer: My take on it is that trans women should not participate in major women’s sport events (allowing trans men in men’s events would not make any difference whatsoever). But Khelif is not a trans woman. In fact, not much seems to be known about her gender issues, if there are issues at all (besides Russian trolling). In fact, I could not find any reliable source that states she is an XY (technically a man), although this might be the case as DSDs include congenital conditions in XY patients which look very female on many levels (think Jamie Lee Curtis), while at the same time enjoying male genitals, such as undescended testicles and the like. People like Elon Musk have reacted furiously on Khelif’s case, blatantly assuming that Khelif was born as a man — which we simply do not know. And even if she would suffer from Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS), she would be an XY — a technical man — and her body would produce testosterone (if the testicles would still be there), but lacking testosterone receptors, it would not help her in any way as a boxer. It would not make any difference. So people like Musk can say what they want, scream what they want, write what they want, and smell what they want — without any medical information whatsoever there are no grounds to condemn Khelif. And let’s be honest: sharing an opinion with Elon Musk is rarely a good thing — He’s the one with a congenital condition. SOURCES: Google images.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Have you ever gone into your sister's home and found something unexpected?
Answer: One day we visited my oldest sister, and as usual, she “urgently” needed a helping hand — there was something in the trunk of her car, and she couldn’t lift it so that I was the one who had to take it out. There was an appalling smell in the air, and it badly worsened as I approached the car. And knowing my sister, I had already figured out that what was inside the trunk was very, very dead. When I opened the car, besides putrified surprise, the thought also immediately entered my mind that this would be a Mission Impossible (nr. VIII). A dead donkey. A stinking and bloody mass weighing more than 500 pounds, with long lifeless ears and white lifeless eyes that stared at me with distracting contempt, as if I was the one who had put it in its uncomfortable predicament. (A couple of weeks later, she would ask me to sit on a living ostrich and keep its neck and head still while she would perform surgery on the monstrous beast, but I did not know that yet.) I will not even try to explain to you, my dear friend, what happened afterwards and how it happened, but I can tell you this much: my stinking-dead-donkey-lifting days are over and done with. (I hope.) SOURCES: painting by Guang Yang.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are the common behaviors of a person with dementia in their final days?
Answer: In many cases, it starts with the most unexpected bang which will make family and friends happy, rather than sad. But that’s because they do not know what is ahead. Take uncle Jessie. For years, his mind has been deteriorating up to a point that he hardly talks anymore, and if he talks, it is mostly confused nonsense. Sometimes he recognizes his children, sometimes he does not. Sometimes he just stares at the empty walls in his room in the nursing home where he resides. He thinks he always lived here. He thinks his parents lived (and live) here as well. But one day, everything changes. Because uncle Jessie is lucid again all of a sudden. He calls the nurses by name, and recognizes his children again, and starts asking about his grandchildren for the first time in more than 6 years. He still knows their names. He starts asking about his friends, about politics and says that he wants to re-read one of his favorite books. Uncle Jessie is back. In fact, he is so back that his awakening shows many similarities with the patients who woke up from their Encephalitis Lethargica (EL) coma following the EL pandemic in 1915–1926, after having been administered the L-dopa medicine.[1] The transformation is so shocking that it is nothing short of a miracle. It isn’t a miracle though. Around about the same time tomorrow, a nurse will find uncle Jessie in bed, not breathing and already cold. His sudden awakening is his body’s last stand — it is its very last try to stay afloat, before his condition will finally pull him down into the darkness. His sudden lucidity is nothing else than his entire system’s despair — sheer panic in which its every energy is bundled together into one last major beam of life, before the final fall. It is the infamous end-of-life hiccup. The final flickering flame which always brings new hope — Before the light goes out. SOURCES: the footnoted site. Painting by Beksiński.

Question: As a doctor, what has a patient done that caused you to burst out in laughter?
Answer: The patient was wheeled into the ER with a broken hip, only 52 years old and looking even much younger. And still, something was going on. The surgeon on call told the nurses that the patient had to stay in bed until the operation, and that no matter what, this patient might prove to be a nuisance. Less than thirty minutes later, the patient asked one of the nurses what he was doing in the hospital, and demanded that he leave ASAP — “There is NOTHING wrong with me !” And so the nurse explained that he had an accident and broken his hip, and that he must stay in his bed at all costs until the operation. The patient did not understand his predicament, and became even angrier because he was obviously held here against his will, and for some reason he had forgotten what had happened earlier this week. But in any case, one thing was sure (because he was not crazy): “He had NOT broken his hip, and he was leaving the hospital ASAP !!” And then he jumped off the bed. At first, some of the MDs laughed the whole issue away when they heard about what had happened, but soon after they understood that the patient really had jumped off the bed. And they all knew what happens to a broken hip when it hits the floor again. But this particular patient suffered from young on-set dementia, and he simply forgot what he was told, and then reacted as if he never heard the question. He never had a broken hip though. (Those crazy people.) SOURCES: the medical scans were taken from The Lancet.

Question: My son got sentenced to 15 years in prison. He is 20 years old. I don’t want him to feel depressed and give up. Is there anything I can do for him while he is in prison?
Answer: My grandfather was imprisoned in a concentration camp in the second World War, and he spent the better part of three years in that camp. He survived it in the end, but lost one lung and a most of his smiles by the time he got out. In the camp, he obviously was never visited by his loved ones, but in some way he virtually was — he received letters from his wife (the paternal grandmother whom I would never meet), and through these letters news about his two young boys (one of whom was my father). A second thing which saved his life — apart from the fact that my grandfather was an exceptionally determined man who proved to be almost impossible to break (his mind was impenetrable) — was the power of reading. In the camp, he learnt German very quickly, and he started to read German books whenever he could. And in some sense, he found a way to escape the horror of the camp through the power of words. And he made it. Your boy on the other hand is still very young — barely adult — and 15 years is a very long time (although we can hope his sentence be eventually reduced if that would be possible), but you can make a huge difference. You are one of very few people who can help him survive being caged for whatever he has done. Visit him as much as you can, write him letters, and keep contact through social media whenever this is possible. Send photographs of the things he misses (even if they are trivial), and talk to him every which way. And send him books — even when he hates to read. He’ll fight you in the beginning, but especially in confinement, reading is more useful than most anything else, and it is perhaps the only way to escape being on the inside. In between the letters, he will be as free as a bird. So encourage him to read your letters and to write letters himself, and convince him to start reading books, even when he thinks he hates them. Once he is in, he will discover the true magic of the way letters dance in books to form words, sentences and stories to take him far away from his prison cell, and make him forget about the cage he is in. Because that’s what letters can do, if combined well enough to form the magical bridge between the paper and sheer fantasy, as if a dancing dervish is whirling his mysterious ways into your head to let the bad stuff out — If even for a very short while. SOURCES: GIF found through Tenor.

Question: What is the rudest thing your OB/gyn has said to you (or you heard directed at someone else)?
Answer: A wedding party. He told us that he performed digital vaginal examinations on his female patients, every single time they visited him. And (upon some questioning from our side), he confirmed that he also performed the DVEs in teenagers, even — and as he admitted after much more wine: especially — on their very first consultation. It gives him some sort of control over their medical gynecological/urological life, and he is not ashamed about it whatsoever. He also knows that the patient would be ashamed to ever admit what he was doing down below. (He is the urologist, right ?) Question: What is your opinion on transgender people?
Answer: Transgender cases are always dramatic beyond anything we ever get to see or read in the media. It might appear controversial, but not a single patient who wants to have sex reassignment surgery (for example) is psychiatrically okay. Actually that should not be as awkward as it sounds: if for most of your life you have been convinced that your gender does not align with your body, the pure psychiatric weight your psychology is endowed with is nothing less than brutal. Every such patient has to through a number of psychiatric evaluations to see if the patient is really fit for what is to come medically, and if the patient will be able to handle his or her new body in the end. Because we should be very clear at one point: the new body of the patient ALWAYS is a mess, and it virtually ALWAYS really messes up the patient. A new penis or a new vagina never looks even remotely like a natural penis or vagina, and they function ever worse. My girlfriend is a urologist — and she was partially trained by a world famous pioneer in transgender surgery — and she has told me time and again that the physical state of these patients after surgery is depressingly bad, and what is even worse: their psychological state is often beyond help. Imagine that you have carried the burden of having been born as a man in a female’s body, and then, finally, after all the required stages of medical and psychiatric therapies, you are ready for the surgeries. You are all fired up, and ready for your new and true life to finally begin. And then you see and experience the total reconstruction mess down there. A penis made from skin flaps which feels like it is almost paralyzed. The patient cannot voluntarily erect the thing whatsoever — there’s a mechanical prosthesis needed for that. To add insult to injury, the top is tattooed so as to make it look like a glans penis. The sight is absolutely horrible, and the psychiatric impact on the patient is often devastating: the new life they so hoped for will never happen. I personally know one Indian patient who went through the whole process of becoming a physical woman, having been born as a physical man. He/she was so revolted by her new body that after less than five years, she decided that she was a man after all, and so he/she went through the entire “inverse” process to be reconstructed as a man again. Needless to say, a double sex change is beyond disaster, and it basically looked as if a bomb had exploded down there. And as in so many transgender patients who go for the total physical transformation, he/she/he understood that it would never be as hoped. And killed his broken self. These cases always come with great expectations — But they never come true. SOURCES: Dissection of the male genitalia, lower abdomen and thighs, with the arteries and blood vessels indicated in red. Colored lithograph by J. Roux, 1822. Wellcome Collection. Source: Wellcome Collection. (© public domain)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: At what stage in your life did you realize, "No, I can't do this any more" and walk out? Why?
Answer: “He does not fight for me anymore, and it’s not what I had expected. He simply gave me up — just like that.” This is what Jenny told Anne’s mother. Both of them were befriended Math teachers at the same high school, and Anne worked in my department. (I also knew Anne’s mother very well.) To me, the news came as a shock. For half a year I had tried to keep our marriage afloat, while she acted erratically, outright strange, and differently, and never did she even try to explain what was (really) going on. She kept me in total darkness during a period which seemed to last forever, until she broke the news that she had been seeing another guy. From January through April, she had even been living alone, in the empty house of friends, and only on weekends she was home. Only then, I was allowed to talk to her. Only then, I could try to keep us together. But as the weeks and weekends passed, she seemed to be drifting further away from me, whatever I said and whatever I tried. And now I was supposed to fight for her even more, after she had moved in with that creep (while I was in Germany) ? After all the lying, and the pain ? So no, I couldn’t do it anymore. The fight was over and done with. When Anne’s mother died from breast cancer a couple of years later, I saw the two of them one last time together — Jenny was sitting in between colleagues, crying tears over the demise of her friend. The remains of Anne’s cremated mother were lying in a casket, quiet and unmoved. The image of seeing Jenny again in this horrible context was mystifying, as if I was seeing a movie about my own future which didn’t feature me. To add insult to injury, Jenny already had breast cancer herself, but she would only find out two or three years later. By then, she would learn that the cancer had metastasized, and that she would never see her children grow up. And near the end of the Summer in 2022, her own cremated remains would lie in a casket in the very same room in the crematorium, only weeks after the oncologist had told her that all was lost. But she did not know that yet. SOURCES: photographs by Ramon Lehmann.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the meanest thing someone has said to you about your personal appearance?
Answer: I was born with webbed toes on both feet (very symmetrical defect, if I may say), and since I was a young boy both children (of all ages) and adults have mentioned them time and again as a curiosity. Yes, it looks as if my feet only have 4 toes (with 5 nails) each. Yes, I cannot pull them apart, and no, it does not better me in the slightest. Yes, I know you find them ugly (but do you really need to keep staring and pointing at them ?). Yes, I look like a duck, and maybe I am a duck (hahaha). Do I swim faster than other people because of my defect ? Hahaha, very nice one (and so original) ! My dad has them as well, by the way — it runs in the family, which is still a tad better than stupidity — but mine are much worse than my his, and mine are really ugly. Like in the left-hand side of the photograph, but (much) more crooked. So yeah, I have been exposed to more than some mockery over the past decades, but as of today — as a father and a son — I could not care less. And again: I do admit that my feet are really awkward and outright ugly, but I can also admit that sometimes clichés are very true — I actually do swim like a fish or duck, and I simply swim faster than the best of the rest. (Quack.) SOURCES: Google images.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's the most embarrassing thing you've ever said in a foreign language by accident?
Answer: My dad was in a scientific conference in Germany — which was attended by international guests and local German scientists, a number of whom were Jewish — but due to a very urgent meeting he needed to attend in The Netherlands, he had to leave ASAP. So after his plenary lecture, he apologized to the audience and the organizers for his sudden departure, in the kind of broken German people sometimes speak to non-English speaking Germans: “Ich muss zu einer dringender vergasung gein !” Which basically said that he had to leave the conference because he urgently needed to attend a gassing. (Sigh.) His announcement was ill-received, and only much later (in the plane) did he realize what he had said (or how it must have sounded to the older attendants). Obviously this was an innocent mistake, but humor often is in the eye of the beholder, and this type of error can sound conspicuous to some. Still, it wasn’t as bad as that one time in Israel in which, as an incoming foreigner (again to attend an international scientific conference), he answered the question “Is your name Joseph ?” (which it is) with: “Yes indeed. Joseph from Nazareth !” (My parents lived in a little town called Nazareth at the time.) It did not fare well. SOURCES: Google images.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What does finding out you have cancer feel like?
Answer: When this particular patient visited her general practitioner, she was as healthy as a fish (with the occasional back pain, but that was nothing out of the ordinary for someone who practiced a lot of sports). She just wanted him to examine a small lump in one of her armpits. That was the only thing. The GP is not worried about the lump, but he still orders some further tests to be on the safe side. And the tests reveal a new truth: the tiny lump is a message which has to be decoded very carefully. It is a cancerous lymph node, whose cancer cells originate from a primary breast cancer tumor. This is where the story becomes tedious. The woman is still young (and she has two young children), and it turns out that she had an aunt on her mother’s side who died at roughly the same age from aggressive breast cancer — she was one of the unhappy few with mutated BRCA genes (only 1/500 women have this kind of bad luck). And this drastically increased the patient’s chances to have these faulted genes as well. BRCA genes help to repair damaged DNA and prevent uncontrollable cell growth, and harmful BRCA mutation disrupt this repair process. The cancer control unit is basically disabled, so that cancer can have its way. The lymph nodes in the armpit can act as a hub for the cancer cells to travel through the lymphatic system to other, distant parts of the body, and the oncologist who is handling the patient knows this only too well. (The back pains are an extra worrisome detail which might not be a detail at all.) So the patient’s body is scanned in search for tumors, and the outcome will determine her destiny. If they find tumors at a distant site, she is doomed. The day comes when the oncologist will finally diagnose the patient. The scans have been analyzed. The information is available. When Jenny leaves his office, she is still crying. The cancer has metastasized to the bones, and that’s what caused her back pain. Most probably, the cancer took years to develop in her body before the first symptoms came, and since she never interpreted her strained back as a symptom, it got extra elbow room to ravage even more. In less than four years, the cancer empties her on the inside up to a point that even her eyes start to look glassy, because there is nothing in this life that she can see anymore. I was married to Jenny, and I was a witness of her demise from afar and in the end from up-close. Until she was no longer there. She just wanted her GP to examine a little lump in one of her armpits — That was the only thing. SOURCES: painting by Mikhail Vasilyevich Nesterov.
