Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's the most emotional phone call you've ever had?
Answer: My father called on the phone. At that very moment, we were having dinner at my mother-in-law’s house, and she was having a fit which even for her standards (she is bi-polar) was staggering. My girlfriend was shocked by her mother’s behavior, and so I answered the phone with my 6-month-old daughter in my arms. While my mother-in-law was calling me names for answering the phone (which I had to take because my father only phoned me when something was dead wrong), I heard what he was saying to me, almost in tears. (It was the first time I heard my dad’s voice break since I was born.) And although I really understood what he told me, the vicious attacks of my mother-in-law towards my girlfriend and me for no reason whatsoever — simply because I answered a phone call while she was suffering a mental breakdown — hardly got to me because I knew what my dad’s words meant. My aunt July had killed herself the night before. She had taken sleeping pills and left some heart-breaking letters, and died while her husband of fifty years was by her side, in bed. By the time he woke up, she was cold. It was her choice, but he had to take the hit either way, and it was very, very, very hard. And cold. In hindsight, it turned out that she had meticulously prepared the whole thing, and I still like to think that after she had laid out her letters (written through a Parkinsonism tremor which she couldn’t control anymore), she finally found some rest when she went asleep for the last time, although the fact that my uncle did not know will always haunt me. And while I tried to take this in — with my newborn baby in my arms — my mother-in-law was shouting, screaming, hitting, throwing, asking, demanding, cursing, hurting, ruining, raging, staging, violating, offending — and in the end, taking most of the letters that I so badly wanted to express my loss. But in the end, I looked in the eyes of my newborn — And found the syllables I needed. SOURCES: the painting is my own (and is called “Contemplation”).

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How would you feel if contraception fails and you have an unwanted pregnancy?
Answer: She has genital warts and does not know how they got there. Her mom does not understand the cause of the itch either. Lisa is 14 years old. Her mom is 30. They do not know how babies are conceived. The urologist immediately notices that Lisa’s boyfriend (Jerry) has genital warts on his tongue and lip. (This will be a long day.) The couple has been an item in every sense of the word since Lisa was twelve years old, and without any form of protection. Lisa’s mom was totally okay with it (and her dad never cared). Her mom never informed them about the many responsibilities that come with acting like an adult. Because she does not know how it biologically works herself, to be honest. These people have no idea what an STD is, nor how babies are made. Lisa thinks one of her friends got pregnant through French kissing, so she never kisses Jerry. Her mom agrees. (“You can’t be too careful.”) After some more questions, Jerry admits outright that he might have had some fun with one trump-et or two. While he was with Lisa. Both Lisa and her mom hardly react because they do not really care (he is a man after all). The urologist is almost desperate by now. How would you feel if contraception fails and you have an unwanted pregnancy ? In the case of these patients, one can only hope that Nature fails every which way even when no contraception is used whatsoever, because one thing is crystal clear — An unwanted pregnancy would introduce Lisa in an even more marginal world than she is already in. And the baby would be doomed. SOURCES: Dissection of the uterus in the latter stages of pregnancy, showing the foetus, placenta and umbilical cord. Colored line engraving by W. H. Lizars, ca. 1827. Wellcome collection.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, what's the saddest experience you've had with a patient?
Answer: The name of the disease sometimes reveals more than it is hiding, even when it’s very rare. The urologist had never seen it before in a patient — only in university text books and the like. The patient was 75 years old, and he was suffering from severe pain in the groin. His condition (increasing pain, a bad fever, and local discoloring) was deteriorating too fast. And the urologist knew immediately what it was — only one condition looked like this, and grew so quickly. FOURNIERS GANGRENE. An acute necrotic infection of the penis, scrotum or perineum (necrotizing fasciitis), which essentially is a flesh-eating disease with an extremely high mortality rate. Less than 1/50,000 males (and some females) get it, and most of them eventually die from it.[1] The man was basically rotting at an exceptionally fast rate. The urologist tried to save the old patient’s life by removing as much rotted tissue as possible from the infected area, including the man’s entire penis and scrotum, but the gangrene had already grown beyond those borders, and kept spreading at a mind-blowing speed, obliterating all tissue it passed through until soon there would be nothing left to obliterate. When the man awoke, the urologist — almost in tears — explained that he only had a couple of hours left (at best), and that he needed to say goodbye to his loved ones, now that he still could. The man gave her a faint smile, and whispered: “Thank you so much, doctor. I am completely ready to go, and I am so glad the agony will be over soon.” There was no time left to say goodbye to his loved ones though. SOURCES: Dissections of the male genitalia and upper thighs: four figures, with the arteries and blood vessels indicated in red. Colored lithograph by J. Roux, 1822. Wellcome Collection. (© public domain)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's your scariest, most disturbing true story?
Answer: A friend of ours noticed one early morning that one of the fingers of her baby boy was badly swollen. After closer inspection, it turned out that some of her hair was wrapped around the little finger. It’s called a “hair tourniquet” — human hair (or some other type of thread) tied around a toe, a finger or male genital. Hair tourniquets often occur in very young children during the night, and are actually not uncommon. Usually things turn out all right, but as the term “tourniquet” clearly suggests, the affected digit cannot receive enough blood, nor can blood be drained through the veins. In (very) rare cases the digit even has to be amputated. In the case of our friend — who was a nurse, of all people — her baby boy’s little finger top was so badly swollen and discolored that she immediately tried to free the finger (as any mother or father would do). She succeeded in unwrapping it, but an instant later her baby boy started to convulse, and went into cardiac arrest. When the paramedics arrived, there was nothing they could do for the boy. Most probably a blood clot from the finger top was released into his little body when the hair tourniquet was removed, and this caused severe thrombosis in the end. (Fatal sepsis caused by gangrene in his little finger could have been another, less likely explanation.) The only thing our friend wanted to do was to unwrap the finger, and see her little baby boy smile again after an uneasy night. But that smile was gone forever. SOURCES: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What male/female double standard do you hate the most?
Answer: Jamie Lee Curtis was technically born as a male, but she was born with a condition called Testicular Feminization Syndrome. This is where the double standard begins. Curtis made her camera debut as an eight-week-old baby in a newspaper article published in Daily World (January 18, 1959 edition), where she was announced to be a boy. (And so it began.) TFS patients have internal, undescended testicles and no uterus, fallopian tubes, or ovaries, but externally the labia, vagina, and clitoris all develop. Typically, the labia and clitoris are indistinguishable from those of a normal (46, XX) female, but the vagina is shorter than usual or sometimes absent. (It’s possibly a combination of the latter symptoms that caused her parents (and their medical staff) to think she was a boy at first (which she was). Or the medical staff already knew more.) Other components such as breast development and pelvic shape are as in normal females, but armpit and pubic hair are markedly decreased or absent, and last but not least: patients with TFS cannot have children. (For your information: Jamie Lee Curtis does not have children on her own — both of her kids are adopted.) And here is where the confusion sets in: despite her congenital disorder, Jamie Lee Curtis looks and always has looked like an extremely handsome woman. But if someone dares to mention that she was born as a man, the world is on fire. (Please explain.) SOURCES: Wikipedia, Daily World, and Google images.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do you think it is disturbing in many cases for a ‘live and kicking’ baby to be killed via abortion at 22 weeks plus gestation?
Answer: We have good friends whose first child was born with a congenital condition which makes the boy almost blind, partly deaf, mentally so retarded that he will never be older than two or three, severely autistic, and he suffers from various other physical defects which make him a very sick child — every minute of the day. Every second. His parents do not know what to do. Most of the time they are worried about their baby, because every single waking moment is a moment of peril for him. He often falls and gets injured (because his impaired mind cannot control his nine-year-old body), he often gets angry and aggressive (because no one understands what he wants, including himself), he often puts dangerous things such as glass shards, stones or needles in his mouth (because that’s what he wants to do). The boy is nine years old today and his life is pure torture. Most of his frustrations are very simple and related to food, and when he gets angry he starts hitting his head — which always is in a protective helmet — against a table or a brick wall, and starts screaming nonsense. His face, arms, hands and most of his body are always covered with lesions, and his constant drooling can be pretty confronting at a dinner table. (Did I mention he was almost blind and dead ?) Although his parents love him with all their heart, they have said time and again that this boy should not have been born — that his every single day is a day of pain and frustration, locked up in a body and mind that were never made to function at all. It’s his constant depression and suffering that make them say that. It’s their dedicated love. Do you think it is disturbing in many cases for a ‘live and kicking’ baby to be killed via abortion at 22 weeks plus gestation ? Live and kicking babies are not killed through abortion at 22 weeks and later. In such cases, either a mother’s life is at stake (and acting upon it is usually the doctors’ call), or a pregnancy is terminated because due to a severe congenital defect or an accident the foetus has no chance to a decent and dignified life whatsoever. In such cases the baby is not killed at all — It is saved. SOURCES: unbekannter Maler, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are some great examples of coincidence?
Answer: My favorite literary work of all time is a book called Turkish Delight — it’s actually an adaptation of a Dutch work called Turks Fruit (by author Jan Wolkers). It tells the story of a man called Eric, who is married to a young woman called Olga. They have an (s)exceptionally passionate relationship, but in the course of their marriage, Olga’s mother — who thinks Olga should marry a rich man, and not a poor sculptor like Eric — slowly mentally poisons her daughter, and at some point introduces Olga to a rich business acquaintance. Olga eventually takes the bait, and starts a relationship with the rich guy. When Eric finds out, it is too late to save their marriage (as Olga is completely brain-washed by her mother), and Eric loses the love of his life through a painful divorce. Afterwards he completely loses himself in the flesh of other women, but he never succeeds in finding the answer he seeks. As the years pass, Eric meets Olga a couple of times, until he finds out she is dying from ovary cancer which has metastasized to her brain. Not long before she horribly dies still very young, he sees her one last time. One remarkable fact about the story is that most of it literally happened to Jan Wolkers. The book is actually an autobiographic approach to his failed first marriage, his passion for his first wife and the extremely painful demise of their relationship. Almost everything is true, except for one thing: Anne-Marie (on whom Olga is based) did not die young from cancer — that was one of his good friends (and I guess he took poetic revenge on Anne-Marie by staging her ending). I saw the R-rated movie based on the book as a nine-year-old kid (in the house of friends of my parents during a dinner party), long before I read the book, and I never forgot it. Later, I must have read the book — which is one of best romantic novels of all time — more than I want to admit, and each and every time, it’s as heart-breaking as the first time. It’s good that the story is not real (it would be too devastating). Many years later, I went through my own painful divorce after my then-wife started a relationship with a better man. After the marriage — which showed many similarities with Eric/Jan’s marriage — I lost myself in the flesh of many others (but the answers never came). Then my story deviated from Turkish Delight because I realized that my former wife was not the love of my life at all — she had ruined that image with a sledge hammer. And so life continued its funny ways, but I never stopped reading the book. And then a weird coincidence happened: I found out that my former wife had metastasized breast cancer, and was actually dying, after I accidentally had met her and could see her fading away into the shadows without needing words. My favorite book suddenly became the true story of my life. (And then she horribly died.) SOURCES: painting by Gustav Klimt.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Has a doctor ever made a mistake while treating you? What happened?
Answer: Not me, but a very recent new patient in my girlfriend’s urology ward. He claimed that his former urologist had noticed some deformations in one of his testicles on an MRI — the patient had contacted the urologist because he had felt some painful irregularities himself — but instead of acting upon it, the urologist had simply proposed to meet again in 6 months, “to see how things evolved.” The patient became extremely worried in the following months — so worried that he decided to go for a second opinion. When one of the new urologists opened him up, he found a cancerous tumor mass in the testicle, and the testicle had to be removed on the spot (big mistake of the former urologist). But that wasn’t the end of it. On new MRIs, suspicious irregularities were also noticed in the other testicle, so in the second movement of this fallacious symphony, his second new urologist again opened him up, only to discover that there was a cancerous tumor too, so that the second testicle also had to go. (VERY big mistake of the former urologist.) If there was any good news to this case, it must have been that the cancer hadn’t spread yet (which it could have, taken the procrastination of the evil urologist). And secondly: the patient already had children. SOURCES: Dissections of the male genitals, upper thighs and pelvic region: two figures, with the arteries, blood vessels and veins indicated in red and blue. Colored lithograph by J. Roux, 1822. Wellcome Collection. Public Domain Mark. Source: Wellcome Collection.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Doctors and nurses, has a patient ever diagnosed you and been correct?
Answer: The patient enters the consultation room with her mom. She has genital warts and does not know how they got there. Her mom is also clueless about the cause of the itch. Lisa is 14 years old. Her mom is 30. Lisa’s boyfriend is also part of the gang, and the urologist immediately notices that he has genital warts as well. On his tongue and lips, that is. The urologist knows that this will be a long, long day. Lisa and her boyfriend have been sleeping together since Lisa was twelve years old, and without any form of protection. Her mom has no problem with this whatsoever — in fact, she humorously adds that she was only a little bit older when she had her first “real” boyfriend. (As the urologist can count, she is not really surprised.) They have no idea what STDs are, nor what protection is good for. When the urologist asks Lisa some standard questions, it turns out that Lisa does not know how babies are made (Lisa: “I know you can get pregnant if you swallow some semen, because my best friend Mary-Beth became pregnant when she did just that. And she was still a virgin.”) Then, after some specific questions, Jerry admits outright that he might have had some fun with some women of ill repute — unprotected, of course, since Jerry does not know what STDs are, and protection ruins all the fun. While he was with Lisa, by the way. And both Lisa and especially her mom do not really mind because “boys will be boys, and Jerry is a man.” The urologist suddenly blurts out that Jerry is NOT a man, that it’s totally irresponsible for kids to sleep together if they do not know how these things work, and what the consequences are, that some STDs are really dangerous, and that this kind of behavior could lead to Lisa getting pregnant while she is just a child. Lisa’s mom looks at the urologist, and says: “Well, if that is your opinion, then maybe YOU are the one with a problem, and YOU should be a better mother than me, if that’s that what you’re saying. Maybe YOU should be the one who talks to a professional because I am a bad mother, if that’s what you are saying. Maybe YOU should help Lisa, if I am so bad, if that’s what you are saying.” And for once, the patient of ill repute might be right. SOURCES: Dissection of the uterus in the latter stages of pregnancy, showing the foetus, placenta and umbilical cord. Colored line engraving by W. H. Lizars, ca. 1827. Wellcome collection.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Who has the most surprising net worth?
Answer: The most improbably candidate would be American singer Dave Matthews. Matthews (who is of South-African descent) and his band are virtually unknown outside of the US — I literally personally do not know anyone in Europe who knows this guy — but in the US, he is an absolute superstar:[1] During the period from 2000 to 2010, his band sold more tickets and earned more money than any other act in North America. Furthermore, the band's 2012 album Away from the World made The Dave Matthews Band (DMB) the only group to have six consecutive studio albums debut at number one on the Billboard charts, and this record was extended even further with the 2018 release of Come Tomorrow. His net worth ? A staggering $300 million dollars.[2] The DMB is a jam band with an almost unmatched live reputation, having released 85 live albums as of today (which sell really good), most of them under DMB’s own Bama Rags label.[3] I happened to see them a couple of months ago, and they blew us away. Matthews also owns ATO Records (which is part of his BMG label). He loves to play and record and does it all the time, but he is also the guy in control — the musical brain who gets the dough in the end. You wouldn’t give it to him — he is nice, idealistic, a bit autistic and weird, introvert, likes to help people and hates people who hate people (hopefully not including himself) — but this man has it all. And he easily beats most Hollywood actors, producers and directors, and singer/songwriters at the heart of their very own game — Olympic Dollar Counting (Paris, 2024). SOURCES: the footnoted sites. For the photograph: Rick Wood/Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Can you sleep peacefully knowing there is a cockroach lurking somewhere in the bedroom and which you have not been able to chase out?
Answer: More than a decade ago, I was doing a road trip in the US with an ex-girlfriend, and we passed through one of these typical tiny villages in the West, which consists of a gas station, a saloon, one motel and a couple of houses centered around one main street. The motel host was a very peculiar man, with a very peculiar sense of humor. Upon checking in, he sold us some dinosaur dung (the place was near Dinosaur National Monument), and then warned us that the hotel had been recently infested by cockroaches, so that if we heard mysterious sounds in our room at night, or felt that the carpet was moving, it was cockroaches all the way (“hahahahahahahahaha”). We thought he was joking. He was not. We first grabbed a bite in the saloon, and then returned for some well-deserved night rest. Before turning out the light, I had seen a huge cockroach crawl away in one of the curtains, but I did not mention that to my ex-girlfriend (as she would go berserk). (I had also stepped on a dead one before we went to the saloon. Anyways.) But then the sounds came. Whispers of a thrill which clearly indicated that some large insects were running around in the room, hissing. My ex-girlfriend turned on the light again, and the she noticed what was going on while uttering some of the grizzliest screeches I had ever heard. They were hissing in the curtains, on the carpet floor, on the bed, in our clothes on the ground — some were even sitting on the ceiling, waiting to fall on our heads. We were so tired though that we soon fell asleep, surrounded by hoards of cockroaches, as if we had ended up in Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom. The awful sounds of insects oozing out of nowhere, waiting to enter the bed and swim in your hair, our find an ear, an open mouth or some other cavity to enter. (And don’t you think they won’t.) In my dreams-turned-into-nightmares, the motel host was chasing us on a giant cockroach while throwing petrified dinosaur dung at our heads, and sounding his barbaric yawp over the rooftops of the world. (“Hahahahahahahahahahahahahahaha !”) Can you sleep peacefully knowing there is a cockroach lurking somewhere in the bedroom and which you have not been able to chase out ? Sure you can, my friend. If you sleep with your mouth closed. SOURCES: photograph by Mick Ryan. It is not a cockroach, but a Summer cicada — I am in Hangzhou, China at the moment, and these monsters (which have the size of a child’s hand) are everywhere.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why do European people stop travelling to the USA?
Answer: My parents are in Las Vegas and my dad starts to feel really sick. Since that in itself is very awkward, my parents decide to go to a hospital, and about an hour later, they enter the ER. Upon entrance, my dad is ordered to sit in a wheelchair. (He has no idea why.) Then the waiting begins — minut after minute, hour after hour. In between other people who are also sitting in wheelchairs. Every single one of them is sitting there for ages. At some point, a trainee approaches my father and asks him some standard questions. And then the trainee is gone again. Two hours later, a proper doctor enters the waiting room, and listens to my father’s heart with a stethoscope. Without lifting my father’s shirt. He asks one or two further questions, says he will prescribe some medication, and then he is gone again. After two whole minutes. My parents are notified that they can leave the hospital, upon paying the bill of a sum North of $1,000. The are absolutely baffled — more than a thousand dollars for five questions and an over-the-shirt stethoscope. My dad is obliged to leave the hospital in a wheelchair, by the way (he has no idea why). It sums up a major part of the US in a nutshell: the wheelchair is not about my father, nor about any other patient. It’s about insurance companies who could sue the hospital if my father would fall when entering or leaving the hospital. The doctor asks a fortune for next-to-no medical service (nor any interest from his side) — the wheelchair is much more important. For my parents it’s not a problem: they can afford to be very well insured, but if you are not, you can forget about the hospital. About the hypocritical stethoscope exam for 1K a piece. Without the money, you don’t exist. It’s the US in a nutshell. And it’s NOT the land of the free. No citizen of the free world is as caged as the American — he is the only one who does not see it, though, because he so believes in the twilight’s last gleaming (broad stripes and bright stars through the perilous fight). Even with a bad case of late stage cancer, you can forget about surgery, radiotherapy or chemo if you don’t have the money to pay for your existence — You are ruined, every which way. “O! say can you see by the dawn's early light, ⁠What so proudly we hailed at the twilight's last gleaming, Whose broad stripes and bright stars through the perilous fight, ⁠O'er the ramparts we watch'd, were so gallantly streaming ?” SOURCES: Image taken from Lincoln (by Daniel Day-Lewis / Steven Spielberg).

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What kind of dares have you been asked to do?
Answer: We were eleven years old, and our school had acquired a brand new anatomy model. And Nelly, the most beautiful girl in our class, had dared us to dismantle the doll. On the most mythical weekend of the year for our primary school — Mussel Weekend ! — Dicky and myself decided to hit, and hit hard. On Mussel Weekend, the school cook, teachers and volunteering parents prepared mussel dishes on Friday and Saturday to support the school. Afterwards, parents could have wine, beer and what have you in the improvised school bar, while their children were having a ball on the school’s playgrounds. These were easily the best evenings (and nights) of the entire school year. So on Friday (the first day of Mussel Weekend), Dicky and myself had slightly opened two windows in our sixth grade classroom (but so that they appeared to be closed), and on the same evening, we returned to the classroom after dinner when our parents were ordering drinks in the school bar. It was around midnight when we broke into our classroom, and subsequently we abducted the anatomy model to the floor, so that nobody could see us. And we dismantled it completely, until it lay down on the floor without its major organs, crying for help in silence while it was bleeding to death without every having blood. When we started to reconstruct it — nervously, because the school janitor was doing his rounds — we discovered that it was much harder than we thought, and that if one piece of the organ puzzle was wrongly placed, the rest didn’t work either. It took us at least two hours to finish the puzzle (in almost total darkness, only helped by the moonlight), but we made it in the end. And on Monday, we handed Nelly a kidney to show her that we had succeeded our quest, so that it was her turn now to keep her side of the bargain. She succeeded with grace. SOURCES: Nyam Center for History (through Google images).

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Doctors: Have you ever diagnosed another doctor who was not aware of their problem?
Answer: The worst excuse for a doctor in the entire hospital (but a very good internist) insisted on consulting my girlfriend (who is a urologist) for “an urgent matter.” He was the kind of man who thinks that his every personal concern was an urgent matter, but who did not have the least bit of problem with letting his cancerous patients wait for a very long time for the next bit of news about their condition. (He was a monster. Was.) In the last couple of weeks, he had experienced some peeing problems, and had even seen some blood in the toilet bowl, and since he was the hypothetical patient now, he needed urgent advice on what was going on. So he was scheduled for a consultation and various physical tests, but the eventual diagnosis was not what he had expected. Because he had expected your typical enlarged prostate — he knew so much about urology that this had to be the case — while the diagnosis sentenced him to a secondary stage prostate cancer of a very aggressive type which needed urgent handling. That is to say: the prostate — all of it — had to go as fast as possible if he wanted a decent chance to be alive in 10 years. But here was the problem: Dr. Redding was a ladies’ man (he had a wife and various nurses on the side), and he knew all too well what could happen to his libido and erectile performance if the prostate would radically go. (And let’s not even talk about the urinal incontinence thing.) So he refused. And behind the back of my girlfriend, he consulted not one, but several other urologists to shop for different therapies (doctors are often the worst patients of them all, and Redding was not an exception to the rule). When he finally came back, his condition had worsened and the cancer had started to spread. And the game changed altogether. The prostate was removed and Dr. Redding suffered from all the possible side effects he initially planned to evade in the first place, but this time hiding under a feeble umbrella that was supposed to protect him from the cancer that had almost reached distant organs in his body — And about to turn his diagnosis into a sentence. SOURCES: Wikimedia commons (Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons).

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are the types of people that you should always avoid?
Answer: My friend Stan — an American mathematician who looks like Santa and smells like Santa too — wanted to introduce his new wife to us. It was the third time around and he was pretty nervous, because “Angela could be a bit tense from time to time.” That must have been the understatement of the century. It started before we even ordered, when Stan mentioned that he really loved the Neil Diamond song which was playing in the restaurant. Angela immediately stopped saying whatever she was saying, and said bluntly and really loud (apparently everyone around had to hear this): “That’s not Neil Diamond, Stan — it’s ELVIS. How can you even mix up Neil Diamond and Elvis Presley ? (To us:) Stan is so tone deaf, it’s a miracle he even heard the song. Who would mix up Neil Diamond and ELVIS ?” After some hesitation, I told Angela that Stan was actually right. Stan shivered because he knew what was coming. He tried to change the subject, but Angela stopped engaging in the conversation altogether. Instead, she started loudly talking to herself, saying “that she was 100% sure that this was Elvis, that this DEFINITELY was NOT a Neil Diamond song, etc., etc., etc.” Then, she took her cell phone and started browsing to prove her point. After two minutes or so of total surprise, further browsing, frustration (“how is this even possible ?”) and so on, she put away her cell phone. Went to the restrooms. Returned, and acted as if nothing had happened (although she was obviously pissed at Stan). Because Stan had been right all along. This little episode characterized the evening, and every other time we met Angela: she contradicted virtually every single opinion Stan (or we, for that matter) had, and then refused to give in when it turned out — after a cell phone search of her own to prove her point — that we were right. And then she was angry. Other typical things which passed: blatant lying. One time Angela was praising herself because she had quit smoking cigarettes after forty years on the chain — two packages a day, what do you say ? — she was such a strong person ! (I heard Stan silently murmur: “Two packages a day ? — you always claimed you did not smoke more than ten cigarettes on every given day.”) Later in the evening I needed to go to the restrooms, and when I came back, I saw Angela (“who had to go too”) buying cigarettes in the hotel lobby. She did not see me, and proceeded with her self-praise as soon as she was back. What are the types of people that you should always avoid ? The Angelas among us, who thrive on contradiction and self-praise, and who are allergic to the (real) truth. Whatever they do, whatever they say, they will never admit that they are wrong, and they will never give in. In the end there is only one thing one can do — Run, Stanley, run. SOURCES: image found through Rolling Stone.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How common is it for families to stop visiting a relative with Alzheimer’s in a care home, once they’ve stopped recognising them?
Answer: Richard III was once a distinguished professor and one of the best friends of my parents, and for a while, he dreamed of sailing the seven seas (so to speak) once he retired. He and his wife had made some spectacular trips on the fisher boat of a friend, and one never knows what dreams may come. But the eventual dream was different. For Richard III started to forget things — small things at first — but small things grew into more rigorous and recurring things, until it became kind of clear that something was going on upstairs. And the once so formidable professor suddenly avoided public appearances, because his self control had vanished, his mind stopped being what it was supposed to be, and his speech had become slurry. He was afraid now, and that was a first. It took more than a decade for his wife to dare saying the word “Alzheimer’s” aloud, because dementia was considered a humiliation for “a man of his stature.” And over that decade, Richard III (and his wife Anne) worked his way through the many phases Alzheimer forces a victim and its family to go through. And then there are the awkward moments. My parents still have dinner every two months with Richard III and Anne — especially for Anne, because everyone (including her kids) basically stopped coming around. Usually Richard III is the forgetful-60-second-diaper-plant he is today, but sometimes he revives. One day (only a couple of months ago), he wakes up in the restaurant from plant hood, and starts dancing with a random (and much younger) woman, and he can’t stop. He sings and dances, kisses her almost violently on the cheeks, and puts his hand in her undies. He is the nightmare of the fisherman’s wife, and the 60-second-man can’t stop. And now he has entered a new stage. A stage in which he cries all the time, because every single word or thought makes him melancholic and sad. About his dear mom, the old days, his childhood friends, his children who stopped seeing him (“that poor man”), about Elvis Presley, and the dream of the seven seas. And yes, it is very common that family and friends stop seeing Alzheimer’s patients in a far stage, but somehow these patients remember (sometimes) what they should forget. The loneliness, the state of absolute despair, the betrayal of the children — The fisherman’s blues. SOURCES: The Dream of the Fisherman’s Wife. Katsushika Hokusai, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. (© public domain)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What went through your head when the doctor said there was nothing more they can do?
Answer: When she was diagnosed with breast cancer, it had already spread to nearby lymph nodes, but her OB/GYN had said that there was no reason to panic. First, some medical imaging had to be performed to see if the cancer hadn’t spread. (Part of the normal routine.) The cancer diagnosis already had been quite a shock, but as a mom of two young children, my former friend Nadine wouldn’t let her head down. (Still, she had seen something in the eyes of her OB/GYN when she told him that her aunt had died young from breast cancer, but she couldn’t pin it down.) Her constant back pain didn’t make life much easier. “Part of a life filled with competitive sports,” — at least, that was what her general practitioner had said (before prescribing paracetamol). When she had to meet again with the OB/GYN to speak about the results of the MRIs, she was nervous, but she had never expected what came next. Black dots of various sizes, scattered over the medical images — she didn’t understand. And when the OB/GYN said they were metastasized tumors, spread to her bones, the world disappeared under her feet. (The part of a life filled with sports. Paracetamol.) In the few years that passed, she tried to live with a life without living, trying every possible therapy that might slow down the monster inside. My former friend Nadine had four or five years left. Then, in June a new update came which would paint the very last part of an unfinished portrait. She had two months left — at most. She would not make it till her next birthday. She would not see her youngest boy go to elementary school. She would not see her boys grow up. She would stop seeing altogether. And in the weeks that followed, her life seemed to crumble into little pieces — as if she had become a puzzle of which most pieces were already gone. And whatever she tried to hold on to the last pieces, that woman who I used to know slowly obliterated until a few final pieces were left. And while the final gloom was setting in to fetch the final pieces, she could only feel the ground getting colder in deep despair with the emptiest eyes in the world. As if they had never seen a thing. SOURCES: Volume Rendering of a contrast enhanced abdominal CT scan. Rendering done with a Carestream workstation. (Through Google images.)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: If someone cured an incurable disease, would they be made a doctor?
Answer: The urologist had diagnosed his brother with a bad case of prostate cancer, and she had threatened to partially remove the prostate, possibly making his brother impotent, or incontinent. And that would never happen. His brother was in his early twenties, you know. And never mind, Matata was a doctor himself — he could cure through home-made herbal preparations, and that’s exactly how he would cure his brother. So he talked to his younger brother, again and again, and although his brother was hesitant because he really trusted his urologist (who was female, if you believe it), Matata could convince his brother in the end to stop with all the proposed classical Western therapies, and to start with the herbal approach. But after a while, his brother’s symptoms worsened, and he went to the urologist again despite Matata’s warnings. The urologist claimed that the prostate tumor had considerably grown — which Matata did not believe — and that his brother needed an urgent radical prostatectomy (which would ruin his life altogether). So Matata convinced his brother again to not listen to this woman, and his brother listened. But then his brother got even more sick and was in so much pain, and died in the worst agony in less than a year’s time as a living skeleton, screaming and begging for his life, and Matata simply could not understand what happened because he had done everything just right — Except for listening to a real doctor. SOURCES: GIF found through GIFer.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What would happen if a patient refused intimate treatment/ care from nursing staff? How would that be documented and how would that patient be viewed?
Answer: This was a middle-aged patient who had entered the Emergency Room with a broken hip, in a lot of pain. He needed to rest and stay still before he would have an operation, and the orthopedist warned the nurses that this guy might be a bit stubborn, and had to be taken care of cautiously. Within the first hour of waiting, the patient became outraged that he was in a hospital, and he demanded to leave the hospital, because “there was NOTHING wrong with him !” The nurses reminded him that he had broken his hip, and that he must stay in bed until surgery — which he vehemently denied. He then screamed that he was leaving the hospital ASAP, and jumped off the hospital bed (and screamed like he had never screamed before). What would happen if a patient refused intimate treatment / care from nursing staff ? How would that be documented and how would that patient be viewed ? The patient’s hip was splintered, and he would need many surgeries in the future to walk (fairly) well again. His case was especially shocking and unpredictable, since next-to-no patient would jump off the bed with a broken hip ? On the other hand — this patient had young-onset dementia, of course. SOURCES: X-ray of the pelvis of an 86 year old male patient with a fractured hip. Image by Du Cane Medical Imaging. (Through Google Images.)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What surgery should you always decline?
Answer: My girlfriend is a urologist and she has said it time and again that she would never want a hysterectomy and certainly not a more complex gynecological operation like a Wertheim-Meigs procedure. Performed by an OB/GYN, that is. In a Wertheim-Meigs operation, the surgeon has to do a radical hysterectomy (total removal of the uterus and the ligaments that hold it in place), remove pelvic lymph nodes and also the upper part of the vagina, all in the context of cervical cancer. It requires surgical skill, and that is exactly what most OB/GYN totally lack. The vast number of surgeries performed on female patients that have been messed up by OB/GYNs is absolutely staggering. It is a well-known hospital secret among OR nurses and surgeons how OB/GYN often butcher their patients, and how general surgeons and urologist subsequently are summoned to save the day. The patients never are informed afterwards by the OB/GYN (I call it the “Hospital Hush”). Ruptured bladders, severed ureters, punctured uteri — they are all part of the ever growing list of messed-up operations by your average OB/GYN. So think twice if your OB/GYN proposes to perform a complex procedure such as a Wertheim-Meigs on your body. His surgical skills might determine how the cancer will fare in the end. And it might fare really well. SOURCES: Graves, William Phillips, 1870-1933, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How do I live alone with no love, friends, or family?
Answer: Four years ago, I noticed a hunchbacked figure standing in my front yard, and noticed that she seemed to be pulling weeds. And then she was gone again. I had seen her before — she lived a couple of houses down the road — standing alone in the middle of the road, as if she was waiting for someone who wasn’t there. The woman reappeared on an irregular basis, always pulling weeds, slowly and decidedly, but also absently. Sometimes, I heard her singing. Sometimes, she was talking to herself (or to the same someone who wasn’t there). One day, we approached the old lady to have a chat, and she she told us that she was a widow who lived all alone for almost ten years, and in total lack of friends and family (except for a son who only surfaced when he needed money), she had decided to pull some weeds. And she had chosen our front yard. She asked us if it was okay that she turned up once in a while to pull some weeds, and we happily embraced the idea. And so it began — a curious front yard relationship which consisted of (watching) pulling weeds, (listening to) old forgotten songs, waving hallo to each other with a smile, occasional short chats, and more pulling weeds. It lasted for a couple of years. One day, the weeds kept on growing and the old songs stopped being sung, and in front of an old house further down the road, a TO SELL sign had appeared. In between the high grass, long thistles and ragwort in our front yard, you could still find some musical notes if you had some luck. Until they were finally gone. And still, we could not suppress a smile when we realized that we would never see her again — our old front yard woman of ragwort and thistles. She had been all alone with no friends and family for almost ten years. But then she started pulling weeds. SOURCES: drawing by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are you banned from? Why?
Answer: For some reason unknown to me, I was explicitly asked from beyond the grave to not attend the funeral of my ex-wife. And for some even stranger reason, a family member demanded me to go as well. (What would you do ?) I never planned to go — that much is true. Our divorce was painful, unscheduled, surprising — did I mention painful ? — and then it ended with a bang. And it was like a decade ago. (But still.) But then she died, and people started to have opinions. Opinions about the past — which was kind of surprising since the very same people often did not even produce the tiniest piece of the puzzle I tried to fabricate during my quest to survive this absolute detail in the realm of human poetry — knowing all too well I was not even worthy of even one verse. The people who never showed up suddenly showed up. With an opinion. And with many verses. And yes, I was completely banned. And a family member refused to talk to me anymore because I did not attend the cremation (while I was not allowed). Banned for life. . Sometimes life is not about more — It’s about so much less. SOURCES: painting by Stephen Early.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the most shocking thing you’ve seen an adult do to a child in public?
Answer: I was in Verbania, Italy for a conference and one evening, we were enjoying one of these absolutely mouth-watering lunches which made every mere mortal swoon, and thinking “Only in Italy.” An American family was sitting nearby our table, and even without talking they could never blind in into the Italian context. The mother was morbidly obese (the American way), the father was pretty average, and they had one teenage daughter who looked more like her father than her mother. And that’s what bothered the mother. At some point, the daughter’d had enough to eat, so she shoved her plate aside and was happy with that. And the mother got really, really angry. “So you had ENOUGH, have you ? You think you are BETTER than me, ha ? Don’t want to be FAT like your mom, and you think you are BETTER, ha ? ASHAMED for me, ha ? You will live a BETTER life than me, ha ?” And then the most astonishing thing happened: the mother started to force-feed her daughter two other plates, while the girl was almost crying, and the dad did not know what to do. Looked the other way (but clearly in denying pain). We tried to intervene, but we immediately faced an American fat-shaming fire wall which could bounce back to the girl in the end — it was really very sad, and extremely painful. This was a mother who knew only too well that she was morbidly obese, that she was the one with a huge (pun intended) problem, and instead of looking into the mirror, she projected her every frustration on her innocent teenage daughter — And made her eat, eat, eat. SOURCES: Google images.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What things were discovered accidentally?
Answer: My mother-in-law is a retired radiologist, and one time she slipped while taken medical images of a patient’s broken collarbone. Instead of throwing the images away, she had an accidental peek at them, and discovered that the patient had lung cancer. Of course, this is not a bug which has become a feature — although it certainly wouldn’t hurt for radiologists to study images in their entirety, instead of only looking at the parts ordered by the protocol. Many cancerous tumors (and other “malformations”) have been missed by radiologists because they did not look at the bigger picture. (Anyways.) Still, an “accidental slip” actually sometimes is the way how big discoveries are made. Take X-rays. Wilhelm Röntgen was not looking at all for a system to scan the insides of a human being — rather, he discovered them (in 1895) while testing whether cathode rays could pass through glass:[1] His cathode tube was covered in heavy black paper, so he was surprised when an incandescent green light nevertheless escaped and projected onto a nearby fluorescent screen. Through experimentation, he found that the mysterious light would pass through most substances but leave shadows of solid objects. Röntgen quickly discovered that X-rays would pass through human tissue too, rendering the bones and tissue beneath visible. Within a year, doctors in Europe and the US were using X-rays to locate gun shots, bone fractures, kidney stones and swallowed objects — Röntgen’s accidental discovery changed the course of medical history in no time, and it’s still going strong as of today. We can even see USB-cables turning up in someone’s bladder. (Figure it out.) SOURCES: the footnoted site. The medical image was taken from Teen gets USB cable stuck in penis in backfired attempt to measure length.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the coolest line in history?
Answer: “Every damn thing you do in this life, you have to pay for.” It was uttered right before the most legendary French singer of all time died at the age of 47. Her body was empty, her life deflated. Already at the age of 14, she joined her father in his acrobatic street performances, and started to sing in public. For Édith had an exceptional voice which in the course of her life, was sculptured by the very experiences she had to live through. As a 17-year-old, Édith gave birth to her daughter Marcelle in 1933, but she found it very difficult to take care for Marcelle. Édith appeared to lack maternal instinct and chose to perform on the streets while the little girl was all alone. Marcelle died not much later of meningitis at the age of 2.[1] At the age of 20, Édith got her nickname “little sparrow” (in Paris slang: “La Môme Piaf”), due to her exceptionally short stature (at 4 ft 8 / 142 cm). She quickly became the most popular French singer of all time (“Non, Je ne regrette rien”; “Milord”; “La Vie en Rose” — need I say more ?). But her life was overshadowed by pain. Fourteen years after her daughter had died, in 1949, the love of her life — the married boxer Marcel Cerdan — died in a plane crash while flying to New York City to meet her. And in 1951, she was seriously injured in a car crash along with French singer Charles Aznavour, breaking one arm and two ribs — later this appeared to be one further reason for her morphine and alcohol addictions (although her love for alcohol had been born much earlier).[2] After many years of alcohol and drug abuse, she ended up with a dying liver, in a dying body. On October 10, 1963, the little sparrow finally passed away — she was only 47. Here last words were:[3] “Every damn thing you do in this life, you have to pay for.” And I’ll second that wholeheartedly. SOURCES: the footnoted site. For the image: Studio Harcourt, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is an experience you had with a patient you'll never forget?
Answer: A 14-year-old patient enters the consultation room with her 30-year-old mom. (Usually, this is a bad start.) She has genital warts down there, and has no clue as to how they got there (says her mom). Her boyfriend Jerry is also present. (He is fifteen.) The urologist sees right away that Jerry has genital warts as well. On his tongue, and lips. Lisa and her mom have not noticed this (and nor has Jerry). The urologist already has a lot of clues as to how this medical mystery will evolve. Lisa and Jerry have been (sleeping) together since Lisa was twelve. Without any form of protection (as the urologist has already observed without them telling her). Mom tells this without the least iota of hesitation — she seems (too) comfortable with her daughter having unprotected fun with a boy. These are patients who do not have a clue what STDs are. What protection is good for. How babies are made. (Even the mother seems rather clueless about pregnancies once that subject is brought up.) These are patients who think they can get pregnant because they swallowed some semen, patients thinking they get pregnant because they kissed, patient thinking they got pregnant because they had a digital vaginal exam two years ago. And it’s obvious that Jerry is the bad guy (since Lisa only had Jerry as a lover). After some specific questions, Jerry admits (or rather, states) outright that he might have had some fun with some women of ill repute — unprotected, of course. While he was with Lisa. The urologist, shocked (and thinking of her 11-year-old daughter) does not know what to say — these people seem beyond help — and to add insult to injury, mom starts laughing and blurts: “Boys will be boys !” SOURCES: Dissection of the uterus in the latter stages of pregnancy, showing the foetus, placenta and umbilical cord. Colored line engraving by W.H. Lizars, ca. 1827. Wellcome collection.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I found a lot of blood on my husband’s underwear. He is a serial cheater. What should I do?
Answer: More than a decade ago, I was sleeping over with one of my best friends, during a very dark period in my life which was essentially characterized by my divorce. We talked a lot, drank a lot, and sang a lot. And his wife did too. A recurring item on such evenings was that at some point his wife became very angry with him for no reason — she was a nasty drunk — and then she started to ridicule every aspect of his persona (especially in the context of horizontal refreshment). My friend (drunk himself) simply laughed with it, and never really understood the vastness of her conduct — until the day on which he found her secret cell phone in a cupboard. And that was basically the end of his marriage. The divorce and its after-life had really exhausted me, and after a night of serious drinking, I decided to call it a day, and went to my room. I remember weird nightmares in which my friend’s wife stood in my room, drunk and undressed, bothering me while I was sinking in and out an alcoholic coma. When I woke up the next morning, my underwear was really bloody, and I could not explain how this had happened (as I was not wounded). But I remembered suddenly that my friend’s wife very recently had had an appendix operation, and still was bandaged and the like. And then I realized that the nightmare had not been a dream at all, but was becoming an even worse nightmare instead. (She r@ped me.) That does not mean that I think that your serial-cheating husband was r@ped by a nasty drunk. But maybe you could ask ? SOURCES: Annals of Surgery, vol. 197, No. 5 (1983), pp. 495–506.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: You find out you have cancer and the doctor gives you 2 weeks to live. What do you do in that time?
Answer: During a late night dinner with friends, one of them told me that my former-wife had been diagnosed with breast cancer (I wrote about her case before on several occasions). I think it was in 2018. After our divorce was finalized, there was no contact between us whatsoever — the divide had become too deep after what had happened. So it’s hard to pin down the details, because news about her came in unpredictable waves through common friends, and I had no idea about how bad the diagnosis really was. One family member told me some time later (in 2020, at the funeral of an uncle) that my former-wife was terminally ill, but since that family member was known to be hysterical (and typically overreacting), I did not know what to think of it (and to be totally honest, it wasn’t of my concern — or so I thought). Then, in the Summer of 2022, I noticed my former-wife standing at the counter of a coffee shop, ordering a drink. That is to say, I knew it must be her based on how she moved and how she dressed, but she was almost unrecognizable — something had happened to her skin (which was pitted, like the skin of an orange, and yellow), and her hair seemed different. And it’s then that I realized that the terminal claim of my family member was right after all — the cancer must have spread to the liver (as far as I understood). Later, I heard that her oncologist had broken the news to her that she had a couple of months left — maybe even a couple of weeks. Which brings me to your question — You find out you have cancer and the doctor gives you 2 weeks to live. What do you do in that time ? What I found out later that in the weeks that followed, she was basically on a tour saying goodbye to friends and family, trying to stretch time until the pain got so bad that she needed palliative sedation. The cancer obliterated her every chance. And what I saw in her eyes on that fateful afternoon in July, is exactly what would happen in the foreseeable future. Because there was nothing left besides despair and the bleakest prostration I had ever seen. The woman who I had known was gone. That is what happens when there is no time left — After the goodbyes, you are grimly reaped. (As if you were never there.) SOURCES: painting by Rhys Knight.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do you sleep with your bedroom door open or closed? Why?
Answer: We sleep with the door open. (Thanks, Tarzan.) Main reason (now): our daughter sleeps some yards further down the hall, and I love the harmony of sleeping sounds she produces. I also want to know when she has nightmares, so that we can soothe her if they get too bad. Main reason (then): Johnny Weissmuller. A seventeen-year-old tomcat dumped at the vet by the children of his old female owner who had to go to a nursing home. They promised to take care of Johnny, but they didn’t (this happens all the time). We adopted him, and I can tell you this: I have never seen a cat so scared. He just wanted to be with his companion, and he hid under the bed, producing the saddest melancholic sounds we ever heard. He stopped eating as well. One day we had a breakthrough when I gave him some bacon, and since then he started to trust us, step by step. Johnny liked to walk around at night, so we decided to keep our bedroom door open. But at some point he started showing signs of dementia, and first irregularly, but later on a daily basis, he got disoriented, and lost his way in our house. Then he started meowing loudly and sadly because he did not know where he was, and he needed help. So we decided to closed the main hall door, so that he could be more at ease in the living room. People who suffer from Alzheimer’s often suffer from the same problem — they wander around, not knowing where to wander to, and panic. In Johnny’s case, he stopped retracting his front paw claws (as many old cats do), and then walked around in circles in our room, not knowing where he was, and making his characteristic sound — Tick tack, tick tack, tick tack. The Alzheimer thing was exactly what happened to Johnny Weissmuller, the famous Tarzan actor who happened to live in our house when he was already very old, with a couple of marbles rolling around upstairs. One day, in a bad rain storm, he decided to sit outside in the garden in a bad episode of confusion, and the damage the storm did killed him through a lung disease. He was twenty-four years old. (Tick tack. Tick tack.) SOURCES: the image is my own (and features Johnny Weismuller).

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a nurse, what are some common mistakes you’ve witnessed doctors make?
Answer: This was a patient who needed a hysterectomy, and her husband had asked his best friend — who happened to be an OB/GYN — to remove her uterus. The next day she was feeling really bad, so the OB/GYN friend opened her up again to see what was going on inside. And he discovered that her bladder was severely ruptured, and he was the one who butchered her. So he called a surgeon — he should have called a urologist (my girlfriend), but he had called her so many times for the many surgical mistakes he had made over the years, that he was too ashamed to admit it. The surgeon could not fix the bladder either, so in the end the urologist was called for reconstructive surgery, and the patient was opened a third time. But after the operation, the patient’s condition deteriorated, and she became so sick that she was actually almost dying, on the verge of going into sepsis. An emergency operation was scheduled right away (by the urologist and surgeon — the butcher was not allowed although he insisted), and to add insult to injury, they found out that the OB/GYN friend had cut off one of the patient’s ureters, besides rupturing her bladder. All this had happened when performing a standard hysterectomy. This is something that many OR nurses have seen over the years — OB/GYNs starting surgical procedures whom they actually can hardly perform, then messing up the patient and needing urgent “assistance” in the end to save the patient’s organs, or the patient’s life. Many a patient have ended with a urine pouch because of the sheer surgical incompetence of OB/GYNs, and many a patient have been saved by general surgeons or urologists (but the latter never received the praise). This is the best kept hospital secret so many OR doctors and nurses know about, but never dare to mention. (Hush, hush.) SOURCES: Diseases of the kidneys, ureters and bladder, with special reference to the diseases of women (1922), Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, what is the most difficult news you have ever had to break to an expectant mother?
Answer: She already was a mom, albeit from a six-month-old baby. As a patient with a very rare case of kidney cancer (which had already spread to nearby lymph nodes), Cynthia already’d had two surgeries to remove the kidney (first surgery), and to remove further growth of new cancerous lymph nodes (second surgery). (She had been pregnant when the first symptoms occurred — peeing blood and recurring back pains which could be intense. That was when she was diagnosed with a rare case of cancer. She was in her early twenties, by the way.) During the second operation, the urologist had seen that the cancer tissue was very close (too close) to a large cardiac vein so that there might not be a third procedure if the cancer came back. Unfortunately, not much later it did, and this time the cancerous lymph nodes embraced the cardiac vein in a gruesome embrace that would be lethal in the end, and nothing could be done. So one of the most difficult conversations in the urologist’s career came when she had to break the news that Cynthia had one, maybe two years left before the vein would be obliterated by its metastatic constrictor. Although the cancer spread rapidly, Cynthia fought it every which way, in the hope that she could know her baby as long as possible. But it didn’t last. I would never know you, don't get to understand. No answers to questions — it's too late for that. But I was in your arms, once, just for a moment. I was in your arms. SOURCES: painting by Nicola Samori. Last quote based on the song “In your arms,” by Birdy.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's your conspiracy theory?
Answer: In her early childhood, she was considered a boy by her parents and siblings (see the newspaper article below). Her Testicular Feminization Syndrome (TFS) case had been well known in the medical world for a long while — that’s how I heard it for the first time — and served as a standard example in several medical grad schools in the US, and other countries. (But apparently, specialists can see it without further notice.) She was born with Testicular Feminization Syndrome (TFS), having the usual male pattern XY chromosomes, but as with all TSF patients her body did not respond to testosterone fully or at all. This prevented the sex development of a typical male — and in Jamie Lee Curtis’s case, this aspect is even more pronounced. Patients with TFS have internal, undescended testicles and no uterus, fallopian tubes, nor ovaries, but externally the labia, vagina, and clitoris all develop.[1] Many other sexual characteristics such as breast development and pelvic shape are also normal. On the other hand, armpit and pubic hair is decreased or absent. And as patients with TFS have no uterus, they cannot have children. Her father Tony Curtis has addressed “her secret” a number of times in public in the past, and in her early childhood she was actually considered (and called) a normal boy. What bothers me the most about this “conspiracy” (because that’s how it is received by many) is not that she was born with XY chromosomes — that doesn’t bother me at all and doesn’t change my opinion about her (as a big fan) whatsoever — but rather how violently people react if you mention her as a medical case with XY chromosomes. Because according to these people, this MUST be a conspiracy. For these people — who ironically “defend” Jamie Lee Curtis (against what ?) — she would apparently be a lesser person if the TFS claim would be true. That is what bothers me the most about her case — Hypocrisy. SOURCES: the footnoted site. For the images: Jamie Lee Curtis at the 1980 Cannes Festival. The newspaper article was published in Daily World (January 18, 1959 edition)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's the most surprising thing you discovered about and with a patient as an obstetrician and gynecologist?
Answer: This happened only yesterday. As a urologist (not an OB/GYN, but hopefully close enough), you see many unexpected patients with unexpected stories, but some are even more surprising than others. This patient was a middle-aged man with a wife and kids, and he had a problem downstairs. His testicles were swollen and slightly wounded, and so was the skin of his glans penis. My girlfriend felt that the patient was hiding something, and asked him to tell the entire story — not a selected part which blurred the bigger picture. He hesitated for a while, but then opened his backpack to take out a device, while he obviously was getting a wee bit aroused (but she tried to ignore it). A little metal birdcage with a round opening at the back — my girlfriend had no idea what it was. “It’s a chastity cage. I wear it at certain parties, and it’s the only thing I wear at those parties.” It was the kind of party his wife did not know about, and he planned to keep it that way. The cage was the obvious cause of his genital condition, and my girlfriend did not even try to ask what the cage was for. But this was obviously one for the books. A patient with a secret life, wounded, and aroused — And caged like a bird in more than one way. SOURCES: Dissections of the male genitalia and upper thighs: four figures, with the arteries and blood vessels indicated in red. Colored lithograph by J. Roux, 1822. Wellcome Collection. (© public domain)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What was the most memorable thing a patient has said while drifting into sleep under anesthesia?
Answer: My girlfriend was still an absoluter beginner, and this was one of her first serious cases as a trainee of a surgeon. Maybe the most serious case of all, come to think of it. People come to the Emergency Room all the time for minor reasons, and this patient was not much different. A bad stomach ache and vomiting — probably a bad case of stomach flu. On the other hand, he was also in his mid-seventies, so every minor variation on a standard condition had to be taken seriously (just like in every other patient). But he deteriorated at an unexpected pace, and somehow something else was going on. His vomiting got worse and worse, and it never seemed to stop. The abdominal pain was suddenly beyond control. The surgeon on call deciding on the spot to open this man up, because basically his instinct told him that they could not wait for medical imaging and the like. And that’s exactly what he told the patient’s wife, before the patient was wheeled into the OR. Before leaving his wife’s sight, the patient told her that he loved her (a standard thing), and that he felt really good now that he knew the surgeons would solve his problem, as minor as it was — “I’ll see you in an hour, darling. And then we can go back home again.” When the surgeon and his amateur trainee opened him up, they found out that his bowel was blue-ish black, and they immediately knew what was going on. So they looked at each other and closed him up again. A bad case of bowel infarction — and nothing could be done. He would die without waking up some time later. His wife didn’t have a clue. SOURCES: the image is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What do lifelong cigarette smokers say when they are diagnosed with an incurable lung disease? Do they say it was worth it?
Answer: One of the most famous cases to which this question applies is certainly Patrick Swayze. He did not die from a lung disease though, but from pancreas cancer. And boy did this man smoke (and drink, for that matter). But did he regret it ? Swayze refused to admit in public how bad his condition really was. In reality, his cancer had spread and his personal clock was clicking, but he still believed that he could fight it — he still believed he could survive in one way or the other. But did he stop smoking, or drinking ? Well, he tried battling his alcohol addiction in the last year of his life after the diagnosis, but he never quit smoking (although he knew very well that his chain-smoking habit might well be related to his condition) — the very reason being that he knew that he was facing sudden death. The pancreas cancer was obliterating him no matter what. Still, he did say that if he ever got to the point “where he's going to live more than 5 minutes, he'd quit in a heartbeat,” in an interview with Barbara Walters.[1] To me, this seems like an indirect way of expressing regret. He did not like that he was dying, and that he was turning into a skeleton in a matter of months. He died on September 14, 2009.[2] Patrick Swayze was not alone. It’s incredibly hard for people to admit in the mirror that their end is really near, that what is hiding inside is eating them, and that it can’t be stopped. And that maybe — just maybe — they caused what is killing them. So some of them keep smoking, some of them keep drinking, some of them do not. One thing is extremely common though among those who finally start seeing certain death in that very same mirror, those who will become a still life soon — the final image of their fading reality. Regret, regret, regret. SOURCES: the footnoted sites.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Has Shannon Doherty, 53, actress of "Charmed" and "Beverly Hills, 90210" passed away?
Answer: Yes she did, and for about four years, she had been sitting in the waiting chamber for this drama to happen. In 2015, she had been diagnosed with breast cancer, but two years later she went into remission. Mind you: this does not mean she was “cured” (whatever this means in the cancer context) — it means the MDs could not detect cancer anymore through standard imaging and other tests. Mind you, again: you could have millions of cancers cells in your body which are trooping together in some location in your body, and which are still not detectable by today’s medical means. A tumor, but it’s hiding under the radar. And you are still living in remission. So yeah, in 2020, Shannen Doherty was diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer, meaning that it had spread (beyond nearby lymph nodes), and also meaning that she was beyond being cured — a death sentence. By the middle of June 2023 she revealed that it had also spread to her brains, and the fact that the culprit was now literally in her head maddened her for obvious reasons:[1] “My fear is obvious. I am extremely claustrophobic and there was a lot going on in my life,” said Doherty. “But that fear …. The turmoil ….. the timing of it all …. This is what cancer can look like.” In early 2024, she still hoped really hard that she could squeeze out another three to five years, but that did not work out in the end.[2] Hope springs eternal — Before a cold Winter tale. SOURCES: the footnoted sites.[3]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the saddest thing you experienced while working in a hospital?
Answer: She is a young mother, only twenty-one years old. But she is also sick. She has an extremely rare kidney tumor whose progression is extremely worrying, as it has spread to nearby lymph nodes. And spreading is always bad. The kidney and lymph nodes are subsequently removed, but the mere aggression of this patient’s cancer means trouble. Not much later, new positive lymph nodes are detected, and this time the lymph nodes mass is dangerously close to the vena cava, a large vein which carries blood to the heart from other parts of the body. And this is worse than bad news. Still, another surgery is planned, the cancerous lymph nodes are removed, and the patient is still a mother afterwards of her six-months-old baby. But there always is a next time in this type of cancer progression, and now new cancerous lymph nodes are about to penetrate the vena cava, and surgery is not possible anymore. The patient is about to be constricted by her cancer, and her fight will become a loss soon. In less than two months, she will not be a mother anymore. And someone has to tell her. SOURCES: Annals of Surgery, vol. 197, No. 5 (1983), pp. 495–506.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do men forget about women they once loved?
Answer: Sometimes so many things have happened in our past that it would be almost impossible to erase all of them. If I think about Ebba, for instance, she would be very hard to forget because her parents live next door (and they hate me). It was also the very first serious relationship after my marriage had ended with a bang, and the stunning contrast with my ex-wife was probably what I needed to detox from the poisonous soup my ex-wife had tried to prepare with me as the main ingredient. As to my ex-wife, it is almost impossible to forget her, because of the way her life ended after a breast cancer metastasis scare. Apparently she discovered a lump, it turned out to be breast cancer which had traveled to nearby lymph nodes, and further investigation led to the fact that it had metastasized to the bones. A death sentence instead of a diagnosis. (“You have four years at most, ma’am.”) In the last months of her life, I had seen her once in a coffee house, and I needed no further explanation — this woman was dying. And she knew it. Two months later she was gone forever, and her death was everywhere. Then, out of the blue I was explicitly asked from beyond the grave — a very unpleasant experience which shocked my family — not to attend the funeral. (Which never was my plan in the first place. But still.) These are the experiences which make us remember. Even if there are no feelings left. SOURCES: painting by Rhys Knight. (The image is my own.)

Question: What's the dark side of Silicon Valley?
Answer: Some of the most powerful companies in Silicon Valley are ruled by individuals who consider themselves above mere mortals, who are convinced that the laws of physics and the like do not apply to their own self-declared semi-god persona. And if you do not follow this person in the most literal way, you become a rotten apple which will be thrown in the bin rather sooner than later. Take Steve Jobs. This is a man who was and is considered an innovator — a genius, according to others — who was actually a fruit cake. This was a man who soaked his feet in company toilets, who was convinced that he did not need to shower nor using deodorant due to his vegetarian/vegan/fruit-only diet while he actually stank so much that when he worked at Atari, he was put on the night shift so that he would not bother colleagues with his stench.[1] This was also a man who ignored his doctors for the better part of a year after being diagnosed with a rare form of pancreatic cancer which was perfectly treatable, with a very good diagnosis. Because he thought that his extreme diets, natural remedies and literal wishful thinking could and would completely cure him.[2] Only it didn’t. His overconfident self-belief was the very reason why his cancer got enough elbow room to outgrow any proper medical treatment later on. It was the very reason he died a terrible death, never really understanding why the cancer could enter his so-called “reality distortion field” and destroy it. In fact, he also believed he could use his reality distortion field approach to cast spells on people.[3] (Sigh.) In the end, a man who believed he could heal himself from cancer through the good old Jedi method (eating fruit), while soaking his feet in toilets and stinking up the room because he did not believe in showering, led one of the largest and most voracious companies in Silicon Valley and the world. Fruit cake, indeed. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. The photograph was taken by Norman Seeff.

Question: What's the best personal hygiene tip you can give?
Answer: A befriended dentist once told me that bad dental hygiene, and gum disease in particular, can create a portal for bacteria to enter the bloodstream, and infect the heart in the end. [George Washington famously battled with painful dental problems for most of his life. Eventually, he wore a set of dentures made of human and animal teeth, bones and ivory. He could not control the thing, by the way, as it often refused to open, or close.][1] The bacteria found in common oral infections also occur in plaques and blockages that form in our heart arteries. If left untreated, this can even lead to a heart attack. More generically, gum disease is linked to increased inflammation in the entire body.[2] Throw some cardiac risk factors like high cholesterol and diabetes into the equation, and you create a recipe for cardiac disaster. In the end, it is absolutely crucial to take care of your teeth and gums — not only for matters of the heart, but also for your general appearance, body odor and personal comfort. (Ask George Washington.) SOURCES: the footnoted sites. The photograph of George Washington’s most famous set of dentures was taken from Live Science.[3]
