Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's the weirdest question you've been asked when crossing an international border?
Answer: Some time ago I traveled to Denver, Colorado and had to pass customs as an international traveler. A customs officer asked me why I traveled to the US, and I answered that I was a mathematician, and that I was planning to work on a research project with an American colleague. He looked at my earrings and the tattoo in my neck, and remained silent for a while. He did not believe me. “This ain’t no time for joking. So I’ll ask you one more time: what are you doing in the US ?” (He was not very friendly either.) I kept my composure, and repeated my answer. He got mad at me — apparently neck-tattooed scum like me is not allowed to be a mathemagician. “I’ll ask you ONE LAST TIME, and then —” While he was delivering his speech, I took a book from my bag, and laid it before him. A published mathematical research monograph. With my name on it. He stopped speaking, looked at the book, read who its author was, read the name on my passport, looked at me, looked at the book, looked at the printed name, looked at my passport, looked at me again. His eyes widened so much that I was beginning to think they would fall from their sockets. He still could not believe it. Then he grumbled something which I did not understand, and finally said with a smile: “You can go, mister professor.” And off I went. SOURCES: GIF found through Google images.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I used to use toilet paper as sanitary pads for a year because I was too afraid to tell my mom my period started. Now I’m finding out it is toxic. Will it impact my health in any way?
Answer: It’s one of those OB/GYN and urologist nightmares. A female patient suffers from intense abdominal pain and feels sick, and it’s not a urinary tract infection, or a tumor. She is not pregnant either. On the other hand, there is a mass in there, and it doesn’t look good. It happened to Sara Manitoski in 2017. The 11th grader from British Columbia complained of feeling unwell and having cramps while camping out on a school trip. She retired to her shared cabin around 10 o’clock. Early next morning — it was March 15 — the other students in the cabin went for breakfast. When they returned, Sara’s alarm was sounding. But she did not react.[1] She was found unresponsive and was rushed to a nearby hospital, where she died the very same day. The cause was a Staphylococcus infection which had amassed on a tampon which she had carried in place for too long. So be very careful in your own creative hygienic solutions if you are having your period, and if you are dealing with menstrual fluid. Ask your mom (there’s nothing to be ashamed about), or go to an OB/GYN instead — It can be a slippery slope when blood is on the dance floor. SOURCES: the footnoted site. For the medical image: Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is your most frightening emergency room story?
Answer: Pain was the word, but would you go to the ER if that was the only symptom — pain in the groin ? Ask any urologist and they would say NO (capitalized). It’s one of the most generic and undefined pains that usually cannot be explained — and guys, you KNOW (capitalized) what I’m talking about. But hearing the guy was one thing, seeing him was another, and diagnosing him was something else. It was the urologists’ first ever case of Fournier’s Gangrene — an acute necrotic infection of the penis, scrotum or perineum, essentially meaning that the genitals of the affected male patient is being eaten, and very, very fast. It’s also extremely rare, since less than 2,000 cases have been reported in the last 70 years. He was in his seventies, and the urologist was very clear on what was to happen: “We need to remove every single thing of this infection — including your penis. Only then you can survive, but I’m not sure if that is even possible.” The man agreed. The next three days two things happened. And this time, no surgery would help anymore. The infection would take over his body and necrotize every single square inch of his painful body in a matter of days. And so that’s what his urologist told him, in tears, because this was a man who was receiving a sentence instead of a diagnosis — as if the amputation hadn’t been enough already. But he was totally okay with it — The pain had to stop. SOURCES: Abb. 325. Schwellkörper der Rute nach Entfernung ihrer Muskeln und Loslösung der Eichel (4/5). Rauber-Kopsch Anatomy.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are the aspects of dementia that few people know or talk about?
Answer: My father-in-law was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease today. He had an appointment at the neurologist’s office in my girlfriend’s hospital at 4pm, and that’s when he found out. Officially, that is. Because in the last couple of years, it was clear to us — but to nobody else, including his two sons (which is weird) — that his short-term memory had gotten really bad. Sometimes he calls us on the phone to ask about things he asked us about yesterday on the phone. Sometimes he tells a story twice. Sometimes. He also knew something was going on — and the fact that his mother died due to complications of Alzheimer’s considerably narrowed the mental elbow room one so desperately needs before an actual diagnosis. He aced the cognitive tests easily — highly educated people (he is a retired urologist) often do — but the bone marrow biopsy undeniably marked the spot. And that’s what he found out today. His mental capacities could make him hide what was lying beneath for much longer, but the bone marrow never lies. My girlfriend is calling his girlfriend as we speak, to break the news. And she is crying. Because although my father-in-law, as a doctor and as someone who knew that his mom had Alzheimer’s, knew what the diagnosis would be — he even called it “judgement day” — but his girlfriend was still in total denial, knowing (as a nurse) what may be coming in a nearing future. Knowing how everything could fade until no memories can escape anymore from the electric mist which will ever grow, until not a single word is left. That is one of the hardest aspects to understand in the context of the dementia curse — Acceptance. SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the weirdest/grossest/most disturbing thing seen by emergency room staff? Do you ever find it difficult not to faint?
Answer: The patient had experienced pain in the groin area and was really sick even before the first thought came of spending the afternoon in the ER. It’s usually the place seventy-five-year olds don’t want to go to on your average Sunday afternoon. But the pain was bad. And the urologist quickly found out what it was. And there was no turning back. Fournier’s Gangrene — an acute necrotic infection of the penis, scrotum or perineum (a type of necrotizing fasciitis, as some medical would say), essentially meaning that the central part of the affected male patient is being eaten, and fast. For some of us, it sounds like a bad reaction to a Maths course, but unfortunately it’s nothing alike. It’s so much worse. “It was the very first time I saw a patient with this disease since I work in this hospital.” Apparently Fournier’s Gangrene is very rare (totaling only about 1,800 cases in the last 70 years). The MD people acted very quickly and removed as much of the infected tissue as possible — including his entire penis (yes indeed) — but over the next days, the gangrene spread at an uncontrollable rate. Some days later, Freya had to talk to the patient — one of the saddest conversations of her career. And since seconds were becoming minutes, and minutes becoming hours, there was no time to waste. Because hours sometimes become days that fade forever into the electric mist. And in this case, they did. SOURCES: Dissection of the abdomen and thigh of a standing man, showing major blood-vessels. Coloured lithograph by J. Maclise, 1851. Wellcome Collection. Public Domain Mark. Source: Wellcome Collection.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, what is the bravest thing you've ever seen a patient do?
Answer: This was simply a woman who wanted a baby, and nothing could stop her. So she wanted her husband’s sperm to be checked once again because something was going on. Something was dead wrong. And there was. Because his sperm sample was dead. They did not find a single living sperm cell, and what was even more surprising: it had always been that way. It must have, since it turned out that he was subsequently diagnosed with a rare congenital disorder that made him infertile from the start — he had always been infertile. So why was this woman’s insistence the bravest thing you've ever seen a patient do ? Because they already had three children. That is to say, she had three children, and her husband believed they were his biological children. But now it turned out that none of them were his own. Yet back in Egypt — where they had lived prior moving to Europe — she had found mysterious ways in getting pregnant, despite her husband’s congenital twist, whom she did not know of. So back in Egypt, she had found a source of viable sperm. And even now — even when the doctor had made it clear that her husband never was a biological father and never would be — she kept insisting. Because besides being incredibly brave, she was also another thing — Incredibly stupid. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIFER.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Is there someone who got real life superpowers after an accident?
Answer: Most people think that he was born this way, but that is not the case. His world-famous characteristically ambiguous eyes were actually the result of a fistfight in the Spring of 1962 with a good pal (called George Underwood), causing so called Anisocoria — a condition in which a person has different-sized pupils:[1] “Underwood’s fingernail had scratched the surface of Bowie’s eyeball, paralyzing the muscles that contract the iris.” The iris of David Bowie’s left eye was permanently expanded, giving him the famous blue and green/black eyes look — and so actually his eyes really had the same color, although they looked so very different. And I’m certainly not claiming that he would not have become the musical super hero he grew into without the Anisocoria, but his eyes were a very important defining part of his enigmatic and chameleon-like persona, and very often the devil is in the details when it comes to legends and the like. In David Bowie’s case, it all boiled down to one argument with a friend in 1962, which would alter his destiny and change his looks forever — Through a lucky punch. SOURCES: the footnoted site. Photo: CA/Redferns.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a urologist, what's the weirdest thing you've seen?
Answer: A couple of years ago, an old woman visited my girlfriend’s office for a problem she had been carrying around, but she could and would not go into any further details about her predicament. When after a long discussion in which the patient refused to describe what was going on, the patient finally undressed, her problem showed right away. Hanging, between her legs. The patient had a complete uterine prolapse, meaning that her uterus was completely protruding from her vagina. It’s not at all an uncommon condition — it occurs when pelvic floor muscles and ligaments stretch and weaken until they are not longer able to support the uterus, so that it drops down into the vagina. But something was really different though. The old woman’s womb was shriveled, blackish and completely dried out, and its surface showed a number of erosions. So when my girlfriend asked her patient how long ago exactly the very prolapse had happened, the woman again dared not to answer at first. “About … about four years ago, doctor.” My girlfriend knew the patient was telling the truth — the womb itself essentially told the entire story — and so she remained silent because the patient wanted to explain herself. “I needed to take care for my bedridden husband, doctor, and never really found the time.” FOUR. WHOLE. YEARS. For four whole years, this poor woman had slept with her womb hanging outside her body, went to the toilet with this thing dangling down below, had sat on it whenever she was sitting, had felt it while she was eating, had ignored the itches (in the beginning) when doing groceries, and had carefully washed it in the shower when nobody was there to witness. For four whole years. So yes indeed, her womb had dried out and the surface was heavily eroded. The old woman had never been so ashamed in her life, and could not stop the tears from falling. She did not even dare to look at her urologist when she popped her question in a broken voice — “Can you … can you help me, doctor ?” And when she finally looked at her doctor, the doctor only smiled, and made a wish come true — She nodded. SOURCES: The diseases of women - a handbook for students and practitioners (1897), J. Bland-Sutton and A. E. Giles (London: Rebman; Philadelphia: W. B. Saunders). Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: After an inmate has been in jail/prison for a long time, what is the most shocking thing for them after coming out for several years?
Answer: He was finally free again, and he had enjoyed his first days of freedom in a mist of euphoria. He talked to people in bars, drank scotch and soda — it was just perfect. But then he lost that. Felt it slip away like in the old movies where you see a ghost lift out of a body. It simply evaporated. He could feel it go:[1] “I was waiting for the bus in the Omni (Auditorium), watching a convention on the main floor there. There were all these people going to a Hawks game. And I was watching these people — these people who had real lives, backgrounds, histories, girl friends, husbands and families. Who were smiling and laughing and talking with each other. Who seemed to have so much of what I wanted.” That’s when he realized what he had lost in prison, how alone he was again (more alone, and then even more), and that the outside world had not waited. That he had only imagined to have a life in prison, but that this had never been the case. That he was a lesser being. And he felt something drain out of him. The depression came just days before the man — in a drunken rampage — committed extremely violent attacks on five coeds, two of whom were Chi Omega sorority sisters who died shortly after. One girl kept touching her teeth while unconscious, because she’d had a new brace since a couple of days. A nipple had been bitten off, and she also had a nasty bite wound in the buttocks. And while she was dying, she kept touching her teeth. To feel if they were all right. After an inmate has been in jail/prison for a long time, what is the most shocking thing for them after coming out for several years ? That life has proceeded without them. That on the inside, they actually had no life after all. And that on the outside, they are invisible, and empty. Even Ted Bundy realized that during his final escape. Before the darkness inside took over again. SOURCES: Ted Bundy — Conversations with a killer (The death row interviews), by Stephen G. Michaud and Hugh Aynesworth, AuthorLink Press, 2000. The image was found through Google images.[2]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, have you ever accidentally and inappropriately laughed at a patient?
Answer: This happened to a patient in my girlfriend’s hospital near the end of April. The patient was only 52 years old, and suffered from a rare case of young-onset dementia. He had been wheeled into the ER with a broken hip. So the surgeon on call told the patient that he had to stay in bed until the operation (for obvious reasons), and he also warned the nurses that since the man was suffering from young-onset dementia, they might want to keep an extra eye on him. In the beginning he was still a bit drowsy, but less than thirty minutes later, the patient asked one of the nurses what he was doing in the hospital — “There is NOTHING wrong with me !” And so the nurse told him the truth: that he’d had an accident and broken his hip, and that he must stay in his bed at all costs until the operation. To which the patient screamed “that he had NOT broken his hip, and that he was leaving the hospital ASAP !!” And then he jumped off the bed. SOURCES: the medical scans were taken from The Lancet.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How did women with ectopic pregnancies survive before modern medicine?
Answer: In the middle ages, ectopic pregnancies were seen as a consequence of violent emotion — typically fright or surprise — during coitus, quite similarly to the belief that hysteria in female patients was caused by the uterus. Hence the term “hysterectomy.” Early treatments of ectopic pregnancies were designed to kill the ectopic conceptus and included starvation, purging, bleeding, and even treatment with strychnine.[1] Somewhat later, attempts to surgically “disrupt” an ectopic gestational sac, or even to pass electrical current into it, frequently resulted in sepsis and death. In fact, even your average childbirth could be life-threatening at any point in history up to mid 1900, and even today in medically underdeveloped countries. Adding insult to injury, a high number of individual pregnancies (which was typical in the old days) worsened the prospects. It was only in the mid-1800s that surgeons such as Ignaz Semmelweis[2] recognized the importance of antiseptic and hand washing procedures — the theory that some invisible germs could cause diseases was not widely accepted yet, and Semmelweis’s brilliant idea that he and the medical students carried “cadaverous particles” from the autopsy room to the female patients in the obstetrical clinic, was not accepted by many of his peers. Unfortunately, his mental struggles with his medical adversaries killed him in the end. But that was the mid-1800s — a time in which 1 out of 200 ordinary pregnancies resulted in a childbed death (in England).[3] In case of ectopic pregnancies before this modern era, the prospects were obviously even much more dramatic. Even in as late as 1880, the mortality rate in ectopic pregnancies was 72–90%.[4] But before modern medicine ? (Silence.) SOURCES: the footnoted sites. For the medical image: COLLINS, Samuel (1618-1710). A Systeme of Anatomy, treating of the Body of Man, Beasts, Birds, Fish, Insects, and Plants. London: Thomas Newcomb, 1685.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the brutal truth about life after marriage?
Answer: You finally start your new life and move in with your new partner. Every day in the final six months has been torture, but now the truth is out and the lies are over. (You will miss the old house and its magic though.) The new house is smaller but it has to do. And in any case, what could be worse than your old life whom you betrayed in all its senses ? (Don’t try to think about the good things. Old scars can hurt for a long time.) Then the kids come and your new life REALLY starts — diapers, innocent tears and much wider smiles, laughing out loud, the first steps, the first word, car holidays and children’s songs. These are the very steps on the ladder to eternal happiness — and you are taking them, one by one. And there is so much more to come. Then, one day you feel a tiny lump in an armpit and it’s probably nothing. But the GP is not sure and refers you to an OB/GYN and medical imaging is scheduled. The diagnosis is breast cancer, and further medical tests reveal that it has metastasized to your bones (which explains your recent back pains in hindsight). The ladder to eternal happiness has collapsed. And time has too. The children’s tears taste different now, and there will be no more car holidays. A dystopian overtone flute is playing notes that only you can hear. And your ex has seen you listening. Four years later, a crematorium technician runs a magnet over your remains to remove ferrous materials that did not combust during the cremation process. The few hinges, staples and screws which are the last witnesses of an illustrious sports career. (You don’t need them anyway.) And then he grinds them so that you can fit into your final resting place. Because this is what you have become — Crushed bones, and casket ash. SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Should I attend my ex-husband’s funeral?
Answer: I did not attend my ex-wife’s funeral. Our divorce was painful (she cheated for half a year, lied about it till the very last day of our relationship, and then wanted money for our house that I did not have), and we never reconnected again. She turned out to be a person whom I did not know, and of all people I have ever known, she shares the gold medal amongst those that hurt me the most. So to me, it was clear that there was no place for me at her funeral. My presence would have been weird, and perhaps even inappropriate to some people, as given our history, my hypothetical attendance could and would be interpreted as a poetic revenge. And last but not least, I received a message from beyond the grave (through intermediaries) that explicitly asked me not to attend. Especially this aspect was awkward to me — why would she even care ? The last time I saw her alive was, accidentally, in a coffee shop, where we both waited for our children (who apparently did gymnastics in the same gymnast hall). I barely recognized her. Here eyebrows were gone, her face was jaundiced and had turned into a so-called “Peau d’orange mask.” (Her skin was pitted like the peel of an orange.) That was two months before she vanished. What struck me the most was the empty look in her eyes, and her broken posture — as if she literally was waiting for death, feeling its cold breath ever so near. She had seen me while I was ordering coffee — she was standing next to me — but it was too late for one very last meaningful conversation. Everything had already been said. SOURCES: I consulted the website Popular Mechanics for the image.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What has shocked you the most about a patient's past medical history?
Answer: An older patient entered the ER with a bad case of stomach flu. He was gracious, patiently, but also obviously in pain. And since he was having a fever as well, they — his wife was with him — did not want to take any risks. But while waiting for an emergency physician, his condition worsened. The abdominal pains became almost unbearable in less than half an hour, and he reached a point at which he could not stop vomiting anymore. Although emergency medical imaging had been scheduled, the surgeon on call decided that since the patient’s condition was so unstable, he had to be opened as soon as possible. One of the most shocking things about this patient was that he never had a medical problem whatsoever in the past — he was a patient with a clean sheet, and he came in running so to speak. My girlfriend was a surgical trainee at the time, and so she assisted. And this very operation turned out to be one for the books — almost unbelievable if you are not active in the medical world. Because his insides were black. His bowel was totally inactive because the poor man was suffering from an acute case of gangrenous bowel — also known under the name of “bowel infarction” — an irreversible condition resulting from insufficient blood flow. And there was nothing they could do. By then, the man had gone into sepsis (blood poisoning), and was literally lying on his death bed in a cold and hospital-bright emergency room, accompanied by a surgeon and his trainee who would close him again, and prepare for a bleak conversation with the patient’s wife who was patiently sitting in good spirits in the waiting room. Because her husband caught a bad case of stomach flu. And he was going to be all right. SOURCES: the image is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Is a colonoscopy as bad as they say?
Answer: The secret word is Propofol. I had a colonoscopy some time ago, and admittedly I did not really look forward to the procedure. And adding insult to injury, I knew every single person in the OR when I was wheeled in, “dressed” only my hospital gown. The day before the colonoscopy, I was only allowed to drink water, and near the evening I had to take strong laxatives which kind of messed up my rectum (because that’s where the problem was located). That was the hardest part. The next morning, I was ready (in my gown) in the OR for the show to begin. The friendly anesthesiologist said “Sleep tight 🙂,” and then intravenously injected Propofol into the IV line. I did not really understand, but after a few seconds my eyes closed just like that. When I woke up, it was over and done with. The culprit in my rectum had been found (a necrotized polyp the size of a mushroom) — it would have to be surgically removed later on — my behind was on fire (and that would last for a week), but for the rest I felt really great, thanks to the Propofol. (This is the sedation Michael Jackson’s personal physician Conrad Murray gave to Jackson “to help him sleep.” As if you want to dry your dishes with a hammer. Anyway.) So is a colonoscopy as bad as they say ? Not at all. It’s a walk in the park. SOURCES: Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a medial professional, what is the worst thing you've smelt coming from a patient?
Answer: When I read the question, I could not stop myself from asking my girlfriend’s professional opinion, right before dinner. Unfortunately she answered. “Oh, without the least shred of doubt, perianal abscesses during my time as a surgical trainee. The pus inside from the anaerobic bacteria beats everything. The worst cancer rot cannot beat a PA — not by a mile.” Perianal stands for peri-anal by the way: it means that the abscess is formed in the tissues surrounding the anus. I knew I should not consult Google images on this matter before dinner, but I had some time to spare, and I did it anyway. Big mistake. Never will I sleep again without the image of a large perianal abscess chasing me and catching up, ready to burst in my face, drowning me in anaerobic pus. Dinner was chicken roast with crispy potatoes and apple sauce, by the way. But I had stopped caring about food about twenty minutes earlier — When the world still made sense. SOURCES: the image is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Does it matter if a woman has a high body count?
Answer: I’m probably the guy you want to talk about, so let me answer it from my personal perspective. If we are talking about body count, we are actually talking about the infamous C. U. M. coefficient. Rarely a woman scores high on more than one of the three axes. Scoring high on all three spells “jezebel.” “C” stands for Collapse. If a man or woman has died under your spouse’s supervision in one way or the other, I guess we could say that we are off to a bad start. In my own case, there are indeed some patients who have died when my girlfriend was responsible in the end — be on the operation table, or afterwards. Maybe a dozen, I’m not sure. It’s an unhappy number, but it certainly counts. Next ! “U” stands for Urology. From the moment I started dating a urologist, many a man have asked me if it bothers me that my girlfriend professionally handles males genitals. Then the same question is always (always !) posed: “How many has she even seen and touched during her career ?” First of all, she has female patients as well. And no, it does not bother me — and yes, I know some men who would be bothered. (Thousands.) Next !! “M” stands for Meat. The meat score is a game changer for many guys (as many of the answers to this question clearly show). With how many men (and women, although this is a lesser issue), has your partner procreated with ? And alas, despite the fact that the C- and U-score in my case are already positive and very high, the M-coefficient does not spare me either. In the case of dr. Freya, we are talking about a 200+ coefficient (thank you very much). So in the end, my girlfriend’s C. U. M. coefficient is so excessive on all counts, that I should be deeply embarrassed according to many. But I’m not. Does it matter if a woman has a high body count ? To me it doesn’t, obviously. Never has for a second. A low body count seems to harm more marriages, if you ask me. (And you did.) SOURCES: Marilyn Monroe photographed by Milton Greene, the Hooker Sitting, Fox Studios, 1954.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Have you ever had a public wardrobe malfunction?
Answer: For a while, I had a relationship with the youngest daughter of my neighbors (her name was Ebba, and I suppose it still is), and she nip slipped all the time. It’s not that she did it intentionally, but she also did not do it un-intentionally. She simply created situations in which a nip slip could perfectly happen, and she would do nothing to prevent it as well. Shit happens, and a nip slip happens just as well. Sometimes people really noticed it, sometimes they did not. And she simply never cared. Years after the end of our relationship, my girlfriend and I saw her walking in the town where we live, with yet another baby. Her ever present anorexia obviously had tightened its grip on her body, and she looked lethargic and bored — The nip slip days were over. SOURCES: the photograph is mine.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Have you ever been taken advantage of in a club when you wore a mini skirt and no panties?
Answer: It was a sunny Tuesday afternoon. We had engaged in a urological debauchery involving five gentle men and one gall — sometimes one thing leads to another (don’t ask) — and were drinking coffee afterwards in a coffee shop nearby. Suddenly my girlfriend Freya ran to the restrooms without saying a word. When she was back, she said rather cryptically: “One of the hound dogs apparently did not wear a medical glove. So I had to remove my undies again because I was leaking down there. I need a beer.” The sneaky dog had certainly abused the open invitation for his own relief, but there was nothing we could do about it now. So I ordered a beer for her instead to wash away the taste. Sometimes urology sucks. SOURCES: image credit to StarTraks photo.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What assumption did your family doctor make that ticked you off?
Answer: A patient with a kidney stone called my girlfriend’s office and insisted on getting an appointment without delay. She suffered from severe abdominal pain, and could not hold it anymore. She had already seen a family practitioner, but he simply concluded that it was the kidney stone, and that she should take some Ibuprofen. But when she described her pain to my girlfriend and showed the location, Freya knew right away that this was definitely NOT the kidney stone. Then, the patient said something interesting: “It’s really painful, doctor, I even asked my dad to drive really slowly because of the pain.” My girlfriend immediately asked a surprising and very non-medical question: “Did it hurt more when the road was bumpy ?” It did. Bumps made the pain much more intensive. Subsequently my girlfriend applied pressure on a specific point on the right-hand side of the patient’s abdomen and then quickly released the pressure, and the patient’s reaction — she screamed — was exactly what Freya had expected. The problem was not urological. “You have acute appendicitis. You will need urgent surgery today.” The patient, reminiscent of her GP’s diagnosis, did not believe it at first and even refused surgery, but the pain was growing ever so worse, and she was getting a fever as well. So she agreed to be examined by a general surgeon in the hospital — just in case. Not much later, a double-check by the surgeon and an emergency ultrasound confirmed the diagnosis. And her appendix was removed on the same day. Due to the extreme sloppiness of her GP, the patient could have died from her condition if she would have believed him and chosen the Ibuprofen pill, but she asked for a second opinion instead. And was saved by the bumps. SOURCES: Annals of Surgery, vol. 197, No. 5 (1983), pp. 495–506.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How did you react when you discovered that your spouse was cheating?
Answer: In the final phone conversation I had with my ex-wife before she filed for divorce — that is to say, she finally admitted on the phone that she had been cheating all along, and that she had decided she wanted a divorce — she did not mention any detail. Not who. not why, not when. “Dear Thomas. When I was contemplating our marriage, I happened to meet someone, and one thing led another, and I developed feelings of love for him. So, you know, I want a divorce.” She did not even dare to tell me in my face — she waited till I was abroad for work, and then called me up, while she was taking stuff from our house. I was shocked. And in Germany. I asked her right away with whom she had been cheating on me. She immediately answered “that in her head, she had never cheated on me since she considered our relationship to be over before she had started her new relationship.” (She only forgot to tell me.) That is how cheaters always think, by the way: they are always innocent. After I repeated my question a number of times, telling her I had every right to know after all the things she had done, she said his name. (And she knew that he was the one I had suspected all along.) And when I asked her — blatantly — when they slept together for the first time, she again turned to silent modus because every new truth made her a worse person. “On my birthday. We first met in Bluesette.” Bluesette was the pub where we had met on our very first date. It was then that I started to realize that she was ruthless, that by the very act of meeting with this man in “our place,” she was erasing me from her past. She was creating new truths, and I had to be obliterated. And that was just the start. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIFer.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, what is the saddest thing you've been asked by a patient?
Answer: Sometimes patients do not ask the impossible, but something quite different which is not impossible at first, but becomes harder as the condition evolves. Sometimes they ask to keep things quiet — simply to save them from the stress their own sickness would endow on them. Sometimes they ask nothing because they cannot speak anymore. Sometimes they are dead. Sometimes. Sometimes they admit they smoked 3 packs of cigarettes per day for three decades, plus the additional amount of alcohol which would have killed most any of us in much more time, while still looking like a ball room dancer in the waiting room while everyone watches, only to reduce to a wreck when the consultation room door closes. Because they are in pain. That is the saddest thing besides the most aggressive conditions — The lies. SOURCES: Google images.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Have you ever been invited to dinner at someone's house and you were not served any food?
Answer: We knew them quite well, so when they invited us we were sure the evening would be a ball. And that was an understatement in all the many meanings of the word. The starters were really very good, and after the starters they proposed we go sit in their royal jacuzzi “and have entrees and desserts in the water.” We had no idea what they meant, but when our hosts completely undressed and jumped in the water, we were kind of startled by the food they had to offer. Eventually we ended up in the jacuzzi as well (they had bathing suits), but when our hostess served us new portions of champagne while showing off her bosomy character near my face, I felt my ex-girlfriend stiffening (and not in a good way). Our hostess only smiled, and sat down nicely beside me, while her husband was fetching a new bottle of champagne. My ex-girlfriend was even more shocked when she saw him running after the bottle, and then coming back, dancing like a dervish while completely standing still. Still, I felt her hand down there in the pool, so I thought she was easing up because these people were good people really, and because besides their exhibiting, they gave us enough free space to feel comfortable. The fact that my ex-girlfriend was much more assertive than usual was also a surplus. She was not like that at all. Never was. In the end, we dressed up again after too much champagne, and went back home. The jacuzzi had been a winner, and rarely had an unplanned enterprise ended so well for me — be it under water, with not enough food but certainly enough liquid. Our hostess waved us off with a generous smile. When I enthusiastically alluded to our secret encounter in the water, my girlfriend looked at me as if I was demented, and so I dropped the subject altogether because I knew this conversation was going nowhere. And I remained silent in the car for the rest of the ride. (She was a bosomy soul indeed.) SOURCES: Shunga Ukiyo-e woodblock print by Keisai Eisen (1790-1848), c. 1825.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the saddest picture you've ever seen?
Answer: She was one of our friends, and her baby had died in the womb at seven months. It was her first pregnancy, and the only picture of her daughter was taken right after birth, when the baby lay lifeless and pale in her arms, as if sculpted in cold marble like Michelangelo’s Pietà — the mother crying. (I’ve seen the picture, and it was absolutely devastating.) One day, her busy baby girl stopped kicking, and over the weekend the baby remained silent as well. She went to her OB/GYN as soon as she could, but she knew what he would say to her. Because she felt it so badly, as if she was bleeding from an invisible hole deep inside. And the news was ever so bleak. The baby had to be removed as soon as possible, since a stillborn at seven months is essentially a mass of dead flesh — and we all know what dead flesh does in a moist environment of 99°F, right ? In the days before labor was induced, our friend suffered from immense psychological trauma, because she did not feel inside what she was supposed to feel, and because she realized what she had become, and what she would always be, no matter how she would look at it in the future — A coffin for her own deceased daughter. SOURCES: the painting is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How long can a woman keep a fetus (dead or alive) in her body?
Answer: Not very long. Actually, it has to be removed as soon as possible, since a stillborn baby is essentially a a mass of dead flesh — and we know what dead flesh does in a moist environment of 99°F, right ? One of our friends experienced exactly that: one day, she felt that her baby girl stopped kicking, and over the weekend, the baby remained ever so silent. She knew something was wrong, and went to her OB/GYN as soon as she could. The message was harsh: her baby had died in the womb at seven months. It was her first pregnancy, and the only picture of her daughter was taken right after birth, where the baby lay lifeless and pale in her arms, as if sculptured in marble like Michelangelo’s Pietà. (I’ve seen the picture, and it was absolutely devastating.) [In the post Roe vs Wade era, some women — such as Deborah Dorbert (photo) — are forced to carry their non-viable baby to term, which is even worse. Deborah’s baby boy died in her arms immediately after birth, without kidneys.][1] In the days before labor was induced, our friend suffered from immense psychological trauma, because she did not feel inside what she was supposed to feel, and because she realized what she had become, and what she would always be, no matter how she would look at it in the future — A coffin of flesh for her own deceased daughter. SOURCES: the footnoted site. Painting by Stephen Early.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What cancer treatment is a scam?
Answer: This young African patient needed a radical prostatectomy, or radiotherapy and hormonal treatment, in a curable case of prostate cancer — but it could have been any cancer. He understood that both of the proposed therapies could possibly influence his libido, and could cause erectile dysfunction in the future. He was very worried about this, as in his family it would be considered as a major disgrace. Now I told this story a couple of times before, so I won’t go into much details, but in short: he went all Steve Jobs on himself under the influence of his older brother — For his doctor, it was one of the hardest things she ever experienced. The man basically committed suicide by listening to his brother. And that’s also what happened to Steve Jobs: he deeply believed in alternative therapies and theories, and even was convinced that a reality distortion field existed, in which something (anything) could become true if you believed in it fanatically enough.[1] As an alternative to classical medical therapies, we could also call his approach denial. Because once you are taking the real medicine, undergoing the real (and hard to endure) therapies, once you are starting to feel nauseous and your hair is falling out, once all this is happening to you in between ever so tiring hospital visits, there is no more room for denial. You are forced to look into the mirror and acknowledge what is really happening inside, instead of trying the fruit-cake diet for an easy way out. And once the final round of alternative denial is over, it is too late. The cancer has taken its course, and it never cared about your herbal scams, fasting panics and other bed time stories which actually made you very sleepy in the first place. And it’s too late to wake up. SOURCES: photo/Getty images.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I gave my son up for adoption and I want him back. His parents don't want him to stay in contact with me. Do I have the right to be in his life when he wants me to?
Answer: A boy called Aemon and his older sister entered yet another new school. Aemon was the new kid in my daughter’s class, and he had been given up by his mom for adoption. That is to say, Aemon and his sister had been taken away from her because she neglected them. His new parents were Foster parents, and really cared for him and his sister — and that was a first. His biological mom, who had a severe drug and alcohol problem, was jobless, mindless, clueless, lifeless and loveless, and more than once, Aemon and his sister had lived days without food in a cold, cold house. His mom simply didn’t care — she had her own problems, you know. But one day, mom was back. And she had decided all by herself that she had every right to take care of her biological children, and that she could be a good mom if she really tried. (My own take on it was that she targeted the child support to pay for her addictions. Anyway.) And somehow she took legal action, and quite easily succeeded in convincing a judge to have her biological children back — or from Aemon’s point of view: to be abducted by this horrible person who almost killed them more than once, and to be taken away from the only parents who had really loved him and his sister, and to be pulled away from his new friends, and their warmth. And so he was essentially removed from his own life — as an ever fading portrait that never had the chance to grow to its full glow — and thrown back into that cold, cold house. (I hope this answers your question.) SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's the weirdest thing a guest has done at your house?
Answer: We had spent most of the evening in a fine-dining restaurant, and our table guest was one of my best friends at the time. (Later, he would move to Washington D. C., and our friendship slowly shrunk into the usual biannual e-mails.) As usual, he was having the time of his life, and after dinner — after all the champagne, and white and red wines — he insisted on paying me (and himself) two double portions of Chartreuse, a strong green herbal liquor not suited for the faint of heart. On the way back home — which was merely a stopover, because we had planned to attend a party later in the evening — his enthusiasm decreased, and his speech became a tad too slurry. In the end, he was dead silent, and perhaps even a little pale. So once we were back home, his announcement that “he was a bit too t-t-tired to go to t-t-the party, and that he was h-h-heading straight to b-b-bed,” wasn’t such a big surprise. So we wished him goodnight, and went to the party some time later. The next morning, I went to our spare room to see if he was still asleep, and to my astonishment he wasn’t there. Vanished, like a fart in the wind. What was there, was an enormous amount of vomit, smeared on the walls and covering the bed sheets, and half of the carpet. And a letter — in which he deeply apologized for the mess — accompanied by a $100 bill. To this very day, I do not know what really happened in that room (and on the walls). And maybe that’s okay. SOURCES: the drawing is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a surgeon did you ever have a "Oh man this is just nasty!" moment during an operation?
Answer: A new patient had entered the hospital in excruciating pain, and needed an urgent physical examination. He was known to have prostate cancer, but his previous had urologist ignored his predicament altogether. Something was clearly going on though. And so when the general surgeon who examined him — at that point it was thought that his pain was unrelated to his prostate cancer — called my girlfriend in total amazement, saying that she really had to see this patient, she came over right away. And she was equally amazed. When she so much as touched the patient’s rectum, stinking pus oozed out of his body, and when they subsequently had a more detailed look inside, they discovered a new surprise which was even bigger than the first one: “A prostate tumor which filled his abdominal cavity — the biggest I’ve ever seen.” It was so big that it was about to protrude from the patient’s rectum, as if the tumor was trying to get away after it had virtually constricted his insides — revealing also at once why the patient couldn’t defecate anymore. The pain must have been mind-numbing, and it was incomprehensible what his former urologist had been thinking while putting this poor man on hold. His new urologist promised him one thing, though — The pain was almost over. SOURCES: medical image found through Google images.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a medical professional, what are some unusual objects you’ve removed (or seen removed) from patients’ bodies?
Answer: She was a very young woman who had been experiencing pain whenever peeing, and a cystoscopy had revealed a large polyp with calcification inside her urinary bladder. It had to be removed because her urologist thought the bloody thing was cancerous. Due to the size of the tumor and given the patient’s age, the operation was scheduled ASAP since the MDs might be dealing with a life-threatening situation if the cancer got too much elbow room to turn into metastasis. When the patient was opened up, a big surprise was waiting — possibly the biggest of every single person present in the OR. The mass was not a cancerous polyp, but an IUD — an intra-uterine contraceptive device — and this particular IUD had started its journey in the womb, had then migrated through both the uterine wall and bladder wall, and ended its travels in the bladder of the patient. And there, it had calcified into something which looked like a polyp. The patient’s body had refused to except the IUD, and had tried to remove the foreign object — which worked pretty well until it got stuck in her bladder, and was covered by calcium. (Sometimes similar things happen with piercings, which in some cases are completely spit out by someone’s body after a while without ever being opened.) And although the surgery had started as an alarming and confusing intervention, the diagnosis could not be better in the end — “Dear Vera, it wasn’t cancer at all. Just a traveling IUD !!” SOURCES: sculpture by Sarah Lucas.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why are there male gynecologists when many females are comfortable with a female doctor?
Answer: A Muslim nurse in my girlfriend’s hospital was forced by her boyfriend to stop as an OR nurse, because “she touched the genitals of other men (in the OR).” And he didn’t like it one bit. People tend to sexualize the medical profession because often patients have to undress for medical examinations and surgeries — and that’s exactly what the current question is all about — but people are also dead wrong. Since the very day I started a relationship with a urologist, hundreds of times — and I do mean literally hundreds of times — have I been asked: “Doesn’t it bother you that she touches the genitals of other men on a daily basis — that she must have seen thousands of them ?” (It doesn’t, and she touches female genitals too for that matter.) People seem to forget that these are the genitals of patients, and since these genitals have to be examined, it means that something is wrong with them somehow. Doctors see these genitals as medical objects — and that’s also how they touch them. In American hospital series, half of the patients look like models (“Please lower your pants, patient Clooney ?”), but in real life, examining a patient’s genitals often includes bad smells, pus, painful lesions, lumps every which way, scared or ashamed patients, and other very non-sexy stuff. Why are there male gynecologists when many females are comfortable with a female doctor ? Because they are medical professionals — and that should do. SOURCES: Vaginal examination in vertical position, J. P. Maygrier, 1825, Wellcome Collection. License: CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the most heartbreaking message/text you ever received?
Answer: It was the first weekend of September in 2022. The weather was splendid, and I was working on my laptop in the shadow of our old cedar tree. A text message came in, and a new shadow was cast. It was my friend Anne, who once had been a colleague for more than ten years, but whom I already knew well before she became a colleague. “Hi Thomas. I’m not sure you already heard, but your ex-wife died a couple of days ago. Thought you wanted to know.” Heartbreaking was not the word — my heart had been broken a long time ago when she filed for divorce after a dark period in which she had hidden her cheating through six months of lying — but that scar was gone. And the divide between us was way too deep afterwards for new scars. But it was shocking nonetheless. (My girlfriend became very silent when I told her the news. She had never known my ex-wife personally, but she did know that there were also two young kids with a trauma for life.) Only slightly more than two months ago I had seen my ex-wife for the last time — the very last time, as it now had become clear (and which was weird in itself). I was ordering coffee (and soda) in a coffee shop, and I noticed a woman standing next in line. She looked like a ghost, because every trace of life in this woman was gone. She was staring into nothingness — with glassy, dull and empty eyes — jaundiced, strange and unrecognizable. As if something was coming which was impossible to avert. And I know it was her. And only then I realized how bad her condition was, that the cancer had spread to her liver, and that she was succumbing to her destiny. (As an ex-partner, you only hear so much.) She had noticed me as well, but we did not speak. Ever again. SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: My sister's 10 year old son has autism really bad and nobody really likes him. The kid is a total nightmare. How do I politely exclude her from an upcoming family gathering?
Answer: We have a friend whose first child was born with a congenital condition which makes the boy almost blind, partly deaf, mentally so retarded that he will mentally never be older than two or three, autistic, and suffering from various other physical defects which make him a very sick child. And it annoys him. He is nine years old today, and he gets really angry when he wants something but does not succeed in telling his parents what he wants. Usually these things are very simple and related to food, and he can easily gets beyond a point of frustration in which he starts hitting his head (which always is in a protective helmet) against a table or a brick wall, and starts shouting incomprehensible words and broken sentences. His face, arms and hands are always covered with lesions, and his constant drooling can be pretty confronting at a dinner table. He is a baby in the very sick destructive body and mind of a nine-year-old, so somehow I think that I understand what you are talking about. Or you know what — maybe I don’t. Because we invite his parents all the time to parties, and we really enjoy their company, and the company of their sick baby boy, and his little sister. (Can you even try to imagine how much it would hurt these parents to stop inviting them because their boy is sick, and never had a chance ?) So yes, we let him trash our place, let him get angry when he wants chocolate, and let him twist and shout when he has an episode. And we also entertain him, show him things he doesn’t understand but really likes, and more. His parents have aged so very much due to the condition of their firstborn, which worries them day and night. We have seen his mother cry so many times, and we have seen his father totally clueless in life — as if he simply has no idea anymore how to proceed in life, not knowing what the next step is, if even very small. So why not let them smile — if even for a brief amount of time ? SOURCES: unbekannter Maler, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do Europeans sit directly on the toilet seat when using a public toilet/restroom? In the United States, a majority of public restrooms have toilet seat covers, whereas there seem to be none in Europe.
Answer: Toilet seat covers — as well as toilet paper, for that matter — are porous, meaning that they contain holes large enough for microscopic organisms to slip through.[1] So the protection is more in one’s head than anywhere else. And in general, unless a toilet seat is overly dirty (with particulate visible fecal matter on it), it is very rare that users would catch anything:[2] In fact, research shows that the average cell phone is coated with roughly ten times more bacteria than the average toilet seat. So cell phones are much worse. But it gets even more interesting … Many women hover over the toilet seat instead of sitting down, for the same reason some people use toilet seat covers — they think it is highly unhygienic to sit down and touch the seat. The problem is that your pelvic muscles need to be relaxed during peeing, or No. 2. And besides the fact that it is bad for pelvic muscles — which in time can contribute to pelvic organ prolapse issues — hovering often also leads to incomplete emptying of the bladder, and ultimately to an increased chance of bladder infections.[3] The standard question of my girlfriend (who is a urologist) to a female patient who suffers from recurring bladder infections is: “Do you hover over the toilet seat while peeing ?” (The answer is virtually always YES.) So please stop covering, and certainly stop hovering, my dear friends. You only make it worse. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. For the medical image: Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Who saved your life without even knowing it?
Answer: My mother-in-law is a retired radiologist, and only recently she told us a story about her biggest “mistake” as a doctor. One of her patients suffered from severe pain in one of his collarbones, and he needed a series of medical images be taken to see what was going on. When she was making the images, my mother-in-law slipped and accidentally made images of one of the patient’s lungs. Before deleting the images — which many radiologists unfortunately do with flawed images before even looking at them — she peeped at one of the images without thinking, and noticed a large dark mass in the lung. A lung tumor the size of a plum — this patient had been suffering from lung cancer without knowing it ! The tumor was operable, and the cancer hadn’t spread yet — and in the end, after surgery and chemo, the patient was declared to be in complete remission. If my mother-in-law hadn’t slipped, if she hadn’t taken the accidental images of his lung and taken a quick peek, the cancer would almost surely have been detected in a more advanced stage which would have destroyed his future. But she did. SOURCES: Volume Rendering of a contrast enhanced abdominal CT scan. Rendering done with a Carestream workstation. (Through Google images.)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Say I walk into a car dealership with the funds to pay in full. I walk up to a salesman, point to a brand new car on the showroom floor, and say: "I want that one." No test drive, no trade in. How long would it take before I'm driving it off the lot?
Answer: We did take a test drive — that much I must admit. But the car looked so awesome that we simply had to try it — if even for a minute. And it was very expensive — I must admit that much too. But driving it was unprecedented, as if we had become movie stars in a movie we had scripted ourselves. It was in the middle of the pandemic, and we rushed to my parents’ house which was relatively near, to show them the car. And bring them the coffee they so desperately needed. And then we drove back, and bought the car — just like that. The car people were deeply surprised by the fact that we could even afford this car. Because I look like a blond blue-eyed gipsy with ear-rings and the like, and my girlfriend looks like a Sami rein deer keeper without a license, but with a heart. And maybe they were right. (But they weren’t.) SOURCES: the image is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's wrong with today's generation?
Answer: I talked with a befriended psychiater the other day at a party of my girlfriend’s hospital, and she confirmed what I had been thinking all along. Parents do not accept their children anymore — that is to say, their children’s lack of capacities. [Some people fight a diagnosis, instead of begging for one.] Instead, they look for excuses. On the last exam I gave (in May), almost 15% of my students (45 students, that is to say) had what is called a “special status” — which means that they get extra time or other benefits, due to some kind of impairment. In almost all cases, it’s ADHD or autism spectrum disorder, and needless to say, this percentage doesn’t add up. In fact, almost all of them have been wrongly diagnosed. The parents — doctor shoppers — know how to find the general practitioners that are “easy” when it comes to diagnosing students with ADHD or autism, but as the befriended psychiatrist explained to me: they also pressure specialists into giving the wrong diagnosis, and it’s an ever growing pest. It’s a manifestation of a phenomenon that we see all the time in nowadays society: parents (and in extension their kids) use a medical diagnosis as an excuse for their children’s imperfections. Have you ever met a parent of the current generation who honestly said that their son Bob wasn’t very good with words, or that their daughter Jan had a hard time at school ? Of course not: Bob is dyslectic and Jan is autistic — special status, two times, thank you very much. (And George is not bad at Maths, he has dyscalculia !) I deeply understand that it is very hard for a parent to accept the shortcomings of their children — I really do. But the blatant denial of this reality has created a monster that does not dare to look in a mirror anymore — The excuse generation. SOURCES: image found through Google images.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are the most misunderstood things about medical doctors?
Answer: This was the end of 2023. The wife of a friend needed to have a hysterectomy. Her husband recommended his best friend — an OB/GYN, of all people — to perform the procedure, and remove her uterus. The next day she became very sick, and her doctors decided to open her up again. It turned out that her bladder had been severely ruptured by the OB/GYN/FRIEND. Instead of doing the right thing, they then called another friend — this time a general surgeon — to save the day. The OB/GYN had messed up so many times that he did not want to call the same doctor who had always saved him. But the general surgeon messed up. And the very same woman who the OB/GYN had “used” so many times, was called yet again. This time to reconstruct the bladder. Still, in the days after her reconstructive surgery, the Ukrainian patient’s condition quickly grew worse and in an episode of almost fatal blood poisoning, an emergency operation had to be scheduled to save her life. It turned out that besides butchering her bladder, the OB/GYN had also cut off one of the patient’s ureters as well. And the same urologist had to save the day once again. And that’s the very thing what is misunderstood about surgery — The doctor you thank afterwards is sometimes not the one who save your life. Especially when the doctor you thank is an OB/GYN. SOURCES: Google images (© Scott Bodell).

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What was your most physically painful experience?
Answer: A decade of pain. It started with a rectal prolapse of something lumpy, which did not hurt at all in the beginning. But after some time, the thing started to hurt. There was pain when it prolapsed during No. 2, there was pain pushing it back inside, but there was also pain when it hid inside my body. I have IBS (irritable bowel syndrome) so my bowel is extremely active, and its every move induced pangs as if someone stuck a knife in my behind. (Painful image.) Throughout the day — all the time — the putrid painful pangs controlled my everyday life until late at night, and often kept me awake during nights as well. I often had to run from meetings because I had to go the toilet and the pain became unbearable, I often almost fainted when the pangs became extreme, I often almost screamed. Toilet visits bathed in blood, and made me feel sick. All the time, more than ten times per day, for over a decade. One day, my (then new) girlfriend — who was an MD — urged me to have myself examined to see what could be done. And a colonoscopy betrayed the culprit: a large, black, necrotized polyp the size of a mushroom. A subsequent operation was planned to remove my pre-cancerous nightmare, and not much later it was gone. The surgeon (whom I personally knew) later said that he had never seen anything like it — “That thing must have caused excruciating pain.” When my rectum had properly healed, the pain was gone, and my life totally changed — I had simply forgotten how great a pain-free felt like. As if a thunderous black cloud had disappeared, and the sun was back. It felt like nothing less than a miracle. And it still does. SOURCES: “Alle de Ontleed- Genees- en Heelkundige werken” by Frederic Ruysch, published in 1744.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are the rarest/strangest/oddest/most bizarre cases in medical history?
Answer: The case of Jamie Lee Curtis probably is. Technically she was born like a man, but medically Curtis appears to have something called Testicular Feminization Syndrome (TFS) from birth:[1] This is precisely the effect in testicular feminization syndrome -- there are internal, undescended testes and no uterus, fallopian tubes, or ovaries, but externally the labia, vagina, and clitoris all develop. Typically, the labia and clitoris are indistinguishable from those of a normal (46, XX) female, but the vagina is shorter than usual or sometimes absent. Breast development is that of a normal woman, as are other sexual characteristics of body habitus, such as pelvic shape. Axillary (armpit) and pubic hair are markedly decreased or absent. In any case: Jamie is what Jamie was — You decide. SOURCES: the footnoted sites.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What was your craziest experience as a nurse in the ER?
Answer: When Mark arrived at the entrance of the ER on his bike, he suddenly collapsed. Simply fell on the floor and had a seizure. This happened on New Year’s Eve, by the way. FLASHBACK This is New Year’s Eve. Mark traveled to his parents’ for a typical New Year’s Eve weekend. Helping his mom making great food. Talking about all the things in his life she didn’t know yet. About his friends, lovers, about his future, about the things that bothered him and only she would care about. And about making the perfect mayo. (And his mom nagging about his dad. Fair deal.) When at some point his mom dropped a napkin on the floor, Mark was the first to bend down and pick it up. And when he did this, something snapped in his neck. (Later on, his mom would swear she had heard the snap.) In no time, a lump the size of a small balloon occurred on the side of his neck, but he had no pain, and felt okay. At least, that’s what he said. Several of his family members proposed (and even urged him) to drive him to a hospital, but he declined the offers, because Mark was a super nice guy, and he did not want to ruin their party. And as there was a hospital nearby, he jumped on his bike and rode to the hospital himself. When he arrived at the ER, he collapsed. FLASHFORWARD In the emergency room, the ER medical doctors discovered that Mark had Syphilis, and that he subsequently had developed an arteriovenous malformation (an abnormal tangle of blood vessels) in his neck. And so when Mark bent over in his mom’s kitchen to help her the best he could, some of the blood vessels snapped under pressure, and caused a heavy internal bleeding. But it didn’t hurt. And when he then jumped on his bike a few minutes later, he was actually bleeding to death and he simply had no clue. Not even when he fell near the entrance of the ER. All alone, on New Year’s Eve. SOURCES: Plate 6, Surgical anatomy of the axilla. Wellcome Collection. (© Public domain)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I found out I have cancer—I have not told my family. We can’t afford the treatment anyway. Should I just say nothing and let nature take its course?
Answer: My girlfriend once had a patient who had been diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer — metastasized to various distant organs. He was sentenced to die, and any form of therapy would only extend his life for a wee bit at best. So he decided — for different reasons than yourself — to refuse further surgery and chemo (and what have you), and he applied for euthanasia instead. But there was a catch. Any GP and oncologist he asked blatantly refused, because the man had obvious psychiatric issues which obstructed his capacity of decision-making. In the meanwhile the cancer did more and more damage, and he started to experience pains he never knew were even possible. Apparently, the pain peaks in metastasis are extraordinary — as if some patients almost literally end up in Dante’s purgatory. And this patient definitely had. Before I go on, I really think you should tell your family, and look for a financial solution if possible. (Or move to Europe, for that matter.) Anyways. Eventually, the cancer spread cutaneously — through his skin and then across the skin over his lower belly and side — and changed him into a bulbous mass of pain. That’s what happens when you let Nature takes its course — Cancer’s nature, that is. SOURCES: the painting is my own. The medical image (of a rare case cutaneous prostate cancer) was found through Google images.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the saddest thing a patient has said to their doctor?
Answer: A couple of days ago, an old woman was wheeled into the ER because she was suffering from a bad urology-related infection. My girlfriend was not on call, but on Monday she acquired more details about the patient in order to decide what would happen with the patient. It turns out she is paraplegic, blind and all alone — “I have no family, no friends, and I do not feel connected to the world anymore. Would surgery really help me at this stage ?” And she is right. Another operation would further deepen her medical predicament (which is already so very bad), and would further alienate her from her surroundings if she even survived. And that wouldn’t be fair. So it wouldn’t be okay to open her up again. She has suffered enough already. SOURCES: image AI-generated by Stable Diffusion on Prompt Hunt.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I am 45 years old. I have no children and have never been married. What is the point to being here?
Answer: My uncle was 40 when his father, whom he lived with, almost died from a bowel obstruction. Although my grandfather survived the emergency surgery and his one year stay in the hospital (a major part in intensive care), he never was the same again, and had to move to a nursing home. For my uncle, a new world opened — a world of freedom. He never married the girl he wanted to marry — she chose another man, and it broke his heart. And he never had children, but he had us — his nephews and nieces. And after his father (who was a tyrant) had moved out, he started to travel without the constant guilt that his father was all alone in the apartment. And he discovered the wonders of the world. My uncle is 75 now, and his health is giving him a rough time, but he still travels (although not that far). In the past years he met a new love in his life in the guise of orchids, every which way. And he systematically started searching rare species in the wild, photographing them in detail and musing about his discoveries in the many writings that he always e-mails us. There’s always a good reason to be here — even if you feel lonely — and lightning could strike in the most unexpected way, and even in the marvelous guise of a bowel obstruction. (Ask my uncle.) SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What was the final straw (incident) that put your elderly parent or grandparent, who still wants to age in place but now clearly can't, into a nursing home?
Answer: The mentor of my father was an old professor who lived with his wife in a large townhouse in an affluent neighborhood near the coast. Besides being a scientist, he was also a classically trained semi-professional cellist, and an avid consumer of literature and art books. But all that changed when his wife started to forget things. Sometimes he caught her sitting silently in the kitchen, staring at the wall as if she had been unplugged. The diagnosis was Alzheimer’s, and since they were both in their eighties, soon he was not able to take care of her anymore. Seeing her fading away broke his heart. Having her moved to a nursing home (in a separate dementia care unit) broke his heart even more. Playing upon their dad’s feelings, his children convinced him in a matter of months to move into the room of his wife in the nursing home, “so that he could be with her again.” As soon as he had moved, his townhouse, including the entire book collection and his old and extremely valuable instruments were sold in no time, and the money was divided. (“What would dad do with a cello in the nursing home ?”) So in his case the last straw was money — he was the final string which prevented his children to sell his belongings. And his wife’s Alzheimer was the perfect excuse. The nurses talked to him as if was suffering from dementia himself. He tried to explain them on a daily basis that his mind was in perfect shape, but they did not listen. He was one of “them” now. And they handled him as if he was a child. All the freedom he still had in his old house was gone, there were next-to-no intellectual challenges (as most cognitive exercises happened on the level of Alzheimer patients), he could not go the theater or to plays, nor play cello or listen to classical music (“that would only disturb the other patients”), and in the end he was essentially reduced to someone without intellectual capacity, forced to look at bad TV programs in between the plants. My dad was the only one who visited his old mentor, but the mental (and physical) decline of this proud man was extremely sad to see. He basically had given up on life. And he died soon after. On the outside, he had been a respectful man with a very rich intellectual life filled with books, music, creativity and love. On the inside — ditched by his own children of all people — he had become a lesser being — One of the plants. SOURCES: Zdzisław Beksiński (copyrights inherited by Muzeum Historyczne w Sanoku), CC BY-SA 3.0 <Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported>, via Wikimedia Commons.

Question: This psychic somehow knew I have a friend that died, and said he’s in the afterlife. I’m an atheist. How did she know I had a friend who died?
Answer: My ex mother-in-law earned some extra money on the side as a psychic. She truly believed she could talk with ghosts and the like, but what she actually always did was guessing. She never mentioned the wrong guesses to us — only the happy few correct guesses. As soon as you visit a psychic, he or she knows that you are vulnerable, that something happened in your life which makes you sad or makes you question certain elements in your existence. Very often, such doubts or questions involve people who are deceased. Psychics have a fixes set of general questions, and through your answers (and reactions on the questions) they sculpt a story which you identify as your own. Sometimes, they even have retrieved some extra information about you in advance through other clients, or common friends. You will buy the story because you are there in the first place, and they know this. You will never see the “noise” in their speculations — you will only remember the things that vaguely resemble what you want to hear. And you will change your experience in hindsight later on, to make it more remarkable and precise. And psychics know that too. It’s the very same game mentalists play, only the latter admit that they are con men. And it’s also the same game levitating Asian monks play — such as the one pictured above. The trick is very simple — he is sitting on a little chair which is attached to the pole his right hand is resting on — but he claims it is magic, as opposed to the magician who does the exact same thing and admits it is a magic trick. Those that want to believe that he is actually levitating, will believe it — whatever the magicians say. It’s also the same psychological trick a certain American felon applies to his followers: he creates new truths by telling the followers what they want to hear. And then magically the claims become really true for the followers. Easy peasy, Japanesey. SOURCES: image found through Snopes.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why do doctors ignore patients when they tell them what they think might be wrong with them?
Answer: Just the other day, my girlfriend told me a horrific story about a patient who was basically neglected by his former urologist. The 42-year-old patient had been diagnosed with testicle cancer and was nervously waiting for therapies to begin, but for some obscure reason his urologist did not make the time to come up with the appropriate medical answer, and brushed the patient off as soon as he frantically entered the consultation room yet again. And so the patient decided to ask for a second opinion in another hospital. When my girlfriend gave him a physical last Friday, she indeed found the tumor in his left testicle — it had considerably grown, and the testicle was bound to be removed. But after further inspection, she also felt a lump in the other testicle which had not been detected by the patient’s former urologist. And this testicle has to be removed too. Fortunately the patient already has children, but in any case some nontrivial permanent hormonal treatments are awaiting him to prevent him to become a female essentially, plus the psychological weight of a life without testicles (which might sound funny, but definitely is not). In my personal opinion, some doctors postpone therapies or even totally ignore the patients’ obvious problems for the sake of convenience, because other patients are more lucrative or because they have no idea how to help the patient without the help of other doctors (and then the ego sets in). So if you really think you are being rushed through your appointments by your MD — certainly if something serious is lying beneath — you may want to ask for a second opinion. It’s your life after all. SOURCES: Anatomy of the penis (Gray’s illustration).[1]
