Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do people with dementia ever know they have dementia?
Answer: Some time ago during the pandemic, we did a hike with my father-in-law and his girlfriend. At some point, he told me something that was entertaining him at the time, and about one minute after he had finished his story, he told me the exact same thing. We had noticed for a while that his memory was playing tricks on him, and lately it has become clear that something is going on with his short-term memory. He knows very well that he forgets many, many things — and has to write everything down on memo pads to “remember” — but currently, he is still in denial that he is suffering from dementia. Still, he agreed to have himself tested and examined, and that is basically going on as we speak. In that phase, once diagnosed, patients absolutely understand that they have a form of dementia, and it is deeply disturbing and painful to go through that phase. But there comes a point that it stops. Patients with dementia virtually always enter a stage in which they ironically forget that they have dementia — they simply become detached from a part of their consciousness (and conscience), and start living more on instinct than anything else. Their understanding of time fades away, and steadily their world becomes more and more blurry, as if they live in a constant mist. Sometimes they recognize things and people in the mist, but often the mist is too thick to see things clearly enough to know what they are seeing. So the answer is: yes, until they don’t. SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's the most unreasonable request you've received from your boss?
Answer: My boss came to my office, closed the door, and popped the question (no, I would not marry him). Before going into the question, you must know that in my faculty there was a tenured professor position for which I would apply, and my boss knew that I was made for the job. But what he also knew was that his best friend — and one-time lover — would also apply. So he came into my office, closed the door, and bluntly asked me not to apply for the job. I was so flabbergasted that I did not say a word. (This was really bad.) Eventually I answered that I would apply for the job, and that his question deeply disturbed me. He did not say another word and left. A couple of days later, I passed by the coffee room, and I heard my boss say “that this time, the quality of the candidate would not determine the winner.” And there was laughter — laughter from colleagues whom I considered my friends. Here was this autocrat stating that he would cheat the system, and they did not object. And indeed, when the whole thing was over — lectures given, interviews done, deliberations over — his candidate came out first. And there was laughter again in the coffee room. But not for long. Because one member of the committee filed an official complaint to the faculty, and described in much detail that the department chair — my boss — had tampered with most every stage of the evaluation process to elect his best friend as the new professor. The faculty discussed the issue, and agreed with the complaint. One year later — after a very dark period in my life, and after an investigation and some parts of the evaluation process redone from the start — I got the position. And my boss’s downfall as the greatest fraud in my faculty’s history began, and never stopped. There was no more laughter in the coffee room, by the way. But the cowards were known. SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the most unforgettable sentence that someone said to you?
Answer: We were lying in bed, and I was still awake although it was far past midnight. Till about two hours ago I had been a very happy man. But then something burst, and I knew it. We had had a fight over nothing in a public house, and I did not understand what had happened. Or rather: why it had happened. Summer had been great, and for the first time we had talked about having kids. But as soon as November set in, our sky had darkened more than ever. It was the middle of November now, and I could hear she was still awake. And then she said the words. “I don’t love you anymore — not like before.” She had never said anything even remotely resembling something like this, and that was exactly why the words were almost inescapable — as if once they had been spoken, there was no way of returning to our original state. We did not sleep again that night. I tried to talk about it, and she fended my every question off as if she was protecting a secret which she had determined not to tell me, well in advance our middle-of-November fight. I remember that the next morning, very early, we sat quiet in the car, both realizing that something had happened. That something had come between us which might never leave. The problem was that she knew what that something was, and I could only speculate. FLASHFORWARD Two-and-a-half years later. She gives birth to a boy with a silly name. I am not the father though. The something-in-between is the father, as I am an official divorcee now, still sometimes contemplating the anger that smolders within me. (If only she had told me the truth.) The words of that one November night are still there, echoing through our common past that has been splintered in bits and pieces by an avalanche of lies. But they do feel even colder than before — As if something has died. SOURCES: the painting is my own work.

Question: As a nurse or doctor, what is the most embarrassing or invasive procedure you have to do to a patient, and how do you help them get through it?
Answer: Most probably digital rectal examinations are top contenders. My girlfriend is a urologist and she performs them all the time. Needless to say, they are very important for tracing prostate cancer (hopefully in an early stage), but unfortunately some men dread them so much that they procrastinate — which in the context of cancer can be disastrous. Waiting for a year can mean the difference between life and death. Patients are often nervous because they know what is at stake on the one hand, while on the other hand they are afraid of the finger — almost more than of the possible cancer. But kindly explaining the patient what will happen next while lubing up, and telling them to relax and not tighten the anal sphincter, certainly helps the patient for what is to invade their privacy. Typical urologists are short men with small hands though — Not tall women with long fingers, like my girlfriend. SOURCES: Alamy through Google images.[1]

Question: As a doctor or nurse, what's the most abusive thing you've seen a visitor do to a patient? How did you handle it?
Answer: It was the patient’s wife. She did not allow her husband to speak, and insisted on his sperm being checked. She wanted to have a baby, and nothing seemed to happen. His semen sample did not contain a single detectable living sperm cell. He turned out to have a rare congenital condition in which patients are infertile from birth. And yet they had three children. None of them were his own, but he did not know this (until now). Instead of listening to the urologist and doing the Maths, the woman became rude and demanded a solution, and all the while her husband was sitting there, quietly, and trying to get his mind around what had just been said. The language barrier (they were Egyptian, and she mastered the local language better than he did) made it even harder. But the sad truth was that in Egypt (where all their children were born), she had found a way to get pregnant, and that was the thing he was trying to understand while she kept on harassing the doctor — as if it was the doctor’s fault that she would not get pregnant again, ever. Because this time, the husband knew. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIFER.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is something brutally honest that needs to be said?
Answer: I once skinned a dead fox on the very same day it had been killed by a big Wedge-tailed eagle. When we (one of my sisters was also present) opened its mouth, hundreds of maggots crawled out — apparently the tongue feeds many mouths. This one is about our final moments. And then a bit later. The five stages of decomposition are, in short: the still-fresh stage, early decomposition, advanced decomposition, skeletonization, and finally extreme decomposition. The second and third stage are the juiciest ones — here is a taste of advanced decomposition:[1] The advanced decomposition phase begins with the appearance of loose, sagging skin and the collapse of the abdominal cavity. The body also shows extensive maggot infestation. The minute you die, you basically become food for worms. (So much for classical burial.) Cremation is much cleaner, but also has its secrets. The biggest secret is a total surprise to most people. The family does not actually get the ashes of the deceased person, but rather something entirely different:[2] “Cremated remains are typically bone fragments and casket ash.” The crematorium people then put the bones and casket ashes that remain into a pulverizer, and reduce them to a more uniform powder-like consistency so that the family really believes that the container does contain the ashes of their beloved one. But it’s nothing less than marketing fraud — SOURCES: the footnoted sites.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I have a hard lump deep in my inner thigh that I just discovered, and when I push on it, it hurts. What could this be and how worried should I be? Is it a tumor?
Answer: At first it was a lump — not in her inner thigh but under an armpit. It did not worry her at all, but just to be sure she called her GP and made an appointment. The GP gave her a physical, and just to be sure, he scheduled some medical imaging and blood tests. (For him, the fact that the patient’s aunt had died young from breast cancer was kind of a red flag. Keep that in mind.) This is what a good GP should do — assess all possibilities. The results weren’t any good. Breast cancer, stage unknown. The lump was not a tumor, by the way, but a swollen lymph node. Because that’s where the cancer had traveled to, and that was not a good sign. Lymph nodes are hubs through which cancer can spread to other, more distant parts in the body. So further tests were needed to determine the stage, just to be sure. Those results weren’t any good either (and that is an understatement). The many black dots on the images were tumors, scattered across her spine, and the stage was known now. (This was a patient whom I used to know intimately, but I only heard about the details in an even later stage.) Less than 4 years later, she would succumb to her condition. The cancer had spread to the liver as well, and had obliterated her body and mind until nothing was left except for the final, empty gaze. That is not necessarily what will happen to you, of course. A lump usually is innocent, but as you understand now, it could also announce a far darker story. So you should go to your GP and have your case examined as soon as you can — Just to be sure. SOURCES: painting by Adida, through DeviantArt.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is one thing you caught your parents doing that you wish you had never seen?
Answer: We were in France (and I think I was about 12 at the time). My sisters and I were asleep in the room, and my parents came in after midnight — they’d had a couple of drinks with the other grown-ups after we had gone to our room. They probably had too much wine, and at some point my mom sat down in the wrong way on the toilet seat, and it broke. She fell on the ground, and she had a bad bruise as a consequence, but that was only a minor detail. Because then she started crying. My sisters did not hear a thing, but I was alarmed (especially by her falling in the bathroom at first), and I knew exactly why she was crying — why she had been crying so much in the last year. Her mother had died the year before, and the pain was just too much. On a Friday near the end of April, we had received a phone call, and although it was finally Summer, my mom did not react the way she usually reacted on Summer phone calls. Her mom had collapsed while trying to lift my grandfather back in bed after a fall. The aneurysm had burst, and my grandmother died one week later. (I wish she could read what I am writing now. Without the aneurysm. Or that fatal Friday.) So my mother was crying now, in a hotel bed, almost one year later. And all I could do was listen, and deeply recognize the tears. Because my grandmother had disappeared. (And I could not find her.) SOURCES: painting by Stephen Early.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How was it possible for the Nazis to burn 4,756 people per day at Auschwitz-Birkenau using 52 ovens, considering that no early 21st-century technology has ever achieved this? 🤔
Answer: I visited Auschwitz-Birkenau in 2012. My girlfriend was with me, and she was (very) pregnant of our daughter. The silence was almost painful. The sheer horror was even worse. It was almost unearthly to walk through the barracks in which so many pain had been experienced, and people — entire families with young children — were lured into showers, only to perish after the last lie. It was extremely hot that day, and that only added to our understanding. The suffering could almost be felt through the silence — as if the final cries had stayed behind to keep a promise. But the Maths added up. It was not hard to understand how meticulous planning could indeed lead to the death of millions — and these guys really had a plan. They must have been so blinded by their own dehumanization formalism — incited by a man who deeply loved animals, of all people — that carrying out the plans seemed nothing more than a well-prepared formality. And in the end, the Nazi guards and higher ranked officers went home and ate a nice late evening dinner meal with the missus and 5 children — a German gramophone playing all along. Daddy never explained what he had done that (and any other) day. (Invited 4,000 females and children to shower, with a smile. Cleaned them up afterwards. How he lived his children.) Dehumanization is what makes us kill much easier without needing to take responsibility for the evil that we do. (We see it in Gaza today.) The Nazis did exactly that: dehumanizing combined with meticulous planning. And they were really good at it — almost ingenious. So yeah, the numbers really add up — there’s no denying that, and it has all been extremely well documented up to the smallest detail. When we left Auschwitz-Birkenau, my girlfriend felt our daughter kicking once again. We looked at each other, and most probably we were thinking the same thing — Sometimes there is life after death. SOURCES: Google images.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, what are some mistakes you've seen common people make?
Answer: A woman enters the consultation room. She can hardly walk, as if something is stuck between her legs. She has a hard time explaining what is wrong, but it is certainly “down there.” The doctors asks her to undress, but she hesitates. In the end, she climbs over the invisible steeple only she is seeing, and undresses anyway. And what is revealed is nothing less than grotesque. Her uterus is hanging between her legs, and it is black. Eroded and necrotized. Only a bit smelly, but there must have been a time where the stench was worse. The doctor asks since when this has happened (and she is afraid for the answer). Again the woman hesitates, and has a hard time finding her words. “Three years.” The doctor does not know what to say. (Three years ? Three years of sitting on this thing. Of going to the bathroom with this thing. Of walking and talking with this thing. Of sleeping with this thing. And didn’t her husband say anything about this ? It’s almost absurd.) This patient will be helped though. Her uterus will be removed, and her problem will be solved. But some patients enter the consultation room with a much more serious problem. With pain, or with a lump. And they knew about it for more than half a year, or even longer. And the cancer turns out to have reached its final stage, and nothing can be done anymore. The patient will succumb, whatever will be done. Because she did the worst thing you can do in the medical context — She procrastinated. SOURCES: Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How do doctors tell you that you are dying?
Answer: Sometimes in the most brutal way. A befriended urologist was in the middle of surgery when his oncologist called. The urologist had been diagnosed with lung cancer only shortly before, and the oncologist was calling to share the results of the medical imaging which had been done to see in what stage the cancer was in. Instead of refusing or postponing the call, the urologist took it because he was so nervous about the outcome, and he simply could not wait any longer — this was basically a life-or-death call, and he knew it. The oncologist said: “Oh sorry man, but this is bad-bad-bad. It has spread to the bones and liver. You know what this means.” The urologist had to stop the operation because the world was turning and he was about to faint. Because the call had been taken, and his future had taken a turn. Because he knew what would happen to his body (and how bad it would hurt), because he knew there was a funeral a-coming, and because he would never know what would happen to his young children. And because he knew that they wouldn’t remember him. All of a sudden, the medical profession made no sense anymore from his side of the table. He was a full-time patient now. SOURCES: picture taken from Popular Mechanics.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What was Steve Jobs wrong about?
Answer: Steve Jobs was convinced of a self-created “reality distortion field” — a term apparently coined in Star Trek — in which he was able to bend the laws of science to his own will. The reality distortion field was a melange of his charismatic rhetorical style, an indomitable will, and an eagerness to bend any fact to fit the purpose at hand:[1] “Amazingly, the reality distortion field seemed to be effective even if you were acutely aware of it, although the effects would fade after Steve departed.” The problem was that Jobs really believed it — not just as a metaphor for developing new products, but as a concrete philosophy for handling life’s larger problems. He believed he could bend reality. So when Steve was hit by a rare case of pancreatic cancer in October 2003, his self-created reality distortion field would in essence take care of it. And instead of attacking the cancer head on through the most advanced medical therapies and technologies, he relied on his fruit-only diet, fasting episodes, bowel cleansing, herbal remedies and acupuncture.[2] The irony was that it was a perfectly treatable and curable case of pancreatic cancer called Islet cell tumor, and Steve gave it the window it needed to grow and spread — in his case to the liver. He died in tragic circumstances from his condition in October 2011, desperate, skeletal and broken. Steve Jobs might have been a marketing genius. But he was a medical fool. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. Photography by Norman Seeff.[3]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How awful was Steve Jobs as a person?
Answer: Steve Jobs was one of the most innovative marketeers in the second half of the 20th century — and I am not alluding to his Apple business alone. We see it all the time: people who are so uncannily successful that they start to believe — believe in their own über humanity, that is. They, and they alone are the very reason that billions of devices were produced and sold over the world in less than three decades, so they must be really special, right ? And Steve was one of these guys who honestly believed that he was one of those special people. Steve was convinced of a self-created “reality distortion field” (a term coined in Star Trek, and I’m really not kidding), in which he was able to bend the laws of science to his own will:[1] "A reality distortion field. In his presence, reality is malleable. He can convince anyone of practically anything. It wears off when he's not around, but it makes it hard to have realistic schedules. And there's a couple of other things you should know about working with Steve." So when Steve was hit by a rare case of perfectly fightable pancreatic cancer (called Islet cell tumor), he did the unthinkable. Instead of consulting professional medical doctors, he went into alternative medicine mode — the reality distortion field, remember ? And while trying to distort his pancreatic cancer into a happy thought and keeping up with his fruit-only diet (which, adding insult to injury, is extremely unhealthy)[2] — he gave his cancer extra elbow room and nine extra months to metastasize, and spread to his liver.[3] By then — when he was finally “ready” to turn to classical medicine — all was lost. He died on October 5, 2011, his last words, sadly, being:[4] “Oh wow. Oh wow. Oh wow.” Steve Jobs became convinced that he had turned divine through Apples — But he ended as fruit-cake instead. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. Photograph by Norman Seeff.

Question: As a doctor, what is your ‘how are you alive’ moment?
Answer: He came into the ER looking really good, in fact. Neatly dressed, 70+ with a lot of grey hair and a sympathetic smile (although much of the smiling had faded now). His wife was with him, and she looked only a little worried. Her husband had turned sick during the day, and he had reached a point where he hardly could stop vomiting. The abdominal pains had increased over time, and so they decided to pay a visit to the emergency room — you never know. His condition worsened so incredibly fast in the ER, that they there wasn’t any time left to wait for medical imaging and the like — this man had to be opened, ASAP. And so the general surgeon on call (who arrived within 20 minutes) and a trainee (who still was in the hospital) started the procedure. And when they had opened him up, they looked at each other and read each other’s minds without saying a thing. And then shrugged. An extreme case of bowel infarction — also known as “gangrenous bowel.” The man’s entire bowel was bluish-black (but mostly black), and had died due to a shortage of blood flow. The abdominal cavity was severely infected, and he was going into sepsis as they spoke. In some sense, it was a miracle that this poor man had walked into the hospital all by himself, looking healthy and in good spirits, accompanied by his poor wife who was currently eagerly waiting for her husband, whom she would never see again. Because apart from dying, he was actually dead when he entered the ER. SOURCES: the image is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why don't people like old people?
Answer: We once had a young chinchilla who unexpectedly died in its cage, and it really affected the behavior of the other chinchillas. They did not understand why the youngster wasn’t moving, and became scared in the end. Instinctively they felt that something was really wrong with the animal — it obviously was a chinchilla, but somehow it also wasn’t. They had encountered death for the first time, and it deeply disconcerted them. Before I removed the chinchilla, some of them had started biting and harassing the little corpse — including its own mom — but once was it was gone, all peace and quiet returned. Death was gone. And maybe that’s precisely why some people do not like old people. They instinctively know that old people represent images of what they will see themselves in the mirror one day, and they are in absolute denial about their own mortality. Every single “bad thing” about old people (which is basically every good thing about babies and toddlers) — little (and not so little) smells, slowness, lethargy, disease, dementia, a general change of thoughts because their world is getting smaller (and more dangerous), controversy and costs, and last but not least: diapers — does not only annoy these people, it also scares them shitless. (In that case, a diaper would be not so bad after all.) For such shitless people, getting older must be a very painful and shameful process of denial which will haunt them till the very end, but not for us — Those who do like old people. SOURCES: photograph/painting by Beksiński.

Question: What was your best moment as a doctor?
Answer: An 83-year-old man and his wife entered the consultation room. The woman explained that her husband often got up at night to pee — sometimes five or six times on a single night — and so she was wondering if his prostate needed a check-up. After an interview with the patient, a digital rectal check and further medical investigations (such as blood tests to determine his PSA levels), the old patient’s prostate appeared to be in an excellent state. The patient’s wife was really surprised, because he often even peed “with less-than-ten-minute intervals,” night and day. The urologist had thought about this a great deal, and so she decided to change tactics, and give it one last, but very different shot: “Mister Redding, can you tell me what day it is ?” The patient’s spouse did not understand and was utterly perplexed. Mister Redding answered: “Why, it is Monday doctor !” But actually it was Thursday. The urologist then took a piece of paper and a pencil and asked Mister Redding to draw a clock, put in all the numbers, and set the hands at ten after eleven. And he simply could not do it. The urologist’s eyes met the eyes of the patient’s wife, and read the question the old woman was trying to ask, not understanding what was happening all of a sudden. And so she answered. “Mrs. Redding, your husband does not have prostate cancer — which is good. But most probably he has been suffering from Alzheimer’s for a while.” Of course, this still had to be verified by a neurologist, but the case was almost crystal clear. And that’s why he had been peeing so chaotically — he simply constantly forgot that he had already peed. Mrs. Redding, first still perplexed, but then more relaxed, admitted that in hindsight this actually made a lot of sense, and it explained many small changes in his daily pattern which actually turned out to be symptoms now. And more than anything else, she appeared to be relieved. Because the doctor “had solved more than twenty questions at once.” (And it wasn’t cancer after all 🙂) SOURCES: Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Question: How strong is a chimpanzee compared to an average human and is it possible for a really strong human to beat a chimpanzee?
Answer: In some sense, chimpanzees are a lot like big cats, in that they do not control their urges, and hardly have the ability to feel real guilt. So if for some reason a fully grown male chimpanzee gets agitated for some reason, he might attack a human without ever thinking about the consequences. And chimpanzees are infamous for their ruthlessness in attacks. In the wild, chimp troops often rip chimpanzees of other troops to pieces, and start eating the victim while it is still alive. And chimpanzee troops are even known to have been fighting in wars which lasted for years.[1] As for their behavior and strength in combat compared to humans, we might ask Charla Nash what happened to her when Travis, the pet chimp of her best friend Sandra Herold, freaked out. One day Travis got mad, and tore off Charla’s face, eyes, hands and lips. She also suffered from severe brain tissue injuries, and her jaw had to be re-attached again through complex medical procedures.[2] After the attack, Nash looked as she had been drowned in acid for a while. (Chimps tends to go for the soft tissue and the face first, but they have enough raw power to rip off a human’s hands with their own hands, and attack at speeds which are completely out of reach for humans. There simply is no time to react.) While Travis was attacking Charla Nash, his owner tried to stop him by hitting him on the head with a shovel, and then she stabbed him three times with a butcher’s knife. He never hesitated for a second, and then ripped off Charla’s face. The thing is that Travis liked Charla, but he was distresses (and on Xanax), and suddenly — and without a provocation — decided to take it out on Charla. That is how chimps work: they act upon their urges, and are not bothered at all by their conscience, or by a form of guilt, whatever pain they cause. So in the end it’s pretty simple: every single adult chimpanzee can turn into a much stronger and even faster version of Ted Bundy in the blink of an eye. And just like Ted, you’ll never see it coming — No matter how strong you are. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. Question: What are your scariest experiences working in a mental hospital or asylum?
Answer: This patient was not in a mental hospital yet, but well on the way. She came in with an angry face, and her facial expression said that she wasn’t going to take no for an answer. And when she started her speech — which she had tried out in her head for ages — the patient declared that it had all started with the TOT — the introduction of TransObturator Tape to fight her urinary stress incontinence problem. Because it was then, after the procedure, that her equilibrium problems started. At this point, the urologist knew that her hunch had been right. And still, she kindly asked what precisely the connection was between the TOT and the patient’s equilibrium problems. “They attached the tape to my tailbone. And now it hurts.” The patient continued to explain that she had read that tailbone problems can lead to balance issues — “because tails are crucial for balance” — and so the TOT had compromised her equilibrium. The urologist tried to explain that TOT was never attached to a tailbone — and certainly not in the patient’s case, since she had done it herself — but the patient hardly listened. And then shouted that she definitely felt that it was attached to her tailbone, that she knew for sure that this is what happened, and that this was what was causing all her balance problems. The urologist then referred the patient to a staff member for a second opinion, because the patient demanded to see another urologist. After a brief consultation, the second urologist kindly said: “Ma’am, after thoroughly thinking about your case, and after consulting my colleague as well, I can only conclude that you indeed have a problem.” The woman’s attitude changed at once, and she even smiled because this urologist acknowledged what was going on, and he would help her with the tailbone thing. “This the wrong ward for you, ma’am — you do not have any urological issues. You need to see a psychiatrist, and rather sooner than later.” And for some reason, the patient did not so kindly agree. SOURCES: Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Question: What has been the most unusual family secret you’ve discovered after getting older?
Answer: It was well known that my paternal grandfather’s mother had worked for a while, as a maid, at the court of a famous European king. But what some family members also found out that as a single woman, she became pregnant from a man who was not in the picture. And weirdly enough, in a strongly religious Catholic society in which unmarried mothers were seen as sinners and shameful subjects who were often hidden in maternity homes or convents to save their family’s reputation, she was not fired at all. Instead, she even received extra help to make ends meet, and she was allowed to keep working in the palace after she had become a true unwed mother. So those family members (my dad’s oldest brother, his wife and their son) concluded that she had a special protected status because the king must have fathered the child who would later become my grandfather. And they keep persisting on their theory, and never fail to mention my uncle’s and cousin’s royal blood whenever they can. My side of the family rather takes this comical idea with a grain of salt, and we have never seen any resemblance between our family members — in particular my grandfather — and members of the royal family whatsoever. Except the Habsburg chin, of course. SOURCES: Google images.[1]

Question: Is it possible for someone in their 40s, 50s, or even 60s to look (and even feel) like they're in their 20s or 30s? If it is possible, how can it be done?
Answer: It is possible. Look at Susanna Hoffs — lead singer of The Bangles. She looks incredibly young for her age, and never had plastic surgery or used Botox.[1] She is 64 in the photograph on the left (and not much younger than 64 in the photograph on the right). How can it be done ? It can’t “be done.” Most of it is caused by good genes, and that’s the one thing which is beyond our control. What you can do is: A healthy minds can also help (depression tends to take itself out on our appearance), and there’s much to say about food and diet, but most of it is false. (And no, that gluten-free diet will not make you healthier, or better looking.) But in the end, even if you respect all these tips, your genes can ruin the party. Some time ago I went to a school reunion, and it was shocking to see how badly some people of my class had aged — the self-declared prom queen looked as if she could be my mother. And she really wasn’t. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. The image on the left was posted by Hoffs on X on her 64th birthday.[2] The other image was taken from IMDB.[3]

Question: Many people who suffered from cancer or rare diseases that are impossible to cure with modern medicine have been cured through praying to God. How do atheists explain that?
Answer: My girlfriend had (HAD) a patient who turned out to be suffering from stage one prostate cancer. He was a young, deeply religious man, and he needed a partial prostatectomy (partial removal of his prostate) to have a chance to be cured. Instead of taking the upshot pill, he decided to consult his brother, who was a self-declared (they always are) alternative herbal healer, and the brother mixed up some herbs and performed some prayers — he was a man of god, even more than his younger brother — and the religious herbal tea would heal his brother in no time. Only it didn’t. On the contrary, his brother’s problems increased, and that young man worried even more because somehow he knew that the religious herbal brother’s promises were not being validated. Somehow he knew his brother was bogus, because the facts were there. And everything hurt. And still he backed out a couple of times because each and every time his brother could convince him that THIS TIME the prayers and herbs would make a change. (They always do.) Only they didn’t. When the patient finally decided to ignore his brother and listen to his urologist, it was too late. The man — who wasn’t even thirty yet — was dying because his brother had dug his grave. And yet you write: “Many people who suffered from cancer or rare diseases that are impossible to cure with modern medicine have been cured through praying to God.” Then why has not a single one — again: NOT A SINGLE ONE — of these cases has been scientifically validated ? Thousands of these cases have been investigated, and not one has survived the investigation. My girlfriend once had a pastor as a patient (also with prostate cancer), and she could not stop herself from asking him why he simply did not pray instead of consulting classical medicine, and let his god to his thing. The pastor only smiled, and said: “Let’s not take that risk, shall we ?” SOURCES: The circulatory system: dissection of the abdomen showing the large intestine, with the arteries and veins indicated in red and blue. Question: Do ghosts really exist?
Answer: In some sense, evil spirits such as Wendigos do. A mythological creature originating from Algonquian folklore which possesses human beings, the Wendigo causes its victims to suffer from an insatiable hunger and the desire to murder humans and eat their flesh.[1] [A mythological Wendigo on the right. And a true Wendigo — or at least, a manifestation of the Wendigo — on the left.] The spooky and really intriguing part of the story is that Wendigos truly exist. Wendigo psychosis is an extreme case of cabin fever in which affected people start killing other people — often their loved ones or crew members — and then eat them.[2] One of the most famous examples is the case of Swift Runner, a Plains Cree trapper from Alberta. In the Winter of 1878, his family was starving and his eldest son died. Only twenty-five miles away from emergency food supplies (in a Hudson’s Bay Company post), he butchered his wife and five remaining children, and ate them. When he came back in Spring and walked into a nearby Catholic mission, the fact that his entire family was missing arouse enough suspicion for him to be investigate — and he confessed in the end what he had done. When he led authorities back to the crime scene, what they found was staggering:[3] There were bones everywhere, some broken in half and hollowed out. That could only mean one thing. Someone had snapped them open and sucked out the marrow. Their suspicions were confirmed when they found a pot full of human fat. He was hanged on December 20, 1879. The Wendigo was gone for now — But not for long. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. Question: What was the last thing you said to someone before they died?
Answer: I was waiting for my daughter in the little coffee house inside the gymnast hall, where she practiced gymnastics. It was a Wednesday. Usually my father-in-law took the shift, but now it was my turn again, and as usual I loved every minute of it. But this time it was different. At the counter, when ordering my coffee (and sparkling water, as always), I had noticed this woman who was obviously sick, but who also resembled something of my distant past. Something which had been good. Something which had turned bad. (She had also noticed me.) I remembered the clothes. I remembered the moves. But the eyes were different. Not more than sixty minutes were left, so I sat down and started to write down my thoughts related to a mathematical problems which had haunted me for almost ten years. The woman sat down on a stool behind my back, about 4 or 5 yards away. She had stopped haunted me a long time ago, but she looked like a ghost. While I was thinking, I realized that the breast cancer had spread. It explained her altogether beaten posture. As if indifference had taken over, and her soul was broken. This was someone who was waiting for something that was once a reality, but now was a promise. This was someone who was dying. Once or twice, I peeked behind me because I wanted to be sure I was not dreaming. But it really was her. The woman I once was married to. The woman who was now fading into the mists of something only she could see, and clearly very closely. (I remembered all too well that breast cancer ran in the family. The aunt who died too young. The faulted genes.) We never said a word. Two months later, I received a message from beyond the grave that said I was not invited to her funeral. She had hoped I would finally create the closure before she passed, of the void between us that was left behind when our marriage imploded into nothingness. But I simply couldn’t. SOURCES: Google images.[1]

Question: How likely are you to provide life-saving treatment in a crisis to a loved one?
Answer: When I was 14 years old, my parents and some friends had a picnic on Tuttle Creek campgrounds in Manhattan, Kansas, close near the lake. The friends had a 3-year-old daughter, and she and I got along really well. So we played while the parents were eating and drinking, and at some point, suddenly, she jumped into the lake. Although the lake wasn’t a sea, its vastness and the wind gave it some slack, and the toddler — facedown — drifted away on the current, and our parents were at least 10 minutes away on the other side of the lake. So I jumped into the lake, and rescued her as if her (and my own) life depended on it. Due to her eventual screaming (once her head came out of the water and she could breath again), our parents rushed into us as soon as they could — only to find me exhausted and very wet, and the toddler in a very happy shape, crying but still very happy. I was 14 at the time, and I am ready to answer your question now — Very likely. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIPHY.

Question: What was your life's biggest decision, and what was the outcome?
Answer: On a Saturday night more than fifteen years ago today, me and my then-girlfriend were about to cross the street, coming from our favorite pub and heading back home just two blocks away. She was already on the street when all of a sudden a truck driving way too fast approached her at a dazzling speed, and the driver had not seen her because it was very dark. Without thinking, I jumped on the street and pulled her back with all my might. The truck missed her by a hair, and did not even stop. She was so upset she started crying, because she knew she had been within an inch of her life. (Life is full of surprises.) Five years later, this time on a Sunday evening in a pub, she became very angry with me for no obvious reason, and it marked the beginning of the end (in hindsight). That very night she told me, in bed, that her love for me was fading. My world collapsed, although it was not yet deleted. And I did not understand what was going on. (Life and its surprises.) Half a year later, she left me for another man, and what happened between that fateful night and her leaving me was darker than the usual dark. And especially colder. One day, in between discussions without any rational meaning and tears, she blatantly told me that “she wished she never met me in the first place.” Our every embrace had sickened beyond cure. (I kept thinking about the night I saved her life. And what would have happened if I hadn’t jumped.) Life did not turn out as it had appeared to be written when we married. The wedding speech. The many dreams. The tears, again. (What a waste.) So life twisted and turned (and sometimes convulsed), and again some five years later I became a father, and a spouse, of a baby and a woman who had never existed in my previous life. They simply appeared, out of nothing. Still a couple of steps later on the distant comic ladder, my ex-wife died from cancer. She had mothered two children in a happy new life, and then she was obliterated in metastasis not long after the first signs had surfaced. Given her congenital faulted genes, she was destined to succumb in its embrace. But she found out too late. If I once regretted her leaving me, or every little behavior from my part which could have led to our divorce, I definitely do not regret it now. (That doesn’t mean I like it though.) If we had stayed together, she would have died in my arms as the mother of my children. And if I hadn’t jumped on the road to save her life, she would have died in my arms as well. But much more importantly to me: if she had not said those terrible words about her faded love, if she had not started to mistreat me, if she had not become the terrible person she became — if we had stayed an item — I would not have met my daughter, nor my girlfriend. I would never have lived in the circus I live in today, and the magic could never be. There never was and would be music in her notes. Which finally brings me to your question: “What was your life's biggest decision, and what was the outcome ?” I listened to the music with a lot of patience. And became enchanted by its notes. SOURCES: painting by Rhys Knight.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is something that people forget about other people?
Answer: Look at the man in the photograph. He is young, charismatic and good looking. His blue eyes are nothing less than mesmerizing — although sometimes his pupils dilate so extremely that his eyes look almost black, for no apparent reason. It makes him even more mysterious. This man loves women. Liz — the love of his love — can only attest to that. He was her best friend, her fiercest lover, most loving husband and best father of her young daughter. He was her everything, until he appeared to be something else too (in 1975–1976). He loves women so much that he had many girlfriends on the side, but Liz knew that she was always the only one — and maybe that was true. (He tried to call her that very last time. But her daughter would not put her through.) He also dearly loves his mom, his brothers and sisters, his dear friends and some more family. And they loved him right back (well, until they heard the news). His mom never stopped loving him, even when the news was out:[1] "Ted has been the best son in the world.” The best son in the world has a sinister side though — a side so dark that once it awakens, no woman is safe. It will seduce them, lure them, cuff them, engage with them, strangle them, cut them, bite them, engage with them again, and again, and again (even when they are cold), decapitate them, and then haunt them again. Ted Bundy, the story of a charming man. What is something that people forget about other people ? That looks and gut instinct can be promising at first — Until the pupils start dilating. SOURCES: Killer in the Archives.[2]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Have you ever done anything that was actually innocent but came off to others as creepy or inappropriate?
Answer: We made a walk in the woods with school friends and my family for my birthday. I had just reached the fine age of 10, and I was to explain them a thing or two about mushrooms (a hobby of mine). [Pope Clement VII died from death cap poisoning in 1534. Just days before his death he affirmed that Michelangelo should paint The Last Judgment above the altar in the Sistine Chapel. The death cap had spoken once again.][1] At some point, I found a death cap — arguably the most poisonous mushroom in the world — and I explained them just how poisonous it was. And then I took a big bite out of it. My parents (who knew it really was a death cap) froze, and two of my friends starting crying, while the others were flabbergasted by why I just did. Then I spit it out again, and resumed the guided tour as if nothing happened — but for some reason the atmosphere had changed. Some of my friends creeped out and had been convinced that I would die. My explaining them (in all smiles) that “the trick is not to swallow” did not fare well with my parents either. And that basically ended my Mushroom Magic career. SOURCES: the footnoted site, and for the image: Workshop of Bronzino, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What's the strangest case you've encountered as a doctor?
Answer: This is a case I wrote about before, but it is also one of the most striking cases I know of in this context. The patient entered the consultation room, and explained he had experienced trouble urinating and found blood in his urine. That’s how it started. It turned out that this young 28-year-old man had prostate cancer, and needed a radical prostatectomy, or radiotherapy and hormonal treatment, but still his chances were really good to be completely cured in a near future. Both of the proposed therapies could have an influence on his libido, and could also cause erectile dysfunction in his future life. As so many patients he was worried about this, and he explained that in his home tribe this would be seen as a major disgrace. So bad that people would mock him, and consider him a lesser man. So instead of starting with the proposed therapies, he consulted his brother instead. And the brother — who had no medical background whatsoever — would cure the cancer on his own, with herbal preparations. In the meanwhile, the man skipped medical appointments, and procrastinated beyond reason, and beyond his every chance. When he returned to the hospital, the cancer had metastasized to distant organs, and now his chances were almost nonexistent to be alive in five years’ time. That’s how it ended. SOURCES: K. D. Schroeder, CC BY-SA 3.0 <Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported>, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Did smoking kill Patrick Swayze? If not, what did?
Answer: It started with a burning feeling in his stomach on New Year’s Eve 2008. Later, in an interview with Barbara Walters, he stated:[1] “I tried to have champagne and it would be like pouring acid, you know, on an open wound, and then my indigestion issues got gigantic and constant. And then I started thinking, ‘I’m getting skinny.’” He then dropped about 20 pounds in a matter of weeks — a very bad sign. Something was definitely going on inside. Not much later, he was diagnosed with metastasized pancreatic cancer. Swayze decided for himself that he would not communicate his precise condition to the public: YES, he had pancreatic cancer; NO, it had not spread and he was fighting the invisible monster with all his (legendary) might. Near January 2009 though, he was finally ready to “admit” that the cancer had metastasized to his liver, but even then downplayed his condition (as the tumor was only “a tiny little mass”).[2] That was the infamous Barbara Walters interview. When asked if he thought his bad smoking habit — 60 cigarettes per day for more than three decades — had something to do with his cancer, Patrick said:[3] “Ooh, I don’t know … I will go so far as to say probably smoking had something to do with my pancreatic cancer.” And most probably he was right. The risk of getting pancreatic cancer doubles if you are a smoker, and about 25% of all pancreatic cancers are attributed to cigarette smoking.[4] Swayze never stopped smoking though because he knew he did not had much time left anyway, as he admitted in the Barbara Walters interview. He died eight months later. IMAGE CREDIT: Barcroft Media Ltd. SOURCES: the footnoted sites.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What’s an embarrassing pee experience you’ve had in the bathroom?
Answer: About ten years ago, I was sitting in a toilet cubicle at a large American airport. The restroom was full of men washing their hands, brushing their teeth and generally freshening up, and there was a lot of noise and commotion — but I did not mind. Yet. Then, I suddenly noticed my cubicle door opening, and this was an outward door. Apparently I had forgotten to lock it, and it opened spontaneously all by itself. At its farthest point, I was sitting half naked in my cubicle with the door wide open, and a dozen of men were looking in the mirror and freshening up, and not a single man turned around, or noticed a naked man in the mirror. I had stopped breathing altogether. Then the door started closing again, and when it had almost completely shut, I jumped up and locked it (and then sat down). I was safe again. And nobody had seen it. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIFER.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Have you ever met or known anybody who is inbred?
Answer: The parents of one of my cousins were first cousins themselves, and when browsing a bit deeper into his mother’s family history, one could see many similar marriages. Not exactly deeply inbred, but not ideal either. My cousin (his name is Kurt) has a history of moronic behavior, and I often wondered if that had something to do with it. He looked (and still looks) okay, but there is something vehemently wrong with and within this man. Even as a child, he scared the other kids, and nowadays he hates the world and everything in it. (One time, I spent a weekend at his parents’ house, and he basically suggested — as a “game” — to kill the house cat. His house cat, that is. He had already locked her up in a cupboard for a couple of days and his poor folks did not know about it. Anyways.) Closer to home, we had a barn owl who unfortunately was fathered by his brother — I noticed the eggs too late, and one had hatched and I could not kill the owlet because I even have a hard time killing a mosquito — and although the owlet was a beautiful bird, he also had a bad leg and he did not develop as he should have. Contrary to my cousin, he seemed to be a very kind being, but he did not possess the power to survive in a world where his parents — abysmal as they were — decided to stop caring for him because even they knew that he was wrong somehow. They kept laying eggs though. SOURCES: the image is mine.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How does one identify an inbred person?
Answer: Meet the Whitakers, America’s most famous inbred family. The isolated family lives in Odd, West Virginia and due to their secretive nature, not much is really known about them besides the fact that almost certainly their many mental and physical defects have been caused by extreme inbreeding:[1] A report by Discover Magazine found that inbred offspring suffer from reduced cognitive abilities and lung function and are at greater risk from diseases in general. It also found that inbred children are ‘at a high risk of rare recessive genetic disorders. And even if you do not know the Whitakers, you almost certainly heard of the “Habsburg jaw.” [Charles II of Spain (1661-1700).] In royal families such as the Habsburg family — which went entirely extinct in the 18th century due to its infamous inbreeding — many a weird physical characteristic was seen in its family members. In case of Charles II himself, according to contemporaries the Habsburg jaw was so pronounced — “That he swallowed his food without thoroughly chewing, leading to frequent stomach problems.”[2] Despite being married twice, Charles II produced no offspring — which probably was a good thing. After his death, just short of his fortieth birthday, a rudimentary autopsy was performed, with the following results:[3] “A very small heart, lungs corroded, intestines putrefactive and gangrenous, three large stones in the [!] kidney, a single testicle black as coal, and his head full of water.” A very small heart, corroded lungs, gangrenous insides, one kidney, a head full of water, and last but certainly not least — a Habsburg chin. (I hope this answers your question.) SOURCES: the footnoted sites, and for the portrait of Charles II: Juan Carreño de Miranda, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Has anyone ever been completely unaware of their medical condition until they received a checkup from a doctor? Have you or anyone you know personally experienced this?
Answer: This is not the first time I tell this story, but it is a striking case nonetheless because I was once married to her. And only when I saw her for the last time, I understood what was going on. And two months later, after it had happened, more details trickled in which completed the picture that I had only seen in pieces in the years preceding her demise. It all started with a lump in an armpit — nothing special. From what I have heard, her second life was good. Married the second time around, children, a house, a good job and what have you. The good life (nothing less). For some reason, the general practitioner wanted to be sure, so he scheduled further investigation — I guess we are speaking about a biopsy and/or medical imaging. The outcome was not good: breast cancer, stage unknown. And that was the dangerous part. (It always is.) Apparently, the lump indicated swollen lymph nodes, and this means that the cancer had already spread from its original location to nearby lymph glands. So further medical imaging was scheduled to set the stage, so to speak. The black dots on the images marked the places where tumors were growing near and in the spinal cord — it explained the back pains in hindsight. They also marked her future. She had entered the last stage — maybe she had even been it for years — and nothing could be done anymore. Just waiting for it to get worse, while trying to fight the pain. It got worse. When I saw her that last time — four years after the initial diagnosis — we sat back to back in a coffee house without saying a word, and I had seen a person who was almost literally fading from existence. Her eyes looked like empty shells. Her body looked broken. Her posture looked desperate. The horizons were gone. She was locked up in a horrible painting that was about to be finished, waiting in so much fear and ever increasing pain for the final touch which would erase her. Almost three months later, she succumbed. (It was August.) SOURCES: painting by Nikoleta Sekulovic.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is done in secret among nurses?
Answer: Doctor hunting. There is a universal phenomenon in hospitals in which some female nurses actively try to develop a relationship with one of the hospital doctors. The status of such nurses becomes higher when they are married to a doctor (in the end), and as silly as that sounds, it’s an undeniable truth. And as silly as it sounds again, doctor hunters who eventually find their prey, often (but not always) act very differently than “common” nurses — they have a powerful husband now, the husband earns a lot of money, and the latter basically lifts them into another part of society. And so they become arrogant. Some of these doctor hunters are very hard to work with — it is as if they cannot hide the fact that hubby is a medical doctor, which has to make them more important than “ordinary” nurses, right ? One of the big hospital secrets which is always hushed away on TV is that there is a well-defined hierarchy in hospitals, and in that hierarchy the doctors are the pilots and the nurses the flight attendants. Every single hospital employee knows this, by the way. On the other side of the spectrum, we have the nurse doers — doctors that actively search for (secret) relationships with nurses. Some of them utterly enjoy the experience (nurse after nurse after nurse), but never plan to end their marriage in favor of the nurse. The main entry stays at home. In my girlfriend’s hospital, a rather impressive number of (doctor hunter, nurse doer)-couples are known, and some of them are “secret” (because the doctor has a family back home), and others are not (because they got married in the end). In one instance, we witnessed to nurses — both doctor hunters — fight at a party because they found out that they both had a relationship with one and the same doctor (who had a wife and kids). They weren’t even mad at him — only mad at each other ! 🙄 It’s always interesting to see how twisted hospital shows misrepresent what really happens in a hospital, and what I find most striking is how totally different nurses are represented compared to real-life situations. In the end, the truth still is that a doctor title opens doors — And doctor hunters want the key. SOURCES: Plate 6, Surgical anatomy of the axilla. Wellcome Collection. (© Public domain)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How do surgeons deal with death in an operation room, especially when they know they made a mistake?
Answer: She did not die on the operating table, but she could have. She had a cancerous kidney tumor which had already spread to the lymph nodes — an exceptional condition for a 21-year-old — and so she underwent surgery to have both kidney and lymph nodes removed. Unfortunately she relapsed, and a new surgery was planned to remove new cancerous lymph nodes. The operation was a success, but it also revealed a darker cloud. This time the lymph nodes mass had been dangerously close to the vena cava, a large vein which carries blood to the heart from other parts of the body. This would be her last chance, because further growth would be inoperable. Not much later, the cancerous lymph node mass had expanded again, but had now intertwined with the vena cava. There was no way to remove the mass without destroying the vein, and so there was nothing else to do then wait for her sentence to be prepared and executed by the cancerous monster inside. The patient was a (very brave) young mom, and telling her what was happening and what could not be stopped anymore — and as a consequence that she would never see her baby girl grow up — felt as a medical failure altogether, and was one of the hardest talks the urologist had ever had. The feeling was excruciating. (The tears were warm.) SOURCES: Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Question: If an alcoholic only drinks after 5 PM, but does it every night, are they in physical alcohol withdrawal every single day until that first drink at 5 PM?
Answer: Not necessarily. I am an alcoholic myself and I never suffer from withdrawal symptoms. I am so-called “functional” (with a high end job), and have no problems at all with not drinking during the day — it simply would not work out for me. So I guess it depends on the person. I do not suffer from a constant craving, but don’t miss out a day off the wagon. Never been on it, by the way. (It’s way too fast.) SOURCES: the painting is my own.

Question: Who was the most neglected child you ever saw?
Answer: It might have been Amina. She was really doing good when she lived with her foster parents, but she knew that her biological mom was there somewhere. She always knew. (Dad had disappeared in the mists of abuse.) She was one of the best friends of my daughter, and we loved to have her foster parents over at our house — they cared for their children (even not biological theirs), they coped with the many prejudices that came with that, and they stood up against something invisible which should have never been there. One day, Amina was not at school. Her biological hard-drug-addicted mom had demanded that Amina live with her again, and her foster parents had lost the appeal to keep Amina protected against her mom. So she simply disappeared. Vanished, into thin air. And since I need to be sincere about this answer, I cannot say what happened to Amina under the guidance of her biological mom. But I can tell you that a true mom would never do that. Not that. SOURCES: drawing by Jocelyn Juste.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the most deceitful thing you have ever seen a business do to a customer?
Answer: A colleague of my girlfriend is a pulmonologist, and his business is largely based on cigarettes. His patients come and go with a plethora of symptoms, but the greatest common divisor is cancer. And that’s the exact disease he never mentions. He knows how much the C-word scares his patients — they are the people who have paid for his house in Spain, and his Porsche Cayenne (coughing) — so he ignores it. He calls it “(abnormal) cell division” and refers the patients through without mentioning the C-word even once. Not one patient has ever been angry with him in hindsight — they all blamed the oncologist (or urologist, or general surgeon) who said the truth. Not the doctor who knew all along — with the perfect business model. SOURCES: Dissection of the thorax and abdomen showing viscera and the aorta. Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: If a cop hits his light for me to pull over, but I don't pull over for about 10 miles because I want to get into a populated area (seen too many instances of cops abusing their powers, or fake cops), what would the cop do?
Answer: That is almost exactly what happened to my dad. He was driving on an inner state and my mother was fast asleep. Although he had noticed that a car had been driving behind him for more than 10 miles, absent-minded as he was (and probably thinking about some mathematical problem), he never was alarmed by the fact that it strongly resembled a police car. In any case, he eventually woke my mom and informed her that a police-like car had been following them for a while, and that it flashed blue lights. My mom told him to pull over right away, and the police man stepped out of his vehicle, and approached the car. My dad rolled down the window, and the police man said: “Mister, I have been following you for more than 10 miles, and you really need to drive FASTER ! This is an inner state, and you cannot drive it at a pace of 30 mph. That is simply dangerous ! So please drive FASTER. That was all — have a good day.” My parents were all shook up at first, but not much later my mom started laughing out loud and couldn’t stop for a long, long time. Being pulled over by a nice cop who orders you to drive faster — That must be a first 🙂 SOURCES: GIF found on GIPHY.

Question: Does Walmart know when you steal from self-checkout?
Answer: They actually do. [Walmart detective at work. Can you spot him ?] One TikTok user who went by the name of @thewalmartguy69 claimed to be an employee at Walmart, and uploaded a video to TikTok that showed how employees can catch customers red-handed if they try to steal at checkout.[1] Some Walmart employees carry a device that actually sees what self-checkout costumers are scanning, and so they can easily compare the list with the items in the customer’s baskets. (The @thewalmartguy69’s account was soon deleted, as was his TikTok video.) Apparently there are even private security guards snuffing around for bad people. In any case, I once noticed a woman trying on some clothes in a Walmart, and somewhat later I saw her walking out of the store in her brand new outfit. Nobody noticed a thing. Because she had found the only flaw in Walmart’s most secret and sophisticated theft detecting system — She scanned nothing at all. Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a teacher, what is the harshest truth a student has ever taught you?
Answer: I was teaching a freshman Calculus course for Biology Sciences, and accidentally overheard a heated discussion between some students in between classes. One of them was a Muslim student called Anand, and he ferociously objected to the theory of evolution (which was obviously very important in the Biology curriculum). One of the professors had explained the evolution of movement in seahorses — a complex and rather mysterious research domain which utilizes theoretical mechanics and differential geometry — and as soon as the word “evolution” had been mentioned, Anand rejected every word of it. Upon being asked by another student whether those really were Anand’s honest thoughts — even though he had seen abundant proof of the contrary — Anand clearly hesitated and said: “I am simply not allowed to think otherwise.” It revealed the shocking truth that this young man was fighting against choices he did not want to make, but somehow he had started to understand that what was (really) going on in Nature, was vastly different than what had been taught to him since childhood. Still, his hesitance showed that a seed had certainly been planted in the mind of this young man. And maybe, just maybe this one would germinate. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIPHY.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Pancreatic cancer is said to be the most insidious of all cancers. Is it possible to spot it early? How can one prevent it?
Answer: One of my dear friends died of pancreatic cancer only months into retirement. He had been experiencing back pains and wasn’t feeling very well either (but still), and was quickly and unfortunately diagnosed after some medical exams. The thing about pancreatic cancer is that when symptoms do surface, it is usually too late and the cancer has already spread. Early stage pancreatic cancer generically has no symptoms whatsoever, and that’s what makes it so sneaky.[1] And as late stage pancreatic cancer has a 5-year survival rate of a bleak 1 percent, what else remains to be said ? Doctors still performed a Whipple procedure on my friend — surgery to remove the head of the pancreas, the first part of the small intestine, the gallbladder and the bile duct — but even after the Whipple, it turned out that the cancer had spread even further, and that he was sentenced to a gruesome end. And he knew that. On several occasions, he pulled the plug on himself but somehow he was saved every single time (to his great sorrow and regret). So he turned into a skeleton in no time, and totally succumbed to the pancreatic torture in a matter of months. From the very early diagnosis, he knew he was a man swimming into a rising tidal wave. But he never saw it coming. (And neither did we.) SOURCES: Francisco Goya, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the farthest you’ve seen somebody reach to be offended by something?
Answer: There was a party at the house of my ex-girlfriend’s parents, and for some reason we started “the smoking discussion.” There was one woman (whom I barely knew), who was fairly aggressive from the start — she kept claiming that smoking was NOT bad for someone’s health — and who became really aggressive after I had suggested that parents who smoke at home damage their children’s health. “So you are saying I DON’T LOVE MY CHILDREN ?” (She was shouting in caps.) That was not what I had said, and I told her so. But she kept insisting — “So I DON’T LOVE MY CHILDREN — Is THAT what you are saying ?” (I wasn’t.) It turned out that she smoked at home at a daily basis, where she was raising her two young children. And since she truly loved her children, this was the indisputable proof that smoking was not bad for someone’s health. She would never hurt her children, right ? SOURCES: the photograph on the right features painter Frida Kahlo, Mexico City, 1954. (© Werner Bischof/Magnum Photos) The drawing is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: People who did everything right during their pregnancy that ended up having complications with their baby/birth, what happened?
Answer: A good friend of ours caught Cytomegalovirus (CMV) when she was pregnant. And still, she decided not to have an amniocentesis to check if the amniotic fluid (which surrounds and protects a baby during pregnancy) was infected. She felt really good, and the pregnancy was a dream. (“They did everything just right.”) Unfortunately, her baby caught the virus as well, and was almost completely deaf when he was born, and still is. He was also (and still is) too small, and he turned to be slightly mentally impaired. And as happens frequently in babies born with congenital CMV, he might be suffering from various other health issues when he grows older (such as severe immune system problems, and symptoms resembling infectious mononucleosis). The decision not have her amniotic fluid checked is especially painful if you know that mom is actually a medical doctor herself — she knew only too well that she took a big risk. And now her boy is scarred for life. SOURCES: the image on the right-hand side was created by Farid Ghanbari. For the left-hand side: dissection of the uterus in the latter stages of pregnancy, showing the foetus, placenta and umbilical cord. Colored line engraving by W.H. Lizars, ca. 1827.
